This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright <note>The legal right to exclusive publication and sale</note> to expire and the book to enter the public domain. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>Notes written in the margins of a book</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

### Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>The conversion of images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

# P r e f a c e

---

In our current age, given the interest that mystical theology and the research conducted regarding it excite in various ways, it cannot be seen as surprising that a translation of the Areopagite writings <note>The works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational figure in Christian mysticism</note> is appearing, and that explanations of these documents—so significant for mystical theology—are being attempted. Yet the translator must not evade the duty of facilitating the appreciation of his work by indicating the connection in which these writings seem to him to stand regarding the entire history of mystical theology in general. The concept of mysticism itself has been understood in such diverse ways, so often misinterpreted by opponents—where good and bad have been thrown together—and so boundlessly recommended and defended by friends, that it seems necessary to at least suggest something on this matter in this very place. —

The words mystery, mystical, mysticism, and <term>mystics</term><note>The systematic study or practice of mystical experiences</note> generally point toward something secret, not known to everyone, and conscious only to a few. However, linguistic usage has always applied these words particularly to religious knowledge, to insights and perspectives on the relationship of man to God and everything connected with this—

<summary>The author introduces his new translation of the Pseudo-Dionysian corpus, noting the contemporary interest in mysticism and the need to define the term against common misconceptions.</summary>
<keywords>mystical theology, Dionysius the Areopagite, definition of mysticism, religious knowledge, preface</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of the historical development of secret knowledge, moving from Greek antiquity to the early Christian era.</meta>

— IV —

applied in this context. The **Mysteries** <note>The "Mysteries" refers to ancient Greek religious rites, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, which were closed to the uninitiated.</note> of the Greeks taught the initiates the truths hidden under images and symbols regarding the one eternal God, the world, and the destiny of man. To every non-initiate, these teachings were a secret, and the initiates recognized one another by them as if by secret signs. Christianity itself emerged during the persecutions of the first centuries as a secret doctrine—not for its own confessors, but for the pagans and non-Christians in general who took no part in the new teaching. 

However, as the Christian faith became dominant in the fourth century, a separation soon appeared within the Christian communities themselves. The external Church grew on all sides; the acceptance of a creed <note>original: "Glaubensbekenntniß"</note> enabled admission into the great community. Given the multitude of confessors, it was inevitable that many confessed merely with their lips, while others attained only a general, superficial concept of it. Only a few penetrated into the spirit and sense of the Founder's teaching and experienced its healing effects through the transformation of their entire inner being. 

Such was the case among the laity; a similar situation, albeit with different modifications, occurred among the teachers. These teachers had to know the doctrine they presented and understand the content of the Scriptures on which it was based; the path by which they arrived at this understanding depended on their spiritual individuality. If **intellect** was predominant in them, they took from the biblical writings especially that which appealed to it and combined it into a whole; if it was **imagination** or **feeling**, they inclined toward that which suited this prevailing quality of their spirit.

<summary>The author describes how Christianity transitioned from a persecuted secret society to a dominant state religion, leading to a divide between superficial believers and those who truly grasped the inner spiritual essence of the faith.</summary>
<keywords>Greek Mysteries, early Christianity, religious persecution, fourth century, creed, spiritual transformation, intellect vs. feeling, biblical interpretation</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s explanation of how internal spiritual experience differs from external religious observance, specifically focusing on the psychological and spiritual "path of experience."</meta>

To make this clearer, we must go back a bit further. The purpose of Christian doctrine is to make all people blessed <note>The German term "selig" implies both eternal salvation and a state of profound spiritual happiness.</note> through virtue. (Matthew 19:16–17.) Anyone who, becoming acquainted with this purpose, prepares to achieve it, soon finds that his own strength is insufficient. This is because he must struggle against an overwhelming enemy outside of himself, but most especially within himself—with the earthly, the sensual, and the carnal. In the midst of his efforts, he falls and sins, and an inner voice tells him that punishment must follow every sin. He is compelled, for the sake of his sins, to look for comfort, and for the sake of his improvement, to look for assistance. 

Christian doctrine meets him with both. It offers him <term>reconciliation</term> <note>original: "Versöhnung"; the theological concept of being made at one with God after sin.</note> and it promises him the assistance of the Holy Spirit. He can accept both of these teachings in faith, without thinking or feeling anything further, peculiar, or secret about them; or, he can experience their power. In the latter case, the effects of these teachings become <term>facts</term> <note>original: "Fakta"; the author uses the Latin term to emphasize these as objective "inner realities."</note>—internal events of which he is certainly and truly convinced. For him, these possess just as much spiritual truth, reality, and certainty as outward sensory perceptions. 

From these two principal and fundamental doctrines, however, a new light spreads for him over all other subjects of the Christian faith. Every individual part of the dogma—regarding the nature of man and his destiny, as well as the essence of God—attains a certainty for him that only personal intuition <note>original: "Anschauen"; a direct, non-intellectual seeing or perceiving of truth.</note> and personal experience can provide.

This **path of experience** has always been called the purely **mystical** path, thereby distinguishing it from the other path, which [begins] with a general knowledge of faith...

<summary>The author defines the "mystical path" as an internal process where Christian doctrines like reconciliation and the Holy Spirit move from abstract beliefs to "inner facts" through personal experience. This transformation provides a spiritual certainty that matches the clarity of physical senses.</summary>

<keywords>mysticism, path of experience, inner facts, reconciliation, Holy Spirit, spiritual certainty, Christian doctrine, virtue, sin</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s discussion of two paths of religious understanding: the "path of experience" (internal) versus a purely intellectual or external approach. It specifically addresses the relationship between personal spiritual experience and the authority of the Bible.</meta>

...moral teachings and external moral conduct, contenting oneself without thinking of the complete transformation of one’s being and the renewal of the inner self.

But on that first path <note>The author refers to the path of "internal experience" mentioned on the previous page, warning that it can be misunderstood.</note>, one has often gone astray. In all Christian faith and action, the Holy Scripture is always the only certain foundation and the guiding rule of what is right. Many, however, have placed their own <term>illuminations</term> <note>original: "Erleuchtungen"; a term often used by mystical or pietist groups to describe direct insights from God.</note> and their inner revelations on par with or even above the Scripture, even though these should merely support the pronouncements of Scripture and sharpen our understanding of them. 

I do not mean by this those who demand a particular state of mind <note>original: "Stimmung"; suggests a spiritual attunement or mood necessary for reception.</note> for reading the Holy Scripture, and who claim that without it, much therein must remain incomprehensible to us. These people are, rather, completely right. Every piece of writing must be read in the spirit <note>The German "Geist" can mean both "spirit" and "intellect," suggesting a harmony between the reader's soul and the author's intent.</note> in which it was written; only through this does it become understandable. Certainly—though it hardly seems necessary to say—an understanding of the words in the broadest sense must come first; but to grasp the spirit of the writer, he must be read in his own spirit. 

The biblical writings, however, point everywhere to a state of our inner self that is clear only to one who has found himself within it, and for him alone does it receive the proper clarity and efficacy. After all, this is generally recognized in other subjects. One requires a poetic sense to understand the poet, a philosophical sense to understand the philosopher, an appreciation for the visual arts for works of art—indeed, for every single noble and great deed, a kindred sense of the heart. Why then, for the divine writings alone, should there not be a preparation for their insight, a harmonization of our spirit with that of the Holy Scripture?

<summary>The author argues that while the Bible is the ultimate authority, it can only be truly understood by someone whose inner spiritual state is attuned to the spirit of the biblical writers.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Scripture, inner revelation, spiritual attunement, biblical interpretation, illumination, moral transformation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that reading the Bible requires a specific spiritual disposition. ...writers take place; why should one be able to inconsistently grant to them what is rejected in others? For instance, the idea that a mere knowledge of the language is sufficient to grasp Homer <note>Homer is the legendary author of the ancient Greek epics, the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*.</note>, or that healthy eyes are enough to truly see what Phidias <note>Phidias (c. 480–430 BC) was a Greek sculptor and architect, widely considered one of the greatest of all Classical artists.</note> and van Eyck <note>Jan van Eyck (c. 1390–1441) was a foundational Flemish painter of the Northern Renaissance.</note> have achieved.

One cautionary note may be made: the sense for these aforementioned worldly and scientific subjects is only ever granted to a few. However, the capacity to grasp the **Word of God** in its own spirit lies within every human being without exception; it only requires awakening and cultivation. But the path of cultivation that leads to this is none other than the path of change and **inner renewal**.

Another wrong turn is that some, in their consciousness of inner illumination and purification, have presented these experiences themselves as the "one thing needful." In doing so, they have abolished and destroyed all distinctions of external confession <note>In this context, "confession" refers to specific Christian denominations or formal creeds.</note>. This is followed by a contempt for all scientific <note>The author uses "wissenschaftlich" (scientific/academic) to refer to rigorous, systematic theological study.</note> investigations into matters of faith. For those who went even further, it led finally to the rejection of all external **means of grace** <term>Gnadenmittel: traditional church practices like the sacraments and preaching, through which God's grace is believed to be transmitted</term>, the church, the office of the preacher, the sacraments, and public worship. 

As soon as they had once strayed from the secure path of Scripture, they altered the positive doctrines of Christianity according to their own inner feelings—such as the doctrine of Redemption—according to their own sense. Ultimately, the Christ of the Bible dissolved into a substanceless shadow, showing himself in each individual only as the "inner light" which illuminated them. This leads then to the doctrine of the **deification of man** <note>original: "Vergöttlichung"; the mystical concept that a human can become one with God or divine in nature through spiritual practice.</note> already in this life; this was the goal and final purpose of so many mystics. And once they have attained it, the ov—

VIII

...transition to the most dangerous of all propositions is easy: that for one who is perfect and in this way deified, all external actions and dealings are indifferent, and sin is no longer sin.

These propositions—which are assumed to be generally known from church history as having been presented by individual mystics—were already characterized as the main tenets of "unpure mysticism" by a writer from the beginning of the last century, who was one of the most vigorous defenders of **Lutheran Orthodoxy**. (Val. E. Löscher, *Noble Fruits of Devotion*. Leipzig 1741, 8.) <note>Valentin Ernst Löscher (1673–1749) was a prominent German theologian known for defending traditional Lutheranism against the perceived "excesses" of Pietism and mystical movements.</note>

We now return to the first teachers of Christianity. The **Fathers** of the first three centuries cannot be placed into any specific class regarding mysticism. However much they differed in talent, erudition, character, and writing style, a Christian spirit runs through them all, which holds to the central truths of Jesus's teachings, explains them to the best of their ability, and defends them against enemies. They are all pious; they wrote for pious purposes; the business of the writer was not yet a mere trade <note>The author suggests that early Christian writing was an act of sincere faith rather than a professional or commercial career.</note>. They had already begun to use foreign philosophies for their purposes, but with the firm conviction of the excellence of the simple Christian doctrine, as Clausen <note>Henrik Nicolai Clausen (1793–1877) was a Danish theologian; the author refers to his work on the early defenders of the faith.</note> has recently shown very well in his work on the **Apologists** <note>Apologists were early Christian writers who "apologized" for—meaning they defended and explained—the faith against the intellectual and legal attacks of the pagan Roman world.</note> before the time of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius I (reigned 379–395 AD) was the Roman Emperor who made Christianity the official state religion, marking a shift from a persecuted minority to a political power.</note>.

Fundamentally, they are all to be addressed as **pure mystics**. The subtleties of systems that emerged later, and the distinctions made with all the caution of the scholastic tradition <note>The "school" or scholastic tradition refers to the highly structured, academic theology of the Middle Ages and the post-Reformation era.</note>, are foreign to them; people have struggled in vain from all sides to find the "pure" doctrine of this or that specific church denomination within their writings. They did not know the barriers of the schools and wrote of their faith with as much refinement, sagacity, and ord- <meta>catchword: Ord-</meta>

<summary>The author warns against "unpure mysticism" that justifies sin, contrasting it with the "pure mysticism" of the early Church Fathers. He argues that these early writers possessed a unified Christian spirit that predates the rigid doctrinal divisions of later centuries.</summary>
<keywords>pure mysticism, Church Fathers, Lutheran Orthodoxy, Valentin Ernst Löscher, Apologists, Theodosius, church history, Henrik Nicolai Clausen</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page VIII regarding the evolution of Christian thought. It moves from the early "pious" simplicity of the first three centuries to the era of great theological disputes (the 4th to 6th centuries), where Greek philosophy and formal logic began to separate systematic theology from practical, mystical devotion.</meta>

IX

[order] and adornment as each of them had at their disposal. Things changed when the great controversies of faith began to disturb and confuse the Church. Once the subtleties of Neoplatonic philosophy—which had absorbed and fused all earlier systems within itself—were transplanted into the realm of Christian faith with its distinctions and dialectical forms <note>By "dialectical forms," the author refers to the use of logical argumentation and formal debate common in Greek philosophy.</note>, reason and speculation found themselves occupied in their own separate way.

The well-being of the individual, and especially of the teacher, now depended on the belief in or the confession of sharply defined concepts that had been formed about the Incomprehensible <note>The "Incomprehensible" refers to the nature of God, which the author suggests was being overly defined by human logic.</note>; the finest differences formed factions, and there arose an "us versus them." Above the noise of this formal dispute, practical effectiveness <note>The lived, active practice of Christian charity and piety.</note> withdrew into the silence. Most of the prominent teachers who emerged were more or less entangled in the great controversies of the fourth, fifth, and sixth centuries; their public appearances occurred mostly in the service of their faction.

From that point on, the practical theologians of the earlier period were separated from the dialectical ones, who gradually worked toward a closed system. The distinction between **mystics** and **systematic theologians**—or however else one wishes to label this contrast—gained a meaning; even if one must assume that no systematic theologian was, or could be, without that practical, purely mystical element. The synodal decrees <note>The formal rulings made by church councils (synods).</note> gradually prepared the material for a complete dogmatic system, especially as later councils used passages from the earlier Church Fathers as evidence and thereby increased the mass of this material. **Origen** had paved the way in his book *On First Principles* <note>original: "von den Prinzipien" (De Principiis). Written around 230 AD, this was one of the first attempts to present Christian doctrine as a coherent system.</note>, **Augustine** had provided great contributions, and most...

<summary>This page describes how early Christian unity fractured as Neoplatonic logic and formal "Glaubensstreitigkeiten" (faith controversies) turned theology into a battle of definitions, eventually separating mystical experience from systematic doctrine.</summary>
<keywords>Neoplatonism, systematic theology, Church Fathers, Origen, Augustine, dogmatics, religious controversy, 4th-6th centuries</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the historical progression from the previous discussion. While page IX ended by noting the emerging distinction between mystics and systematic theologians, page X describes how these two paths solidified. It highlights John of Damascus as the peak of the systematic approach and monasticism as the primary vessel for the mystical, practical "spirit" of Christianity.</meta>

X

Doctrines had gradually come to the forefront of research; so that in the work of **John of Damascus** <note>Johannes von Damaskus (c. 675–749) was a Syrian monk and scholar. He is often considered the last of the Greek Church Fathers and is famous for "The Fount of Knowledge," which organized Christian doctrine into a structured system.</note>, a complete and rich system for its time could take shape. Others followed, and the era of the **Scholastics** <note>The Scholastics were medieval thinkers who used formal logic and philosophy—largely rediscovered Greek texts—to explain and defend Christian teachings.</note> developed. But the practical theologians had not lagged behind. 

Individuals had reached similar results through the path of inner contemplation—though modified in a different way—as those established by the Church; and an institution created entirely for contemplation and the inner life, **monasticism**, arose and spread. Setting aside what the monastic order achieved as a faction and a mass in the great religious struggles of the time—which usually did not reflect well on its character in history—it nevertheless provided the opportunity, even if in the extreme, to preserve the practical spirit of **Christianity**. A great number of **mystics** emerged from it, a clear sign that it favored above all the meditative activity of contemplative souls.

However, these mystics—as we shall call them—did not feel driven toward a system. In the most diverse forms, they expressed the secrets that had become clear to them, which they had experienced, and for this purpose, they formed their own language, distinct from the language of the system. We find these utterances of theirs in letters, in poems; we encounter them as **exegesis** <term>Exegese: The critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially the Bible.</term>, where the effort to communicate the meaning they had recognized drove them to their threefold allegorical explanation <note>In the Middle Ages, scholars often interpreted the Bible on three or four levels: the literal, the allegorical (what to believe), the moral (how to act), and the spiritual (what to hope for).</note>. They strive to lift the veil that lies over the secrets of the spirit; they find symbols and speak symbolically; they wish to show and interpret the **Spirit of God**, which breathes through everything, everywhere and in every place. ->XI<-

Having now briefly outlined how the mystical perspective developed on the foundation of Holy Scripture and the individuality of particular Christians and teachers, we must also mention an external influence. This influence caused the scattered individual mystical elements to consolidate into a whole and emerge as such.

This influence is **Neoplatonic philosophy**. Here, we can only hint at how this philosophy—in the results of its **speculation** <note>In this context, "speculation" refers to deep, structured philosophical reasoning and abstract thought rather than mere guesswork.</note>—is entirely similar to Christian mysticism. Rising from basic concepts, it eventually reaches the idea of the "One Supreme Being" and makes union with this Being the ultimate goal of humanity. It shows how **ascetic prescriptions** <note>Strict rules for self-discipline and the avoidance of physical indulgence, intended to focus the soul on the divine.</note> pave the way for this union, and how its most respected teachers boasted of heavenly visions, spiritual ecstasies, and even the tangible vision of God. The mystics adopted these experiences, which had been obtained through different means, and the entire wealth of their results. They were kindred spirits who found nothing offensive in a mutual exchange of ideas. However, the primary and most significant bridge through which Neoplatonic philosophy merged with Christianity was the alleged **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>original: "Areopagite Dionysius." A 1st-century convert mentioned in the Bible, but the writings attributed to him (now called "Pseudo-Dionysius") actually date to the 5th century and famously blended Christian doctrine with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> in his surviving writings. We cannot yet concern ourselves with the controversy over when these books originated or who wrote them; it is sufficient for us to know that they appeared and became influential from the sixth century onward. From that point on, they were read, applied, translated, commented upon, and paraphrased as authentic writings of a holy disciple of the Apostles. For their impact alone is important and worthy of consideration for the history of mystical theology. Whether they were written earlier and forged for hierarchical-political or other purposes is irrelevant; history only brings them into its domain at the moment they enter the life of the Church and bear fruit, whether good or bad, that can be clearly traced. Their authority and widespread distribution are evidenced, aside from the **scholia** <term>Scholia: Explanatory notes or commentaries written in the margins of a manuscript.</term> of **Maximus** <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), a key theologian who helped popularize the Dionysian writings.</note> and the paraphrases of **Pachymeres** <note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310), a Byzantine scholar who wrote simplified versions of these dense mystical texts.</note>—

->XVII<-

Theology is the only flaw that must be held against this otherwise excellent writing. <note>The author likely refers to the work of Borger mentioned on the previous page, suggesting that while the historical analysis is sound, the theological bias is a drawback.</note>

For this history of mystical ideas in the Christian Church, the latest work by Schultheß <note>Johannes Schultheß (1763–1836), a Swiss Reformed theologian and educator.</note> has struck an excellent path. In the book which he titles: **The Documents of All Genuine Theosophy <term>Christology</term> <note>The branch of theology relating to the person, nature, and role of Jesus Christ.</note> and Mysticism, Collected Directly from the Sources and Arranged in a Self-Explanatory Order** (Zurich 1820, octavo), he first provides the concept of <term>Wisdom</term>; as it is presented in Job, the Proverbs of Solomon, the Book of Sirach, Baruch, and the Book of Wisdom, within the larger passages of these books that deal with the subject. He speaks of "pseudo-wisdom" and irreligious wisdom in general; of unlearned wisdom, and concludes with the Wisdom of the Gospel. From there, he transitions to "the Word" <note>original: "das Wort"; refers to the *Logos*.</note>, then arrives at "the Spirit," and similarly examines the various meanings of this word in the Old Testament. — He has, in doing so, certainly established the fundamental mystical concepts to which all others lead back, tracing them from their lowest to their highest meaning. If the initial source and foundation of every part of church history is to be sought in the New and Old Testaments, then we must recognize this work as an excellent contribution to the history of mysticism. And even if a researcher proceeding from a different point of view should arrive at different results in specific details, the path set out here—which is taken in all similar investigations—is entirely correct. —

->XVIII<-

What **Neander** <note>August Neander (1789–1850), a pivotal German theologian and church historian known as the "father of modern church history."</note> has accomplished in specific fields of church history regarding the history of mystical ideas is too well known to require extensive mention here. In his work on **Julian** <note>Neander’s *The Emperor Julian and His Age* (1812), which examined the life of the last pagan Roman emperor.</note>, he demonstrated the mystical atmosphere of that era and the entire first period of the Christian Church, particularly among the pagans, and proved its influence on the spread of Christianity. For the **Neoplatonists** themselves, a favorable era has arrived, and we look forward to a rich harvest in this field.

Already **Creuzer** <note>Georg Friedrich Creuzer (1771–1858), a German philologist known for his work on ancient mythology and Neoplatonism.</note> has given us the first parts of **Proclus**; we eagerly await the continuation, as well as the edition of **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of its last major systematizers.</note>, which is desired and expected from all sides. To this, Kopp’s edition of the largely unpublished **Damascius** <note>Damascius (c. 458–538 AD) was the last head of the School of Athens.</note> will be added, shedding clearer light on the ideas of these philosophers by tracing them back to the first **Ionian philosophers** <note>The earliest Greek thinkers from the 6th century BCE, such as Thales and Anaximander, who lived in Ionia.</note>. All these works are closely related to the history of mystical ideas, because the authors being edited became co-sources of Christian **mysticism**, and the latter cannot be understood without an exact knowledge of those sources. A new treatise prepares us for this knowledge, which we currently only know from the *Göttingen Scholarly Reports* <note>original: "Götting. Anz." (Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen)</note>, issues 166 and 167, 1821: *A Review of Alexandrian and Neoplatonic Philosophers* <note>original Latin: "Philosophorum Alexandrinorum et neoplatonicorum recensio"</note>. By carrying out a more precise distinction between the different eras of **Alexandrian** and **Neoplatonic** philosophy and separating Jewish, Christian, and Plotinian-Alexandrian philosophers, the author brings a particular clarity to this entire part of philosophical history; the benefit of this for the treatment of mystical history is self-evident.

Alongside so many significant works and contributions to the history of mystical theology, the present work might also be considered a small supplement without further pretensions. Its purpose is to present the mystical writings attributed to **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a biblical figure from Acts 17:34. This author is clarifying that he is translating the influential mystical texts that were famously, though falsely, attributed to him.</note> purely and in their entirety. It therefore provides a complete translation of these writings and includes separate essays that contribute to their clarification and evaluation. It particularly addresses the controversy regarding the age of these writings

->XXII<-

...could therefore not be avoided, because **Kestner's** <note>August Kestner (1777–1853), a German diplomat and theologian who argued for the early Christian origins of the Dionysian writings.</note> new hypothesis seemed to have rendered the older arguments unusable. It seemed best to provide a concise but complete excerpt of the treatise by **Dalläus** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Huguenot scholar who famously argued against the authenticity of the works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, which presents these arguments in their full sharpness, and to add what was omitted from the relevant works. The relationship to the **Neoplatonists** <note>A school of philosophy founded by Plotinus in the 3rd century AD, which heavily influenced early Christian thought.</note> had to be presented in its main outlines, the reasons for the peculiar delivery and style of these works demonstrated, his **exegesis** <term>exegesis: the critical explanation or interpretation of a religious text.</term> illuminated, and the entire result for **mystical theology** <note>A branch of theology focusing on experiences of the divine that transcend ordinary human understanding.</note> brought into a clear overview.

Such a treatment seemed required for the writer who has been the primary source for all subsequent mystics. A precise acquaintance with him contributes most to the understanding of those who used him and who refined, spread, and embellished his ideas. Regardless of how one might imagine a history of **speculative mystical theology**, these writings will always have to be placed at its head, because in them alone are united all the elements from which the earlier, more speculative **mysticism** was formed, and which the later mysticism found and used as the foundation for its larger and more extensive structures.

# Daillé <note>The author refers to Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Protestant theologian. He was a pioneer of "higher criticism," famously proving that the works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite were not written by a 1st-century contemporary of the Apostles but were composed centuries later.</note>

### on

## the Era of the Author of the Areopagite Writings. <note>The "Areopagite writings" are a collection of mystical and theological treatises originally claimed to be the work of Dionysius, a member of the Athenian judicial council (the Areopagus) converted by the Apostle Paul. Modern scholars now refer to this unknown author as "Pseudo-Dionysius."</note>

<sig>1 *</sig>

# I.

Dionysius the Areopagite was converted to Christianity by Paul and was appointed as the first bishop of the Athenian community. This is the only fact known about him through credible witnesses. Legend, however, has much more to tell of him. The Church of Paris formerly claimed that he was its founder, even though records show that it was actually established under Decius <note>Trajan Decius, Roman Emperor from 249 to 251 AD, known for his systematic persecution of Christians.</note> by a different Dionysius. The falsehood of this claim has been sufficiently demonstrated in dedicated treatises by Jacob Sirmond <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651), a French Jesuit scholar and historian.</note> and Johann Launoi <note>Jean de Launoy (1603–1678), a French theologian nicknamed "The Destroyer of Saints" for his critical historical investigations.</note>. 

Another error was occasioned by an impostor who forged several books under the name of this Dionysius the Areopagite, giving rise to a great dispute between two parties over their authenticity. The books themselves are titled as follows: the first, *The Celestial Hierarchy*; the second, *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. These are followed by a long treatise *On the Divine Names*, a short one *On Mystical Theology*, and ten letters. The same spirit that pervades all these writings and their uniform style sufficiently identifies them as the work of one and the same author; in some passages of his writings, the author even states this himself. Aside from these works, however, the author mentions several others within the surviving texts of which no trace has yet been found, and which therefore seem to have been entirely lost. Among these lost works, he names *Divine Hymns*, a *Symbolic Theology*, a treatise *On Intelligible and Sensible Things*, *Theological Outlines* <note>original: "theologische Hypotyposen." From the Greek *hypotyposis*, meaning a sketch, draft, or model.</note>, and a treatise *On the Just and Divine Judgment*.

<summary>This page introduces the historical Dionysius the Areopagite and distinguishes him from the legendary founder of the Church of Paris and the anonymous author of the famous Neoplatonic "Areopagite" forgeries.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul the Apostle, Church of Paris, Jacob Sirmond, Johann Launoi, Pseudo-Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, Mystical Theology, textual forgery</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Areopagite" writings. While the previous page introduced the physical works and the suspicion of forgery, this page focuses on the "argument from silence"—the fact that no early church authorities mention these supposedly foundational texts for three hundred years.</meta>

One would think that the famous and celebrated name of the author, the immensely important content of these writings—which concern themselves with the highest matters of faith—and the individuals with whom he claims to correspond in his letters, would all have made these writings not only known, but highly famous and sought after, if they had ever existed. Added to this is the sheer volume and scale of the writings themselves, in which no contemporary writer comes even close to him, and the familiarity with Greek literature and philosophy, of which only faint traces can be found in those other early authors. Yet, in the first three centuries—even though so many Christian writers from that era have survived—there is not a single mention of these supposedly Areopagite writings in any of them, much less a fragment or a citation of them; and yet these same writers very frequently cite other works by the disciples of the Apostles, such as the Letter of Clement of Rome <note>Bishop of Rome at the end of the 1st century; his letter to the Corinthians is one of the oldest surviving Christian documents outside the New Testament.</note> to the Corinthians.

## II.

This silence might be explainable if we did not find, in the writers of the first centuries, occasions and even urgent reasons to mention these writings. One would think that writers who cite the genuine Dionysius, or those who wrote about the passage where his history appears (Acts 17:34) <note>original: "Apoſtelgeſch. 17, 34." This Bible verse records Dionysius's conversion in Athens.</note>, or those who wrote against the same heresies that the "false Dionysius" <note>Often called "Pseudo-Dionysius" by modern scholars.</note> opposes in his works, would necessarily have cited the words of the famous disciple of the Apostles for the sake of illustration or confirmation.

Aristides, however, says in his *Apology* <note>Aristides of Athens, a 2nd-century philosopher and Christian apologist.</note> merely of him that he was a man wonderful in faith and wisdom, Bishop of Athens, who [made] a clear confession

Dionysius of Corinth <note>A bishop of Corinth who lived in the late 2nd century AD.</note> had merely said of him that he had been converted by Paul and was the first bishop of the Athenian church.

Both intended to exalt and praise the church by mentioning Dionysius; yet they say nothing of his writings. This is particularly striking in the case of Aristides, who addressed his *Apology* to the scientifically-educated Hadrian <note>Roman Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD), known for his intellectual pursuits; Aristides was one of the earliest Christian defenders of the faith.</note>, and would therefore have had ample reason and occasion to speak of the excellent writings of the Areopagite.

Neither Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> nor Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his eloquent preaching.</note> mention the slightest thing about the works of the Areopagite converted by Paul in their treatises on Acts 17:34 <note>original: "Apoſtelgeſch. 17, 34." This verse mentions Dionysius joining Paul after the sermon on the Areopagus.</note>.

Irenaeus <note>Bishop of Lyon in the late 2nd century and a primary hunter of heresies.</note>, in order to prove the church's faith in one God and Creator of the world—the Father of Christ—as the teaching of the Apostles against the heretics (who assumed multiple gods or "Aeons" <note>In Gnostic belief, Aeons are various levels of divine beings that emanate from the supreme God.</note>), appeals to the uninterrupted tradition of the communities founded by the Apostles. For this purpose, he cites the letter of Clement to the Corinthians and that of Polycarp <note>Bishop of Smyrna and a direct disciple of the Apostle John.</note> to the Philippians as evidence. Why does he not use the passages from the Areopagite’s *The Celestial Hierarchy* <note>original: "de coelesti Hier."</note> 2, 3; *On the Divine Names* <note>original: "de divin. Nomin."</note> 11, 6; 12, 3; 13, 3–4; 28, 29, 30, and 4, 18 etc.? He was, after all, a student of Polycarp, who—according to the letter from Dionysius addressed to him—was his intimate friend. Therefore, Irenaeus did not know these Areopagite works; and they were thus not in existence; for had they existed, it would have been quite impossible that Irenaeus did not know them. Likewise, Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note>, in his book against the Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a prominent Gnostic teacher in the 2nd century.</note>, lists all the Catholic writers who had written against the fantasies of the Gnostics

And why did Irenaeus <note>Bishop of Lyon (c. 130–202 AD) and a key defender of orthodoxy against Gnosticism.</note> not cite the striking passage from the fourth Areopagite letter against Saturninus <note>An early Gnostic teacher who claimed that Christ only appeared to be human (Docetism).</note>: "Christ, who was man according to his entire essence" <note>original: "Christus, als der nach seiner ganzen Wesenheit Mensch war."</note>? The same applies to the long dispute over the readmission into the Church of those who had fallen <note>Often referred to as the *Lapsi*, these were Christians who renounced their faith or committed grave sins under Roman persecution and then sought to return to the church.</note> after baptism. The letter from Dionysius to Demophilus explains this subject so clearly and distinctly that a mere reference to it would have sufficed to end all dispute. Must these Areopagite writings not have been completely unknown at that time, if they were not used in such heated controversies?

The same observation presents itself regarding the heresy of Artemon <note>A 3rd-century teacher who taught "Psilanthropism," the belief that Jesus was a mere man and not divine.</note>, according to which Jesus was a mere human and did not exist before his birth by Mary. In opposition, the defender cites the authority of Holy Scripture and the Christian writers who lived before Victor <note>Likely Pope Victor I (reigned c. 189–199 AD), who was involved in major early theological disputes.</note>, but mentions nothing of Dionysius.

Similarly, *Tertullian* <note>An influential early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note>, in his writing against *Praxeas* <note>A teacher who promoted "Monarchianism," the belief that God is only one person, effectively blurring the distinction between Father and Son.</note>—who conflated the Father and the Son—fails to cite the key passage from *On the Divine Names* <note>original: "de Diuin. Nomin. II. §. 5."</note> (Book 2, Section 5): "The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father."

How could *Papias* <note>An early 2nd-century Bishop of Hierapolis and an important figure in the transmission of oral traditions about Jesus.</note>—who, according to *Eusebius's Church History* <note>original: "Eusebius Kirchengeschichte III."</note> (Book 3, last chapter), was the originator of Millenarianism <term>Chiliasmus: The belief that Christ would establish a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth before the final judgment.</term>—have dared to establish this doctrine if these Areopagite writings had already existed? In those writings (*Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* <note>original: "Hierarch. Eccl. cap. 7."</note>, chapter 7), it is quite clearly stated: 

> Others have, I know not how, fallen into thoughts and opinions that betray an earthly and physical origin, by assuming a most blessed and holy state similar to this life is promised to the pious; and they even dared to wickedly assert that those who shall be equal to the angels will consume foods appropriate for this changeable life. May God prevent any pious man from falling into such error!

### III.

The book *On the Celestial Hierarchy* contains a detailed description of the angels and particularly their division into nine classes. All writers who wrote about angels after the Areopagite writings became known refer to them with one voice; but not a single one of those who touched upon this subject before the appearance of the *Areopagitica* <note>The collective name for the works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> did so.

Thus, *Irenaeus* <note>Bishop of Lyon (c. 130–202 AD) and a key defender of orthodoxy against Gnosticism.</note> says against the Gnostics: "Let them ever recount to us the number of the angels and the order of the archangels, or reveal the mystery of the Thrones..."

<keywords>Pseudo-Dionysius, Tertullian, Praxeas, Papias, Millenarianism, Chiliasmus, Celestial Hierarchy, Irenaeus, Angelology, Church History</keywords>

--- Page 38 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite were unknown to the early Church Fathers. The previous page ended with a quote from Dionysius's "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" regarding those who held "opinions that betray" a lack of understanding of the spiritual realm. This page examines how Origen, Augustine, and Cyril of Jerusalem expressed ignorance regarding the very angelic hierarchies that Dionysius supposedly defined in the 1st century.</meta>

...and teach the distinctions between the Dominions, the Principalities, the Powers, and the Authorities. Yet they do not know what they ought to say about them.

*Origen*, in his commentary on *Matthew*, does indeed acknowledge a distinction among the angels, saying that there were various powers—some who served Christ, others who worked alongside the prophets, etc.; but he knows nothing of the nine classes of Dionysius.

*Augustine*, however, states quite clearly that he does not know Dionysius. For in his book against *Priscillian* <note>A 4th-century bishop from Spain whose ascetic and mystical teachings were eventually condemned as heretical.</note>, he expresses himself thus: "That Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers exist among the heavenly spirits, I believe most firmly; also that some distinction is found among them; but—though you consider me a great teacher, despise me now—which ones they are and what their difference is, I do not know." — He adds that in such matters, cautious ignorance seems preferable to reckless curiosity. In the *Enchiridion* <note>original: "Enchiridio" - Augustine’s "Handbook" on faith, hope, and love.</note>, he even doubts whether Archangels and <term>virtutes (ἀρεταὶ): "Virtues" or "Powers"—a specific rank in the traditional angelic hierarchy.</term> are one and the same, and what distinction exists among those four words with which Paul likely intended to encompass the entire heavenly society. — Against the Arian <note>A follower of Arianism, a 4th-century theological movement that argued Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> *Mariminus* <note>Likely Maximinus, an Arian bishop who debated Augustine c. 427 AD.</note>, who had written that angels were indeed seen by archangels, but archangels were not seen by angels, he asks: "From whom did you hear this? From where did you learn it? Where did you read it? Would it not be better if you paid attention to the Holy Scriptures, in which we read that angels have even been seen by men, whenever and however they wished?" — *Cyril of Jerusalem* says against the Arians, who brought forward much that was improper regarding the begetting of the Son: "Tell me first, you boldest of men, how a Throne differs from a Dominion, and then search into that which concerns Christ; tell me what a Principality is, what a Power is, what an Angel is, and then search after the Creator himself."

Their admitted ignorance of these celestial ranks serves as evidence that the works of Pseudo-Dionysius had not yet been authored or circulated in their time.</summary>

Caesarius <note>Likely Caesarius of Nazianzus (c. 330–369 AD), a physician and brother of Gregory of Nazianzus.</note>, who took his information from Basil, counts only seven orders. There are seven orders, he says, just as Jude has written and as the high Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, whose letters mention various angelic ranks.</note> reckons them.

Petavius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and scholar of the history of dogma.</note> says clearly: one will find the ninefold number of angels in no ancient writer who lived in the first five centuries, for the works of Dionysius—who first established them—were not yet known.

Similarly, although the Syrians in their ritual books have indeed divided nine angelic orders into three hierarchies, they name them in a manner entirely contrary to the Areopagite's classification, calling the first class "Angels," the second "Seraphim," and the third "<term>Watchers</term> <note>original: "Wächter" — a term for a specific class of angels found in the biblical Book of Daniel and the apocryphal Book of Enoch.</note>."

The particular way in which Dionysius (*On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 7, §4) explains the Seraph mentioned in Isaiah 6 is unknown to any of the older commentators, neither Basil, nor Cyril, nor Jerome, nor Theodoret.

## IV.

Historical matters also appear in these writings which no other ancient author has mentioned. Among these is the solar eclipse during Christ’s crucifixion cited in the seventh letter. The alleged Dionysius recounts that he witnessed and closely observed it alongside the pagan philosopher Apollophanes at Heliopolis in Egypt at that very time. Likewise, he mentions a certain Hierotheus as a student of Paul and as his own teacher; a pious and wise man, Hierotheus supposedly wrote several works, many of which Dionysius himself cites. Dionysius claims that, together with this man and the brother of the Lord, James, as well as the Apostle Peter and Timothy, he saw that body which gave the <gloss>primal source of life</gloss> and received God into itself—meaning the body of the Virgin Mary. Also belonging to this category is the story of the vision of Carpus from Crete in the eighth letter.

It also highlights suspicious historical claims within the Dionysian texts, such as a witnessed eclipse and the burial of the Virgin Mary.</summary>

Regarding these four stories, one would believe that all writers who recorded such things must have included them first. However, they are found neither in the works of *Papias* <note>Papias of Hierapolis (c. 60–130 AD), an early Christian author who sought out oral traditions from those who knew the Apostles.</note>, nor *Hegesippus* <note>An early Christian chronicler (c. 110–180 AD) who wrote against heresies.</note>, nor *Irenaeus*, and not in *Clement*. And the diligent collector *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History" for his massive efforts to preserve early Christian records.</note>, who researched everything so carefully and with such great resources to historically clarify the time after the death of *Jesus*, likewise knows not a single word of these tales. Even the commentators on the passages regarding the Passion of *Christ* know nothing of them, no more than *Augustine*, who did not consider this solar eclipse to be a natural one, yet failed to cite this testimony of *Dionysius* in support. *Origen* <note>A prolific 3rd-century scholar from Alexandria.</note> explains the solar eclipse—which supposedly spread over the whole earth—as being limited only to the land of *Judea*, without drawing evidence from *Dionysius* to prove to his pagan opponents that it had also been observed in *Egypt*. The same is the case with *Jerome’s* interpretation of this passage. The two most learned writers of Christian antiquity thus did not know these writings. Their lack of knowledge is a strong proof of the non-existence of the works themselves. — Similarly, no writer mentions the prophecy cited by *Dionysius* in the tenth letter, <unclear>which</unclear> he claims to have given as a comfort to the Apostle *John* while he was living in exile on *Patmos*, predicting that he would soon be freed and return to *Asia*.

So much for the writers of the second and third centuries in this regard. Now for something regarding those of the fourth and fifth. —

## V.

It is well known how many very clear passages regarding the *Trinity* appear in the Areopagite writings—so clear, in fact, that even the *Nicene* formula of condemnation <note>The "Anathema" or formal rejection of Arianism established at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> against *Arius* is not expressed more distinctly. How, then, could certain Fathers, such as *Tertullian*, *Origen*, *Novatian*, *Dionysius* of *Alexandria*, and even *Justin*, express themselves so...

Furthermore, the "Dionysian" writings contain advanced theological definitions of the Trinity that only appeared after the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</summary>

...express themselves so severely regarding the divinity of the Son and the Spirit as they did, if they had known these passages? How did it happen that the defenders of the Trinity <note>The Christian doctrine that God exists as three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> against the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> in the following centuries did not cite these passages—not even Athanasius <note>A 4th-century bishop of Alexandria and the primary opponent of Arianism.</note>, who brought forward many passages from earlier Church Fathers against them—any more than all the other writers on the same subject until the sixth century?

Dionysius uses the word hypostasis <note>original: "ὑπόστασις"; in theology, this term refers to a distinct person of the Trinity as distinguished from the shared divine essence.</note> in a way that signifies the divine person as distinct from the divine nature; he treats it not as a word he invented, but as one commonly used by the theologians of that time. However, according to Morinus <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French theologian and scholar of Church history.</note>, the Greek theologians first used this word in this specific sense at the Council of Alexandria (362 AD). Before then, the term was viewed with suspicion by the Orthodox <note>Those adhering to the established, traditional creeds of the Church.</note> in the West; Jerome <note>A prominent priest and scholar (c. 347–420 AD) best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> also expressed himself very strongly against it. Likewise, in the fourth century, Aerius <note>A 4th-century priest who challenged the established Church structure.</note> claimed that the office of bishop was not superior to that of a presbyter <note>A priest or elder.</note>. Epiphanius sought to refute him without making the slightest mention of Dionysius, whose description of a completely perfected subordination and ecclesiastical order would have served in place of all other refutations. Furthermore, during the Pelagian controversy <note>A 5th-century theological struggle regarding human nature and grace; Pelagius argued that humans could choose good without special divine aid.</note>, Augustine never cited the passage from *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* (Chapter 3, Sections 7 and 11) which speaks so clearly in his favor regarding the corruption of human nature.

One also searches in vain through the records of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon <note>Major church councils held in 431 AD and 451 AD to define the relationship between Christ's divine and human natures.</note> against Nestorius and Eutyches for any citation of the striking passages from the Areopagite, who even uses the specific expressions of the Council of Chalcedon: without confusion, without change, without alteration, without mutation <note>original Greek: "ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀναλλοιώtaus, ἀμεταβόλως." These four adverbs became the standard definition for how Christ's two natures were united.</note>.

Thus, even at this time, the *Areopagitica* were not yet known.

### VI.

As is well known, Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note> cites all the passages known to him from ancient writers in his *Church History* to prove the accuracy of the Canon <note>The official list of books recognized as Holy Scripture.</note>; but he mentions Dionysius nowhere, even though this Dionysius cites all the New and Old Testament books most clearly, and even attributes the much-disputed Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> to the Apostle John in clear words. How could Dionysius of Alexandria <note>A 3rd-century bishop and student of Origen.</note> have so directly denied this book to John (according to Eusebius's testimony) if he had known the Areopagite writings? Eusebius even lists those writers who cited certain books or wrote about them; yet in all of this, there is nothing of Dionysius. The same case occurs with the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Epistle of James.

Moreover, neither Eusebius nor Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible.</note> nor Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Massilia, a 5th-century priest who continued Jerome's biographies of famous men.</note> mention Dionysius in their catalogs of Christian writers. It is hardly believable that Eusebius, since he cites Dionysius [of Alexandria] himself, would have forgotten his extensive and important works; and the objection that he intentionally skipped them because he, Eusebius, was a secret friend of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God.</note> is void. If that were the case, would Eusebius have cited no one from the pre-Nicene <note>The era before the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> Fathers except those who leaned toward Arianism? No; on the contrary, he mentions almost all of them, with very few exceptions, and among them are the true pillars of Nicene Orthodoxy <note>The mainstream Christian belief established at Nicaea, defending the full divinity of Christ.</note>. Even the most zealous defender of the authenticity of the Areopagite writings considers this accusation against Eusebius to be a slander. —

Furthermore, Eusebius could have told the stories of the solar eclipse, of Hierotheus, of Carpus, and of John <note>Specific legendary accounts found in the Pseudo-Dionysian writings.</note> while remaining silent about the source, yet we find not a single word of them in his works. Finally, the charge of Arianism does not apply to the continuators of the Eusebian catalog, Jerome and Gennadius.

<summary>The author argues that the "Areopagite" writings must be forgeries because the earliest Church historians—Eusebius, Jerome, and Gennadius—never mention them, even when discussing the biblical books Dionysius supposedly authenticated.</summary>

and yet they too are silent regarding Dionysius, even though it would have been their duty, as successors, to record and supplement what was omitted or forgotten by Eusebius. The "good cause" <note>Referring to the triumph of Nicene orthodoxy over Arianism.</note> itself, having triumphed at Nicaea, would have demanded this, had any earlier cunning by opponents managed to keep these magnificent works in the dark.

Opponents argue, on the one hand, that Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar and translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> only intended to include the writers already listed by Eusebius in his catalog, and therefore, it does not follow from Jerome's ignorance of the writings that they did not exist at all. Moreover, Jerome cites many writers who were omitted by Eusebius. — As for what is inferred about Jerome’s ignorance from a passage where he says that, living in Bethlehem, he could not know all the *new* writings just coming out unless the authors themselves pointed them out to him; it is self-evident that this could not apply to important, famous, ancient works. However, should the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus was a created being; they were the primary theological opponents of the period.</note> have hidden these books, it remains for the opponents to provide proof that such books even existed to be hidden.

It must also be added that Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Massilia (5th century), who continued Jerome's biographical work.</note>, the successor to Jerome who supplements his work remarkably, also knows nothing of the Areopagite writings.

### VIII.

*Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian who defended the authenticity of many traditional church documents.</note> however, and *Perronius* <note>Cardinal Jacques Davy du Perron (1556–1618).</note>, along with other opponents, maintain that the Dionysian writings were indeed cited by authors of the first five centuries. In contrast, *Anastasius* <note>Anastasius Bibliothecarius, a 9th-century Roman scholar and librarian.</note> says in a letter to *Charles the Bald*; however famous, knowledgeable, and ancient this *Dionysius* may have been, it must nevertheless be noted that no <term>orthodox</term> <note>meaning "right-believing" or following established church doctrine</note> writer made mention of his works until the Roman Bishops *Gregory*, *Martin*, and *Agatho* cited them in their writings and thereby authorized them. Among the more modern writers, *Sixtus of Siena* says that the mystical theology of *Dionysius the Areopagite* likely did not yet exist in the time of *Athanasius*. *Petau* <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian.</note> concedes that in the first five centuries the *Areopagitica* <note>The collection of works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> did not yet exist, and *Bellarmine* even asserts that before *Gregory the Great*, these works were never cited under the name of their author.

Nevertheless, *Baronius* says that *Athanasius* was familiar with the *Heavenly Hierarchy* <note>original: "himmlische Hierarchie"; one of the primary works in the Dionysian corpus.</note> and cited it in the fourth question of his *Book of Questions*. But this book is not by *Athanasius*, but by a much later writer. In that same work, *Epiphanius* and *Gregory of Nyssa* are cited, both of whom lived after *Athanasius*; in the thirty-third question, *Athanasius* himself is even cited; moreover, *Chrysostom*, the *Ladder of Divine Ascent* by *John Climacus*, *Maximus*, *Nicephorus*, and others—even the Romans are called a nation of the Frankish race therein. It is probable that this book is by an *Athanasius* of Antioch who lived three or four centuries later.

Similarly, the Maronite **Abraham Echellensis** <note>A Lebanese Maronite scholar (1605–1664) who helped translate the Arabic Bible.</note> asserted that Bishop **John of Dara** in Syria wrote a Syriac commentary on the *Areopagitica* <note>The collected works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> in the fourth century. This is false, as **Morinus** <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French theologian and scholar of Eastern liturgies.</note> has shown, demonstrating that this writer lived long after the fourth century—even after the **Trullan Synod** <note>A church council held in 692 AD to complete the work of the previous ecumenical councils.</note> (692).

It is also claimed that **Cyril of Alexandria** <note>The Patriarch of Alexandria (c. 376–444 AD), a central figure in early Christological debates.</note>—according to **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian who defended the antiquity of Dionysian texts.</note> citing the *Breviarium* <note>A summary or handbook of ecclesiastical history.</note> of the Deacon **Liberatus**—cited the Areopagite writings in his books against **Diodorus** and **Theodore** etc., *on the incarnation of the word* <note>original Latin: "de incarnatione verbi"</note>, in passages that supposedly fell out or were removed later for reasons unknown.

But **Baronius** cited the passage incorrectly. For **Liberatus** speaks merely of rumors regarding this matter, stating: a deacon named **Basilus** came to Alexandria and handed over certain Armenian books and his own to **Cyril**. This (so the *rumor* goes) allegedly prompted **Cyril** to write four books: three against **Theodore** and **Diodorus** as the originators of the **Nestorian doctrine** <note>A 5th-century belief that emphasized the separation of the divine and human natures of Christ.</note>, and one book *on the incarnation*, which allegedly contained the unadulterated testimonies of the ancient Fathers: the Roman Pope **Felix**, the Corinthian Bishop **Dionysius the Areopagite**, and **Gregory**, surnamed "the **Wonderworker**" <note>Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–270 AD), a famous bishop known for his missionary work and supposed miracles.</note>. Here, then, there is only talk of rumors spread by the **Acephali** <note>A name meaning "the headless ones," used for a group of Monophysites who rejected the Council of Chalcedon and lacked a clear leader.</note>; and **Liberatus** adds immediately thereafter: to this, the Catholics—the defenders of the truth—replied.

Every new and forged book could, after all, be declared ancient and authentic using this excuse of **Bellarmine’s**.

It is asserted without proof that many writings shared the same fate as these Dionysian ones; rather, there has never been a case where works of great scope, written by a very famous man and containing very important content, remained hidden. Instead, the course of such matters is always that such writings become known either during the author’s lifetime or shortly after his death and are cited by other writers on various occasions. After a longer or shorter period of time, they may then partially perish; this continued existence depends largely on their content, and partly on the whim of fate, which happens to rule over this or that book. The common causes that lead to the disappearance of books explain nothing in the case of these writings. They were not poor; rather, they were always highly praised by the Catholics, so they could not have perished as being worthless. — They did not fall into the hands of uneducated, ignorant, or crude people who could not have appreciated their value, but were supposedly sent to **Titus**, **Timothy**, and **Polycarp** <note>These are prominent figures of the early Church: Titus and Timothy were companions of the Apostle Paul, and Polycarp was a disciple of the Apostle John and Bishop of Smyrna.</note>. These honest men, friends of **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian judge converted by St. Paul, to whom these mystical writings were falsely attributed.</note>, glowing with zeal for the cause of the Church, would certainly have carefully collected these writings and shared them with their congregations in **Crete**, **Ephesus**, and **Smyrna**, and these in turn would have shared them with neighboring congregations. Above all, they would have been sent to **Athens** and made known to all of Christendom as a rich treasure and distributed through copies. —

The care of the earliest times in preserving the written records of famous teachers is well known; certainly, they would have done no less than later times for the publication and explanation of our writings, if they had been present. For

The third reason is completely untenable: that the Areopagite writings were far too sublime and obscure for the masses to grasp. # XI.

Dionysius suffered martyrdom under Domitian <note>Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD.</note>; according to a tradition put forward by Sirmond and Launoy <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651) and Jean de Launoy (1603–1678) were influential French scholars who applied critical historical methods to church traditions.</note>, with which all the oldest defenders and opponents of the Areopagite writings, even Marinus, agree. ### XIV.

The evidence for the death of the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a judge of the Areopagus in Athens who was converted by St. Paul.</note> under Hadrian is insufficient. ### XV.

Dionysius must have died under Domitian <note>Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD.</note>. This is proven by the entire course of events; furthermore, by the testimonies of Maximus <note>Likely Maximus the Confessor, a 7th-century theologian and commentator on Dionysius's works.</note>, Methodius, Simeon Metaphrastes, the Menaion <note>Liturgical books of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the lives of the saints for each month.</note>, the Greek Anthology, and a Synaxarium <note>A collection of brief hagiographies or "lives of the saints."</note> which has Dionysius first burned in Athens and then beheaded in Paris; likewise the testimony of the anonymous author on the history of Dagobert <note>King of the Franks in the 7th century.</note>, of Hilduin, Paschasius Radbertus, Hincmar, Vincent of Beauvais, Albert of Stade, and Matthew of Westminster.

# XVII.

The author of the <term>Pseudo-Areopagite</term><note>A name used by modern scholars for the anonymous author who wrote under the pseudonym of Dionysius the Areopagite, a first-century convert of St. Paul.</note> writings also reveals that he wrote after the martyrdom of Ignatius. For he cites (in *On the Divine Names*, Ch. 4, § 12) a saying from a letter written to the Romans, which, according to his own statement, was composed shortly before his martyrdom: “Saint Ignatius writes, ‘my Love is crucified.’” <note>Original: "meine Liebe ist gekreuziget" (Latin: *amor meus crucifixus est*; Greek: *ho emos erōs estaurōtai*). This famous line from Ignatius of Antioch's *Letter to the Romans* is a major chronological problem for those claiming Dionysius wrote in the 1st century, as Ignatius died around 110 AD.</note> Since it is admitted that Ignatius suffered martyrdom in the year 110 or 111, Dionysius cannot be the author of the writings named after him. 

Halloix <note>Pierre Halloix (1572–1656) was a Jesuit scholar who famously defended the authenticity of the Dionysian writings.</note> resorts to the excuse that this citation of Ignatius was not written by Dionysius himself, but was perhaps inserted into his work by a copyist. But already another Jesuit, Vasquez, says on a similar occasion: If such excuses were to hold, then no passage of any Church Father that happened to be inconvenient would be safe. — However, no printed edition and no manuscript omits this passage; even Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), an influential theologian who wrote extensive "Scholia" or commentaries on the Dionysian works.</note> read it, as his <term>scholia</term><note>Brief explanatory notes or commentaries written in the margins of ancient manuscripts.</note> testify. The proofs that Halloix cites for his opinion—that without this passage Dionysius’s discourse would be better connected, that Dionysius did not here cite Hierotheus <note>A legendary figure described by the author as his teacher and a contemporary of the Apostles.</note> alongside Ignatius, that the words do not prove at all what the author intends to prove, that the words of Ignatius were similar to the words of Paul (Galatians 6:14), and that not the whole passage but only a part of it is attributed to Ignatius—are self-refuting. Could no Church Father commit an error against logic or rhetoric!

Thus, even if the letter of Ignatius were authentic, the citation of a passage from it would speak against...

## XVIII.

By quoting a passage from **Ignatius’s** letters, the **Pseudo-Dionysius** clearly shows that he wrote after **Ignatius’s** death. Now, he attributes the book *On the Divine Names*, in which this quotation appears, to his fellow presbyter **Timothy**; he addresses him as someone still living. **Timothy**, however, had already died by the time **Ignatius** wrote his letters. For **Ignatius** himself, in his letter to the **Philadelphians**, speaks of **Timothy**, **Titus**, **Evodius**, and **Clement** as saints who had already departed from this life; and in the letter to the **Corinthians**, he names **Onesimus** as their bishop, implying that **Timothy** must have already passed away. <note>The letters mentioned here—to the Philadelphians and Corinthians—are part of the "Long Recension" or spurious letters attributed to Ignatius, which were widely debated by scholars of this period.</note>

**Maximus** <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), an influential theologian who wrote extensive commentaries (scholia) to defend the works of Dionysius.</note> resolves this difficulty by declaring the Ignatian passage to be an interpolation <note>An "interpolation" is a passage introduced into a text by a later hand, which was not part of the original manuscript.</note>; a pretext which has just been refuted (see section XVII). It need only be added here that **Maximus** found this passage in all copies roughly 100 years after the first appearance of the Areopagite writings; it could not have entered the text from a scholar’s <term>gloss</term><note>A "gloss" is a brief explanatory note or translation written in the margin or between the lines of a text.</note>, because the author of the passage speaks of **Ignatius** as his contemporary. 

**Maximus** offers another excuse: namely, that **Dionysius** had remembered this sentence from an oral conversation with **Ignatius** and thus quoted it from memory. However, the quotation states explicitly, not <term>he says</term> <note>Original Greek: <foreign>φησὶ</foreign> (*phēsi*)</note> but <term>and the divine Ignatius also writes</term> <note>Original Greek: <foreign>γράφει δὲ καὶ ὁ θεῖος Ἰγνάτιος</foreign> (*graphei de kai ho theios Ignatios*)</note>. **Baronius** <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Vatican historian who attempted to reconcile historical discrepancies in church tradition.</note> refuses to accept that the **Timothy** to whom the book *On the Divine Names* is addressed is the disciple of **Paul**; instead, he claims it was a younger **Timothy**, the son of a Roman senator named **Pudens**. **Dexter** <note>Flavius Lucius Dexter, a 4th-century figure to whom a famous forged chronicle was attributed in the early 17th century.</note> even makes him...

### XIX.

The author of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* calls **Timothy** (Chapter 3, § 1) his son <note>original: "ὡ παῖ κάλε" (o pai kale), a Greek address meaning "O child" or "O son."</note> and does so in various other places (*Heavenly Hierarchy* Chapter 2; *Divine Names* Chapter 2, 1). Now, as **Baronius** <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian famous for the "Annales Ecclesiastici," a massive history of the Church.</note> has already shown, it is easily provable that one bishop would have called another "brother," not "son." **Halloir**, however, provides the following reasons why an exception was made in this case: first, because **Dionysius** was much older than **Timothy**; second, because **Dionysius** had instructed **Timothy** in philosophy and the worldly sciences; and finally, because **Timothy** was fearful and timid by nature and required **Dionysius** not only as a teacher in knowledge, but also in virtue and steadfastness.

But the first reason concerning the youth of **Timothy** is false. **Paul** took him as his companion in **Lystra**, certainly not as a boy. This occurred at least three years before the ninth year of the Emperor **Claudius**. If one assumes **Timothy** was twenty-five years old at that point, he was thirty-three at the beginning of **Nero's** reign, while **Dionysius**—according to his own statement in the letter to **Apollophanes**—was forty-three in the tenth year of **Claudius**,

### XXI.

On the occasion where he (in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, Chapter 7, Section 11) defends the ceremonies of baptism against the pagans who mocked them, he remarks: he says of it what the divine teachers, drawing from ancient tradition (having been initiated <note>original Greek: "μυηθέντες," meaning those initiated into sacred mysteries</note>), had handed down to him. — Could this be said by a disciple of the Apostles? If the Apostles had instituted infant baptism, would it have become an "ancient tradition" by the time of their immediate disciple, Dionysius? Moreover, by "divine teachers" here, he does not even mean the Apostles, but necessarily later theologians; for it is quite clear regarding the Apostles that what they taught about baptism they received not from ancient tradition, but from Jesus.

To explain the word "ancient" <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαῖος"</note> used in the passage as if it stood for "from the beginning" <note>original Greek: "ἀπ' ἀρχῆς"</note> contradicts the laws of language.
