"...should not be explained to the uninitiated." This distinction was reportedly established by the very legislators of the worship handed down by God. For this reason, the author sends his book on the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* to Timothy as a gift; he hopes, trusting in Timothy’s holy promises, that both he and others to whom he shares the book will touch holy things with a holy mind. He expects they will share divine matters only with the divine, the perfect only with those capable of perfection, and the most holy only with the holy. Therefore, he says (in the same work, Chapter 2, Section 1): "Let no uninitiated person come to this spectacle."

But neither in the time of the Apostles, nor in the first three centuries, is there the slightest trace of this "acting in secret." Justin Martyr describes both sacraments <note>Baptism and the Eucharist.</note> in detail in his *Apology*; likewise, Tertullian describes baptism in his book *On Baptism* <note>original Latin title: *de baptismo*</note>. Neither in Irenaeus, nor in Clement of Alexandria, nor in Origen and the other Greeks—nor even in Cyprian and the Latin writers before the year 260—is there even a trace of mystery in this regard.

In these writings, the same form and manner of public penance already appears as it existed in the third and fourth centuries. In the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* (Chapter 3), mention is made of both the sinners who are not yet admitted to penance, as well as the two classes of the penitents themselves: the "listeners" <note>original Greek: ἀκροαταί (akroatai); those allowed to hear the scriptures but not stay for the prayers.</note> and the "kneeling ones" <note>original Greek: ὑποπίπτοντες (hypopiptontes); those who knelt in prayer but were dismissed before the Eucharist.</note>. <meta>This page continues the argument that the liturgical practices described by Pseudo-Dionysius do not match the simplicity of the early Church. ...were dismissed from the assembly. All of this was by no means yet determined or brought into its final form in the first two centuries.

Pseudo-Dionysius describes the act of baptism exactly as it existed in the fourth and fifth centuries. The catechumen <term>catechumen: a person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before being baptized</term> goes with his sponsor <note>original: "Pathen", a godfather or witness</note> to the presiding official; the latter questions him, lays hands on him, makes the sign of the cross over him, and has his name written in the church registers along with the name of the sponsor. He then has him undress and stand facing the West <note>original: "Abend" (evening), the direction of sunset, liturgically representing the realm of darkness and Satan</note>, stretch out his hands three times toward the West, blow away Satan three times, and renounce him. He then turns him toward the East <note>original: "Morgen" (morning), the direction of the rising sun, representing Christ</note>, and with eyes and hands raised toward heaven, the initiate accepts Christ and his teaching—just as this entire ceremony is described in detail in the second chapter of the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

To see how this entire description originates from a later period, one should compare it with the account already mentioned above, which Justin Martyr <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) provided one of the earliest surviving descriptions of Christian baptism and worship in his *First Apology*.</note> gives of the same, where everything is conducted quite simply and without pomp.

### XXIII.

No passage from the first three centuries speaks of the specific circumstances regarding the consecration of the holy oil, which Pseudo-Dionysius (*Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, Chapter 4) describes so extensively, placing it on the same level as the Lord’s Supper <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>.

No writer of the first centuries speaks of the incense offerings, which constitute a main part of the ceremony in Dionysius's work. Furthermore, he mentions certain altars which were only introduced by Pope Sylvester <note>Sylvester I, Bishop of Rome from 314 to 335 AD; the author suggests that the use of permanent stone altars is a post-Constantinian development.</note>; indeed, there were no altars at all in the oldest times. Likewise, the mention of temples proves this later age, since—besides the previously mentioned Chrysostom and Isidore of Pelusium—they expressly state that in the earliest times, neither churches nor temples existed.

## XXIV.

Dionysius furthermore mentions monks and describes at length the manner of their initiation, even though, according to the consistent testimony of antiquity, they were completely unknown in the first three centuries. Halloix <note>Pierre Halloix (1571–1656), a Jesuit scholar who famously attempted to defend the 1st-century authenticity of the Dionysian writings.</note>, since it is all too well known that monks only appeared through Hilarion, Paul, Antony, Julian, and Macarius <note>These figures are the "Desert Fathers" of the 4th century, credited with founding Christian monasticism.</note>, attempts to rescue Dionysius by claiming that he spoke of a very special kind of monk, who were neither hermits nor <term>cenobites: monks who live together in a community</term>, but rather lived among the laity in the cities, subject to bishops and priests, partly individually, partly collectively in communities <note>original: "Kollegien"</note> in chastity and abstention from worldly affairs; and these would have held the first place among the laity in the churches, right after the clergy. — But no writer speaks of this kind of people; no one uses the names that Dionysius gives to his monks, namely <term>monachoi: "solitary ones" or monks</term> <note>original: "μοναχοὶ"</note> and <term>therapeutai: "servants" or "healers"</term> <note>original: "θεραπευταὶ"</note>. Only Philo uses the latter term, and Dionysius therefore believed, along with Eusebius, that the "Therapeutae" mentioned by Philo were Christian ascetics. <note>Philo of Alexandria described a Jewish sect called the Therapeutae; later church historians like Eusebius mistakenly believed they were early Christians.</note> —

The anointing of the dead with oil is also a later practice. ## XXVI.

The prophecy that Dionysius puts forward in his letter to John was certainly easy to manufacture, since the later writer knew well from history of John's return from Patmos. Nevertheless, he committed a demonstrable error in this prediction by saying that he would enjoy the Apostle's company after his return to Ephesus. This could not have occurred, since Dionysius suffered <note>meaning he was martyred</note> under Domitian, while John returned under Nerva <note>Domitian reigned 81–96 AD; Nerva reigned 96–98 AD. The author is pointing out that if Dionysius died under the first emperor, he could not have met John under the second.</note>.

Equally suspicious is the frequently mentioned Hierotheus. He is said to have been a disciple of Paul, the teacher of Dionysius, a distinguished worker for the Christian faith, and an inspired expert and orator on the "mysteries" <note>referring to the sacraments or hidden theological truths</note>. At the same time, his excellent writings are highly praised, his concise...

Hierotheus and Dionysius are one and the same person. The alleged Dionysius forged a fake Hierotheus and elevated him as high as he could in order to give his own new ideas a brilliant aura of authority.

## XXVII.

The alleged Areopagite also cites well-known ancient Christian teachers and attributes writings to them that are completely unknown to both ancient and modern scholars. First, he mentions a certain Justus—whom Pachymeres <note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310), a Byzantine scholar who wrote extensive commentaries on Dionysius.</note> identifies as the one mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles—and of whom Dionysius says that he called divine peace and divine rest an "ineffability" which remains unmoved against every "emanation" <note>original Greek: πρόοδος; in this context, it refers to the way God's power flows out into the world.</note>. Likewise, in the third paragraph of the first chapter of *Mystical Theology*, he cites a saying by the Apostle Bartholomew. However, it is very doubtful whether books were ever [written] by either man...

...were once in existence. The ancients carefully collected books by the Apostles or their disciples, citing them and identifying those that were forged. Regarding Justus and Bartholomew, absolutely nothing of this kind is known. To be sure, Pope Gelasius <note>Gelasius I, Pope from 492 to 496, who issued a famous decree distinguishing between canonical and apocryphal books.</note> cites a "Gospel of Bartholomew," but he himself designates it as apocryphal <note>meaning "hidden" or of doubtful authenticity</note>; and since it was not cited earlier, it seems not to have been much older than Gelasius himself. Thus, if Dionysius were to have drawn from it, it provides a **proof** against his supposed antiquity.

When Dionysius speaks in *The Celestial Hierarchy* <note>One of the most influential works of Pseudo-Dionysius, describing the nine orders of angels.</note> about the various opinions regarding the "lot" through which Matthias became an Apostle <note>Referencing Acts 1:23-26, where the early Church chose a replacement for Judas Iscariot by casting lots.</note>, and then offers his own opinion on the matter, Morinus <note>Jean Morin, the 17th-century scholar mentioned on the previous page.</note> rightly observes how so many conflicting opinions could have existed in that early time concerning a matter that had only recently occurred—opinions which could have been immediately corrected and established by simply asking any Apostle still living. The same observation applies to the difficulty he finds elsewhere in the explanation of the vision of Isaiah, where he also speaks of conflicting opinions; in that case, it was merely his own embarrassment that forced him to explain how his "angel-doctrine" <note>angelology</note> could possibly harmonize with the clear pronouncements of the prophet.

Dionysius claims that Paul was the first to teach the division of angels into three classes, each of which has three orders <note>This refers to the famous nine-fold hierarchy: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominions, Virtues, Powers; Principalities, Archangels, Angels.</note>. Yet this division conflicts with clear passages of Holy Scripture, and Paul himself never hints at it in the slightest, which he surely would have had to do according to Colossians 1:28 <note>In this verse, Paul speaks of "warning every man and teaching every man in all wisdom."</note>. —

...difficulties, occur frequently enough, and Dionysius does not even need these in all his writings. Even the anointing after baptism, which he identifies as an apostolic institution, only appears at the end of the second century. Furthermore, neither the Apostles nor any writers of the first three centuries ever call the ointment *myron* <note>original: μύρον</note> as the material used for anointing, but quite simply oil *elaion* <note>original: ἔλαιον</note>.

Dionysius commits a blatant and incomprehensible historical error by making Zechariah <note>The father of John the Baptist; see Luke 1:5–25.</note>, whom the angel Gabriel addressed, a High Priest <note>original: ἱεράρχην - hierarchēn</note>. At the time Gabriel came to Zechariah, either Matthias, the son of Theophilus, or his successor Joazar—under whom Christ was born—was High Priest. This is sufficiently proven by the lists of High Priests in the records of Nicephorus and the librarian Anastasius <note>Nicephorus I of Constantinople and Anastasius Bibliothecarius were influential chroniclers who preserved lists of ancient religious leaders.</note>. While later writers such as Ambrose, Augustine, and Chrysostom commit the same error, it is more excusable for them, as they lived in a much more distant time. How, however, could Dionysius, who supposedly lived so close to those events, overlook this circumstance, which he could have learned upon the first inquiry?

Furthermore, one can note the false explanation of Cherubim, which Dionysius explains as an "outpouring of wisdom." This is incorrect because, according to its etymology, it means "youths" <note>The author is likely referencing an 18th-century etymological theory that linked the Hebrew *kerub* to a root suggesting youth or strength, contrasting it with the mystical interpretation used by Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>.

...thus he calls James the "Brother of God" <note>original: ἀδελφόθεον — adelphotheon</note> and David the "Ancestor of God" <note>original: θεοπάτορα — theopatora</note>. These epithets, however, were not used at all during the first three centuries and did not emerge in the Church before the Council of Ephesus <note>The Council of Ephesus (431 AD) was convened to address the teachings of Nestorius and confirmed that Mary could be called the "God-bearer."</note>. For it was only in opposition to Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a bishop who argued that Mary was the mother of Christ’s human nature only, not his divine nature.</note> that these titles arose to indicate the intimate union of God and man in Christ. Just as people then began to call Mary "God-bearer" <note>original: Θεοτόκος — Theotokos</note>, so too they called James, the Lord's brother, "Brother of God" <note>original: ἀδελφόθεος — adelphotheos</note>; Anna "Divine Ancestress" <note>original: θεοπρομήτορα — theopromētora; literally "the grandmother of God," referring to the mother of Mary.</note>; and Mary herself also "Receiver of God" <note>original: θεοδόχον — theodochon</note>. From this it follows that the Areopagite writings could only have been written after the Synod of Ephesus (431).

The words he uses to explain the unity of the two natures in Christ show quite clearly that he had the heresy of Eutyches <note>Eutyches (c. 380–456 AD) taught that Christ’s humanity was absorbed into his divinity, a view condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.</note> in mind; for, with minor modifications, they are the same words that the Council of Chalcedon used against this heretic. (*On the Divine Names*, Ch. 1, §. 4. Ch. 2, §. 10).

### XXX.

But even the overall tone and the "color" of the Areopagite language—so far removed from the simplicity of the apostles' disciples—shows that the author must have been shaped by other influences in much later times. Dionysius anxiously avoids using simple, common words and instead grasps for grand phrases, majesty, pomp, and splendor. Such is the judgment of Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a brilliant classical scholar who proved that many "ancient" texts, including these, were actually later forgeries.</note> regarding him: that he has shrouded the mysteries in night and darkness, much like pagan writers, as if they were kept in a hidden sanctuary; using new words, and unusual, strange compounds for what could have been expressed with a single word;

He also critiques the author's overly ornate and "pagan" writing style as being inconsistent with the simplicity of the early Apostolic age.</summary>

...is expressed in several grand and resonant words; through this accumulation of words, as Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD) was a monk and theologian who wrote extensive commentaries explaining the difficult works of Dionysius.</note> says, he obscures the meaning. He avoids the words that the Church actually uses, as if they were not suited to his elevated status. Thus Morinus <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659) was a French scholar who scrutinized early church documents and recognized that Dionysius’s style did not match the 1st century.</note> describes his style as full of "Asiatic bombast" <note>A term used in ancient rhetoric to describe a highly ornate, flowery, and overly dramatic writing style.</note>, unusual compound words, high-sounding and exaggeratedly grand terms, long sentences, and an endless array of adjectives and complex structures, always striving for significance and intensity of expression. And he does this, we might add, not only when speaking of divine mysteries, but everywhere—even in letters to his friends. 

He never calls baptism "baptism" <note>original: βαπτισμὸς — baptismos</note>, but rather "divine birth" or "rebirth from God" <note>original: Θεογενεσία — theogenesia</note>; he calls the Lord’s Supper the "rite of rites" <note>original: τελετὴ τελετῶν — teletē teletōn</note>, the "most sacredly-consecrating Eucharist" <note>original: ἡ ἱεροτελεσikωτάτη εὐχαρισία</note>, and the "most hierarchical of all mysteries" <note>original: μυστήριον τὸ πάντων ἱεραρχikώτατον</note>. The place where people were baptized was usually called either the *font* <note>original: fons</note> or the *baptistery* <note>original: baptisterium</note>, but Dionysius calls it the "mother of adoption" <note>original: μητέρα υἱοθεσίας — mētera huiothesias</note>. 

He calls the bishops "Hierarchs" and "the namesake titles of the Hierarchy" <note>original: τὰς τῆς Ἱεραρχίας ἐπωνύμας</note>; the elders he calls "priests" <note>original: ἱερεῖς — hiereis</note>, and only a few times in the headings does the word *Presbyter* <note>The standard early Christian term for an elder or priest.</note> appear. The deacons he calls "ministers" <note>original: λειτουργοί — leitourgoi</note>; the Apostles and Prophets he calls "theologians," and sometimes "interpreters" <note>original: ὑποφῆται — hypophētai</note>, and once even "our divine initiators" <note>original: τὰς ἐνθέας ἡμῶν ἱεροτελέσας</note>. Holy Scripture is called "every sacred and holy-written tablet" <note>original: πᾶσα μὲν γὰρ ἱερὰ καὶ ἁγιόγραφος δέλτος</note>. Thus, he calls Genesis "the [book of] the birth-existence and ordering of beings from God" <note>original: ἡ τὴν ἐκ Θεοῦ τῶν ὄντων γεννητὴν ὕπαρξίν τε καὶ διακόσμησιν</note>; and the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> he calls "the hidden and mystical vision of the beloved and divine [disciple]" <note>original: τὴν κρυφίαν καὶ μυστικὴν ἐποψίαν τοῦ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀγαπητοῦ καὶ θεσπεσίου; referring to John the Apostle.</note>.

### XXXII.

When Halloir <note>Pierre Halloir (1572–1636) was a Jesuit scholar who wrote a significant defense of the authenticity of the Dionysian writings.</note> states that Clement of Alexandria and Gregory of Nazianzus <note>Two of the most important early Church theologians, active in the 2nd and 4th centuries respectively.</note> had borrowed passages from Dionysius, we must conclude—with the help of the preceding treatise—that Dionysius, or the writer appearing under his name, actually knew and utilized the writings of the aforementioned Fathers.

### XXXIII.

The opinion of Hypatius <note>Hypatius, Bishop of Ephesus, famously expressed skepticism about the Dionysian works at a meeting in Constantinople in 532 AD, noting that if they were genuine, they would have been cited by earlier authorities like Cyril or Athanasius.</note> persisted in the Church for over a hundred years after him. The first citation of the Areopagite's writings occurs in the works of Gregory the Great, who says in his thirty-fourth homily on the Gospels: "The ancient and venerable father Dionysius the Areopagite is said to say <note>original: "fertur dicere"—Gregory uses a cautious phrasing, suggesting he is repeating a report rather than citing a definitive source.</note> that from the ranks of the lower angels, some are sent out visibly or invisibly to perform their work"—a completely vague, non-decisive reference. The first to cite Dionysius as a true and reliable witness is Leontius of Byzantium <note>A 6th-century monk and theologian who was among the first to integrate Aristotelian logic into Christian theology.</note>, who says in a treatise against Nestorius and Eutyches: "from the book of Dionysius the Areopagite, contemporary of the Apostles, *On the Divine Names*." However, this Leontius wrote after 591 AD. At about the same time lived Anastasius Sinaita <note>A monk and prolific theological writer from Mount Sinai, active in the late 7th century.</note>, who calls Dionysius a famous teacher and apostolic mystic of divine things; this was not under Justinian, as Halloir and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit cardinal and a central figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> claim, because this Anastasius wrote after the death of Bishop Eulogius of Alexandria. In addition to Gregory the Great and Athanasius <note>This likely refers to a later figure or a mistaken attribution, as the famous Athanasius of Alexandria died in 373 AD, long before these works appeared.</note>, at about the same time, Sophronius <note>Sophronius (c. 560–638) was the Patriarch of Jerusalem and a defender of orthodox doctrine against Monothelitism.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the historical acceptance of the pseudo-Dionysian writings. The previous page ended with a mention of Gregory the Great and began a reference to Thomas of Jerusalem, which is completed at the start of this page.</meta>

omas, Bishop of Jerusalem, regarded the Areopagite Dionysius as the author of the writings existing under his name. However, actual authority was first granted to this opinion by the Roman Bishop Martin at a Roman Synod in 649 <note>The Lateran Council of 649, which was convened to condemn Monothelitism.</note>. At this same synod, several writings by the Monothelite <term>Monothelitism: A 7th-century theological doctrine which taught that Christ had two natures but only one will; it was eventually declared heretical.</term> Patriarch Cyrus of Alexandria and the Agnoete <term>Agnoetae: A sect that believed Jesus, in his human nature, was subject to certain limitations of knowledge or "ignorance."</term> Themistius were read aloud; both of these men had appealed to passages from the Areopagite to prove their opinions. Martin did not reject the citation, but rather corrected it and cited other passages from the same writings in opposition. This is recounted by the librarian Anastasius <note>Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810–879), a prominent scholar and translator of the early Middle Ages.</note> with accompanying praise for the Roman bishops Gregory, Agatho, and Martin, who were said to be the first to mention the Areopagite’s writings. 

Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), a monk and theologian who was a staunch defender of the authenticity of these works.</note> seems to have contributed greatly to this recognition; an ancient report even states that he specifically persuaded Martin to convene this synod. The great fame Maximus enjoyed in the Church as both a scholar and a pious man likely did much to recommend these writings that he praised so highly; and since he died a martyr’s death in 660, the reverence for him and for what he recommended was further increased. However, Maximus himself states that even in his time, many still doubted that Saint Dionysius was the author of these writings, believing instead that a later writer was their creator. —

### XXXV.

Later, the Areopagite writings reached the Latin-speaking West. Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> had cited them only from hearsay; the same seems to have been the case with Bishop Martin, with Agatho, and even with Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note>. Under the reign of Pepin <note>Pepin the Short, King of the Franks.</note>, the Roman Bishop Paul sent the works to him in France, in the original Greek. Paul succeeded his brother Stephen in 857 <note>Historical records usually date Paul I's reign to 757–767 AD; the date 857 in the text may be an error in the source or transcription.</note>.

About forty years later, as the historians Baronius and Halloir relate, copies of these writings were sent as a gift from the Greek Emperor Michael to Louis the Pious. Under the reign of Charles the Bald, they were then translated into Latin by Johannes Scotus Eriugena <note>An Irish theologian and philosopher (c. 810–877) active at the court of Charles the Bald.</note>. However, it was initially thought he had not translated them all, but only the books *On the Divine Names* and *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. This is suggested by a letter from the Roman Bishop Nicholas I to Charles the Bald, in which he writes that he had been informed that Scotus had translated these books, and that they should be sent to Rome for official approval. This was incorrect, as shown by Eriugena’s own letter to Charles the Bald, in which he explicitly states that he had translated all the writings of the Areopagite (including those still available to us today).

As early as 859, the books *On the Celestial Hierarchy* and *On the Divine Names* were cited by Hincmar of Reims; and later, Hincmar explicitly stated: Dionysius the Areopagite, the ancient and venerable Father, as he [was converted] by the Apostle Paul...

# XXXVI.

### XXXVII.

When Halloix <note>Pierre Halloix (1571–1656), a Jesuit scholar who published a massive defense of the writings' authenticity in 1633.</note> appeals to the fact that the Areopagite writings were considered the work of Dionysius the Areopagite for a full thousand years, and wishes to prove from this that they must therefore be authentic, he has forgotten that <unclear>many</unclear> other admittedly forged works can <unclear>claim</unclear> the same for themselves, as they were attributed to Ambrose, Jerome, or Augustine for just as long. In this proof, the point is not to show that these writings have been held as authentic since the sixth century, but rather to provide evidence for their authenticity from the first five centuries. Furthermore, when Halloix says that if one denies the writings to Dionysius, one must name their true author, this is an unreasonable demand. It is enough to show that they do not belong to the one to whom a long tradition has ascribed them; and it follows from the nature of the matter that someone who produced <term>pseudepigrapha; works written under a false name, usually that of a famous historical figure</term> and passed them off as the works of a famous man—wishing them to be accepted as such—would most diligently conceal his own name and authorship.

### XXXVIII.

Another reason for the authenticity of the writings, which is derived from the idea that a pious, learned, and enlightened man, such as the alleged Dionysius reveals himself to be throughout his works, would not have been capable of such a fraud, is easily dismissed. ## First Chapter.

**Contents.** All knowledge of God must be drawn solely from Holy Scripture; the spiritual cannot be recognized from that which is perceptible to the senses, and God even less so.

One must speak of God only according to Holy Scripture; in it, God communicates the knowledge of His essence to us according to our capacity for understanding.

The mystery of God must not be profanely <note>The German *frevelnd* suggests an act of spiritual rebellion or impious curiosity.</note> investigated; He must be praised from the Scripture. An account of what we learn of His essence from the same.

The names of God are mostly derived from divine attributes and emanations <note>original: *Ausflüssen*. In this context, it refers to the ways the Divine "flows out" into the created world.</note>; in this life we see God only "through a glass darkly" <note>original: *im Räthsel*, literally "in a riddle," a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note>; in heaven He is clearly beheld as He is in Himself; just as we here below can no more grasp Him than we can the state of the blessed. God must be praised from All and from Nothing; positively and negatively <note>This refers to the two paths of theology: *kataphatic* (saying what God is) and *apophatic* (saying what God is not).</note>.

God is simultaneously nameless and many-named.

In what way God is nameless, and yet bears all names.

God is named differently not only according to His attributes—but also according to His appearances.

### §. 2.

Regarding this, as we have called it, super-essential <term>super-essential (German: *überwesentlich*): a key term in this philosophy meaning "above all essence" or "beyond being." It suggests that God does not "exist" in the way a chair or a person exists, but is the source of existence itself.</term> and secret Godhead, nothing may be said or thought except what has been revealed to us by God Himself in the Holy Scriptures. For as the Godhead has kindly spoken of itself in the Holy Scriptures, the knowledge and contemplation of it is inaccessible to all existing beings <note>original: *Seyenden*; refers to anything that has "being" or existence.</note>, because it lies super-essentially beyond them all. Many theologians have celebrated the Godhead not only as invisible and incomprehensible, but also as unsearchable and untraceable, because no trace of it exists for those who wish to penetrate into its secret infinity. Yet none of the existing beings is entirely without a share in the Good; instead, while remaining firmly within itself, the Godhead graciously radiates its super-essential ray into illuminations <note>original: *Erleuchtungen*; the spiritual light or insights given by God to help a soul understand truth.</note> suited to each existing being. It lifts pious spirits toward the contemplation, communion, and likening <note>original: *Aehnlichung*; the process of becoming more like God, often referred to in Greek as *theosis*.</note> possible for them—those spirits which strive toward it with all their strength in holy awe. They neither dare to strive higher than the contemplation of God <note>original: *Gottanschauung*; the spiritual vision or "view" of God.</note> appropriate to them allows—which would be a fruitless arrogance—nor do they waver toward the lowly by yielding to what is base. Instead, they aspire firmly and immovably toward the ray shining down upon them, and with a love suited to the illuminations granted to them, they soar upward with holy awe, sobriety, and piety.

Thus, we look toward the radiant splendor shining upon us in the Holy Scriptures, and by it we are illuminated for divine praise—

### §. 6.

# Chapter Two.

## Concerning the unified and differentiated knowledge of God (Theology), and what divine unity and differentiation are.

---

**Content.** The names of the Good, the Beautiful, the True, the Wise, and others of this kind apply to the entire Trinity, because they belong to God according to His nature, which is the same in the three Persons; and not only essential attributes, but also outward <term>emanations (German: *Ausflüße*): the way God's power flows out into creation</term> are named in this way.

What is said of God as a whole in Holy Scripture, according to His <term>essence (German: *Wesensheit*): the core nature of what God is</term>, must not be divided, and what is said separately or personally <note>Referring to the specific traits of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit</note> must not be conflated.

An exposition of what is said in common of the whole Godhead, and what is said specifically of each individual Person.

The unities in God are called essential attributes, while the differentiations are called emanations; an exposition follows, through an example, of how the three divine Persons are completely united with one another without confusion.

However, they call the "distinctions" the good emanations and radiations of the Godhead. And they say, according to the Holy Scripture, that the aforementioned "union" has its own properties, and conversely, the "distinction" has its own peculiar unions and distinctions. Thus, to the divine union or the super-essentiality of the primal-one Trinity, there is united and held in common: the super-essential existence; the super-divine Godhead; the super-good Goodness; the identity of the complete peculiarity that is exalted above all; the unity exalted above primary unity; the Unutterable; the Multitudinous-voiced <note>original: *Vieltonende*; likely referring to the many names attributed to God in scripture</note>; the Unknownness; the uniquely visible; the affirmation of all things; the negation of all things; and that which is exalted above all affirmation and negation; the persistence (if one may say so) of the united <term>hypostases</term> <note>The individual "persons" or distinct realities of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) who exist as one essence.</note> within one another, their thoroughly super-united stability, mixed in no part; just as the lights of lamps (to use more sensory and common examples) which are in a house, and are entirely within one another mutually, yet have a pure and clear, peculiarly determined distinction from one another, and yet are united in this distinction, and distinct in this union. For thus we see, when there are many lamps in a house, the lights of all are united into a single light, and shine as a single, undivided beam of brightness; and no one could, in my opinion, distinguish the light of one specific lamp from that of the others out of the air that surrounds all the lights, nor see one without the other, because they have all mutually passed into one another without mixing.

If now someone carries one of the torches out of the house, its own entire light will also depart with it, but from that of the other lights...

But someone might object that the seal is not complete and the same in all its impressions. ### §. 7.

But regarding the divine causes of these unifications and distinctions, as we have found them in the Holy Scriptures, we have set them forth to the best of our ability in the *Theological Outlines* <note>A reference to a separate, likely lost or theoretical work by the author dealing with primary theological principles.</note>, treating each one specifically. In that work, we developed and revealed some points through truthful discourse, leading the holy and pure mind toward the clear contemplations of the Holy Scriptures; other points we hinted at as mystical, according to divine tradition, being elevated beyond the power of the mind.

For everything divine, and everything that appears to us, is known only through participation <note>The philosophical idea that created things "participate" in divine qualities (like beauty or goodness) without being the source of those qualities themselves.</note>; but the Divine itself, as it exists according to its own fundamental ground and position, is elevated above all mind, essence <note>original: *Wesenheit*; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>, and knowledge. When we, for example, call that "beyond-essential" secrecy "God," or "Life," or "Essence," or "Light," or "Word," we understand by these names nothing other than the powers which descend from it to us—powers that deify us, communicate essence to us, generate life within us, or grant us wisdom. 

We approach the Divine itself only by setting aside all intellectual activities, for we see no deification, no life, and no essence that would be entirely similar to the Cause that is exalted above all exaltation. Thus, the Father is the primal source <note>original: *Urquell*</note> of the Godhead, while Jesus and the Spirit are—if one may say so—offshoots of divine growth, blossoms, and beyond-essential lights of the primal Godhead. This we have learned from Holy Scripture; but how these things actually relate to one another is neither possible to speak of nor even to imagine.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of divine names, specifically focusing on the relationship between "Causes" (the Divine) and "Effects" (the created or celestial order). ...fatherhood and sonship originate from the primal fatherhood and primal sonship which is elevated above all things, and are granted to the celestial powers. From this source come gods, and sons of gods, and fathers of gods, and god-like spirits; they are named as such from that source because this fatherhood and sonship is communicated to them in a spiritual manner—that is, incorporeally, immaterially, and intellectually. This is possible because the primal divine Spirit is elevated above all intellectual immateriality and deification <note>original: *Göttlichung*; the process of a creature becoming "god-like" or united with God, often called *theosis*.</note>, and Father and Son are most highly removed from all divine fatherhood and sonship.

For there is no exact similarity between the causes and that which is produced by those causes. For the latter receives the images of the causes as far as possible, but the causes themselves exist outside of and are elevated above what they have produced, according to the law of their own unique primal ground. To use ordinary examples: we say that pleasure and pain produce joy and mourning, yet they themselves do not feel joy or mourn. And of fire, which warms and burns, we do not say that it warms and burns itself. And if someone were to say that Primal Life lives, or that Primal Light is itself enlightened, they would, in my opinion, not be speaking correctly—unless they meant it in a different way: that in a higher and more essential sense, whatever exists in the effect pre-exists within the cause. —

### §. 10.
### From the *Theological Outlines* of the most holy Hierotheus.

The Cause of all things, which fills all things—the Divinity of Jesus—sustains the parts that harmonize with the whole. It is neither part nor whole, and yet it is both whole and part, in that it encompasses everything—both part and whole—within itself, while being sublime above both and preceding them. For it is perfect in the imperfect as the primal ground <note>original: *Urgrund*</note> of perfection; yet it is "imperfect" <note>In this mystical context, "imperfect" means that the Divine cannot be limited even by the definition of "perfection"; it is "pre-perfect" or "beyond-perfect."</note> in the perfect, as being beyond-perfect and before-perfect. It is the shaping form in the formless as the primal ground of form; yet it is formless in forms, as being sublime above form. It is an essence <note>original: *Wesenheit*</note> that proceeds unblemished through all essences, and is supra-essential <note>original: *überwesentlich*; existing beyond the nature of ordinary being or substance.</note> above every essence; determining all principles and orders, and yet placed above every principle and every order. It is the measure of all beings <note>original: *Seyenden*</note>; — Eternal—

# Chapter Three.

### On the power of prayer; on the holy Hierotheus, and the reverence with which one must write about divine things.

**Summary.** One must draw near to God through prayer; not because God is distant from us, but so that we might be present to God in spirit and mind. For in prayer, it is not so much that God draws near to us, but that we draw near to Him in spirit.
**Reasons** why he, following the holy <note>Hierotheus was a legendary 1st-century convert and mentor to the author; in reality, these texts were likely written in the 5th or 6th century by an author now called Pseudo-Dionysius.</note> Hierotheus, composed these theological books; at the same time, the praise of Hierotheus, and how they were both present alongside Peter and James at the death of the holy Virgin Mary, and what they did there.
**Explanation** of how lowly and modestly he thinks of himself and his own writings. —

We must first draw near to the Trinity with prayers as the original source of the Good, and then step closer to be initiated into the knowledge of the all-good gifts that rest within it. For while the Trinity is present with all things, not all things are present with it. For she is not in space, such that she could be distant from anything, or pass from one thing to another; indeed, even to say she <note>The author uses the feminine pronoun "she" to refer to the "super-good Trinity" (German: *die Dreifaltigkeit*) or "Primal Goodness" mentioned on the previous page.</note> is in all beings does not yet reach her infinity, which is above all and encompasses all. Or just as if someone standing on a ship kicks at a rock in the sea with his foot, it will have no effect on the firm, unmoved rock, but he will distance himself from the rock, and the more he kicks at it, the further he will push himself away from it. Therefore, it is necessary above all, especially in theology, to begin with prayer; not to pull down the power that is present everywhere and nowhere, but rather, through the remembrance of God and the invocations directed to Him, to deliver ourselves into His hands and unite ourselves with Him.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the necessity of prayer as a prerequisite for theological study. The text now transitions into a defense of the author's decision to write this treatise, addressing why he is providing his own explanations when his mentor, Hierotheus, has already written on these subjects.</meta>

...to treat theological subjects, and had gone through the main content of the entire theology through specific developments, then we would not have been so utterly senseless or foolish as to believe that we could cast a clearer and more divine glance into theological matters, or to undertake a superfluous and vain labor by saying the same thing a second time. Moreover, we would be committing an injustice against our teacher and friend <note>The "teacher and friend" refers to Hierotheus, a legendary figure and purported mentor to Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> if we were to appropriate for ourselves through theft his excellent teaching and enlightenment, in which we were instructed through Saint Paul. 

But because he, in truth, presented divine matters in a weighty manner befitting an elder <note>original: "Greisenart"</note>, giving us only short, comprehensive definitions where he compressed much into a single word, I and the teachers working with me on young souls were tasked with developing and explaining the condensed, comprehensive thoughts that emerged from the spiritual power of that man, using language appropriate to our own level. And you yourself have often urged us to do this, and even sent Hierotheus’s book back to me, as it exceeded your capacity for understanding. 

Therefore, we assign him the position of one exalted above the multitude, as a teacher of perfected and profound thoughts—as a second Holy Scripture which takes the second place after those inspired by God. But to those who stand on the same level as us, we wish to transmit the divine according to our own insight. For if "solid food is for the perfect" <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:14: "But solid food is for the mature."</note>, what perfection does it require to feed others with it? This has now also moved us not to stand back despondently from the exploration of the Divine, so far as it is reachable to us, but—not leaving helpless those who cannot look upon the higher things that are clear to us—to set ourselves to writing. We do not undertake to bring forth anything new, but rather through small, detailed explanations, to lay out and explain what was said in brief by the truly **holy and divine Hierotheus** <note>The mentor of the author; according to tradition, a convert of St. Paul and the first bishop of Athens.</note>.

## Chapter Four.

### Concerning the Good, Light, Beauty, Love, Ecstasy, and Zeal; and that Evil is neither a Being, nor from Being, nor in Being.

**Content** Goodness is the primary attribute of God, and all things exist through divine goodness.
From goodness proceed the orders and duties of the **Angels**, as well as souls and their faculties, and both the animate and inanimate.

->§. 7.<-

This Good is also praised by the holy writers as the Beautiful and as Beauty, as Love and as the Beloved, and by whatever other divine names are fitting for the beautifying and graceful beauty. However, "the beautiful" and "beauty" must be distinguished in the Cause <term>The Cause: *Ursache*, referring to God as the source from which all qualities originate.</term>, which encompasses the whole within the One. ### §. 8.

Three kinds of movement are attributed to the divine spirits: circular movement, in which they are unified in the beginningless and endless radiations of the Beautiful and the Good; straight movement, when they proceed to the supervision of lower things, penetrating everything in a direct path; and oblique movement, when, while looking upon lower things, they remain within their own identity without departing from it, moving incessantly around the Beautiful and the Good—which remains the same—as their foundation.

### §. 9.

The circular movement of the soul is its entering into itself away from external things, and the unifying concentration of its powers, which grants it an unerring quality <note>The "unerring" (*das Unirrende*) refers to a state of stability and truth where the soul is no longer misled by the changing physical world.</note> in a circle, turning it away from the many things existing outside and gathering it, first within itself, then—once it has become one—uniting it with the powers that are already united, and thus leading it to the Beautiful and the Good, which is above all beings, as the One and the Same, without beginning or end. The soul moves obliquely when it is illuminated by divine knowledge according to the measure of its powers—not in a purely spiritual and unified way, but through understanding and discourse <term>Discursive: *discursiv*, referring to step-by-step logical reasoning rather than immediate, intuitive spiritual grasping.</term>, as if with mixed and transitioning activities. Its movement in a straight line, however, consists in its not entering into itself or being moved in unifying spirituality (for that is, as mentioned, its circular movement),

### §. 14.

What might the theologians <note>In this context, "theologians" refers specifically to the biblical writers and early Church Fathers.</note> mean when they call God sometimes *Love* and *Affection* <note>original: "ἔρως und ἀγάπη" (eros and agape)</note> and sometimes the *Beloved* and the *Longed-for* <note>original: "ἐραστὸν καὶ ἀγαπητὸν" (eraston kai agapeton)</note>? Of the former, He is the cause, the producer, and the begetter; but the latter He is Himself. Through the former, He is moved; through the latter, He moves—because He is His own awakener and leads Himself to Himself. 

They call Him "beloved" and "longed-for" because He is beautiful and good. But they call Him *Love* and *Longing* <note>original: "ἔρως καὶ ἀγάπη" (eros and agape)</note> because He is the stirring power that leads upward to Himself. He alone is beautiful and good through Himself, and He is, as it were, a revelation of Himself through Himself. He is a "good outflowing" of the union that transcends all things—a movement that is loving, simple, self-moving, and self-active. This movement pre-exists in the Good, flows out from the Good into all that exists, and then winds back again toward the Good. 

In this, divine love clearly shows its lack of beginning and end—like an eternal circle, moving around the Good, from the Good, in the Good, and toward the Good. It moves in an unerring rotation, always proceeding, remaining, and returning in the same way. Our magnificent teacher <note>A reference to Hierotheus, the mentor of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> has spoken of this same truth with divine inspiration in his *Hymns of Love*, and it is only right to remember them here, placing them like a "sacred head" atop our treatise on love.

In this philosophical context, it refers to anything that exists or has a place in reality.</note></term> strives for the Beautiful and the Good, and does everything it does because it considers it good, and every goal of being has the Good as its beginning and end (for nothing does what it does with a view to the nature of evil), how can evil exist in things that have being, or exist at all, if it is without this striving for the Good? 

And if all being comes from the Good, and the Good is elevated above all being, then in the Good, even <term>non-being<note>original: "das Nichtseyende." This refers to that which does not yet exist or lacks form; the author argues that even "nothingness" is held within the power of the Good.</note></term> is [considered as] being. But evil is either not a being, or if it is, it is not entirely evil—not non-being. For that which is absolutely non-being cannot exist unless it is thought of in the Good in a <term>beyond-essential<note>original: "überwesentliche Weise." A key term in mystical theology meaning a way that transcends the normal categories of "essence" or "existence."</note></term> manner. 

The Good will now be equally elevated above both simple being and non-being. But evil is neither in things that have being nor in things that do not; rather, it is even further removed from the Good than non-being—it is strange to it, and even further from essence. 

But from where, then, does evil come, one might ask? For if there is no evil, then virtue and vice are the same, both in their entirety and in the individual sins and their corresponding virtues; or, that which fights against virtue cannot be evil. And yet, moderation and immoderation, justice and injustice, stand in opposition to one another; and not merely as outward appearances in the just and the unjust, or the moderate and the immoderate. Rather, even before the difference between the virtuous man and his opposite appears outwardly, virtues and vices already stand far apart within the soul, and the passions rebel against the <term>intellect<note>original: "Verstand." Here meaning the higher reasoning faculty that perceives truth.</note></term>. From this it follows necessarily that one must grant an opposite to the Good: namely, Evil. For the Good is not in opposition to itself; instead, having sprouted from one <term>primal ground<note>original: "Urgrund." The foundational source of all things.</note></term> and one causal source, it rejoices in community, unity, and friendship.

However, he acknowledges the moral reality of vice and the internal struggle of the soul as evidence that some form of opposition to the Good must be accounted for.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of evil, specifically addressing the philosophical argument that evil might be a necessary part of the "whole" or a creative force through the destruction of existing things. It continues the translation and commentary of Dionysius the Areopagite's *On the Divine Names*.</meta>

Even the lesser good is not in opposition to the greater, just as a greater degree of heat or cold is not in opposition to a lesser degree of heat or cold. <note>The author argues that differences in degree (more or less good) do not constitute an opposition, whereas evil is a fundamental hostility to the Good.</note> Evil is therefore within <term>beings<note>original: "den Seyenden." Referring to anything that has existence or reality.</note></term> and is itself a being, and is opposed and hostile to the Good. And even if it is the destruction of that which has being, this does not yet cast evil out of the realm of Being; rather, it too will be a being and contribute to the emergence of being. Or does the emergence of one thing not often arise from the destruction of another? In this way, evil would cooperate toward the perfection of the Whole, and through itself would make it possible for this Whole not to be incomplete.

### §. 20.

To this, however, true discourse may reply that evil, as evil, creates no <term>essence<note>original: "Wesenheit." The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note></term> and no <term>becoming<note>original: "Werden." The process of coming into existence or changing.</note></term>, but rather, insofar as it is evil, merely worsens and destroys the <term>substance<note>original: "Substanz." In a philosophical sense, the underlying reality that supports properties.</note></term> of beings. Should someone say that it is generative, and that through the destruction of one thing it grants "becoming" to another, the true answer is: it does not grant becoming *as* destruction. Rather, as destruction and evil, it merely destroys and worsens; but becoming and essence occur through the Good. Thus, evil will be destruction in itself, but generative only through the Good. 

As evil, it is neither a being nor a producer of beings; but through the Good, it is a being, and a good being, and a producer of good. For the same thing cannot be both good and evil in the same respect, nor can the destruction and the becoming of the same thing be the same power in the same respect; nor can there be a <term>primal power<note>original: "Urkraft."</note></term> or a primal destruction. For <term>primal evil<note>original: "Urböse." The concept of an absolute, foundational evil similar to how God is the foundational Good.</note></term>—evil in itself—is neither a being, nor a good, nor a generator, nor a producer of being and the good. ### §. 22.

But evil is also not in the angels. For if the good angel proclaims the divine goodness, he is, through participation on the second level, that which the proclaimed thing is on the first level as its cause. Therefore, evil is not in the angels; but it might be argued that they are evil because they punish sinners. But it is not the state of being punished that is evil, but rather becoming deserving of punishment; nor is it evil to be rightfully excluded from sacred rites, but rather to become wicked and unholy and incapable of the pure mysteries.

In this Neoplatonic context, the author is arguing that evil has no independent "being" or substance; it is not a "thing" that God created, but a hole where a good quality should be.</note></term>, but rather as a deficiency, as a void of the Good that is characteristic of perfection.

### §. 25.

But evil is not present in animals lacking reason either. For if one takes away anger and desire, and the other things called "evil"—which in reality are not so according to their nature—then, for example, the lion would no longer be a lion if one took away its strength and pride; and if the dog were friendly to everyone, it would no longer be a dog; for the dog's particular nature is to be watchful, allowing only the members of the household in and driving away all strangers. Thus, it is not an evil that nature is not destroyed; rather, the <term>destruction of nature<note>meaning the failure of a creature to act according to its specific design or instincts.</note></term>—weakness and a lack of natural qualities, activities, and powers—that is what is evil. And if everything existing in time becomes complete through the process of <term>becoming<note>original: "Werden." The philosophical process of growth and development toward a final purpose.</note></term>, then the incomplete will not exist at all within the whole of nature.

### §. 26.

Evil is also not found in nature as a whole. For if all natural relationships arise from Nature in general, then nothing is fundamentally opposed to her. In individual cases, however, some things will be according to nature, and others will not. For what is against nature for one is not so for another; that is generally the case. The <term>badness<note>original: "κακία" (kakia), a Greek term often translated as vice or moral worthlessness.</note></term> of nature, however, is that which is contrary to it—the deprivation of what is characteristic to it. Thus, there is no such thing as an "evil nature"; rather, the only thing that is evil for nature is when it cannot reach the perfection specific to that particular nature.

But evil is not present in bodies either: for ugliness and disease are a lack of form and a privation of order. This, however, is not an absolute evil, but rather a lesser form of beauty. Here referring to moral or ontological defect.</note></term> for the soul is evident because it is possible for this wickedness to exist even without a body, as is seen in the demons. For all spirits, souls, and bodies, evil consists solely in weakness and the falling away from the possession of the good that is proper to them.

### §. 28.

Furthermore, that oft-repeated claim—that evil resides in <term>matter<note>The fundamental "stuff" or underlying substance of the physical world.</note></term> simply because it is matter—is also incorrect. For matter itself participates in and is receptive to adornment, beauty, and form. But if matter exists outside of these things and is in itself without quality or form, how could matter actually *do* anything, since in and of itself it does not even have the capacity <note>original: "Macht hat zu leiden." In a philosophical sense, this refers to "passivity" or the ability to be acted upon by another force.</note> to be acted upon? And moreover, how could matter be evil? For if it exists in no way and nowhere, it is neither good nor evil. But if it exists in some way, and everything that exists comes from the Good, then matter must also come from the Good. If that were the case, either the Good produces evil, or evil—because it comes from the Good—is actually good; or evil produces the Good; or even the Good—as something coming from evil—is itself evil; or otherwise, there must be two <term>principles<note>Fundamental first causes or "gods" of reality.</note></term> that both depend on yet another higher summit. But if one says that matter is necessary for the fulfillment of the <term>universal whole<note>original: "Weltganzes." The cosmos viewed as a complete and integrated system.</note></term>, then how can matter be an evil? For evil is one thing, and necessity is another. How could the Good bring something into being that arises from evil? Or how could evil even exist...

### §. 25.

But evil is also not found in irrational animals. For if one takes away anger and desire—and the other things that are called "evil," though by their nature they actually are not—the lion, for example, would no longer be a lion if one took away his strength and pride. Furthermore, if the dog were to be friendly toward everyone, he would no longer be a dog; for the dog's own nature is watchfulness, and that he only admits those of the household while driving away all strangers. Therefore, it is not an evil that a nature is not destroyed; rather, the destruction of nature—weakness and the lack of natural qualities, activities, and powers—*that* is evil. And if everything existing in time becomes perfect through the process of "becoming," then that which is imperfect will not exist at all within the whole of nature.

### §. 26.

In the whole of nature, too, evil does not exist. For if all natural relationships arise from Nature in general, then nothing stands in opposition to her. In individual cases, however, some things will be according to nature, while others will not. For something may be "against nature" for one individual while it is not so for another; this is generally the case. The badness <note>original: *κακία* (kakia); a Greek term for vice, defect, or a failure to reach excellence</note> of nature, however, is that which is contrary to it—the deprivation of what is proper to it. Thus, there is no such thing as an "evil nature"; rather, the only thing that is evil for a nature is when it cannot reach the perfection proper to its specific kind.

Evil, however, is either not a being, or if it is, then it is not entirely evil, not a complete non-being. The Good will now be equally exalted above that which simply is and that which is not. Evil, however, is neither in the beings nor in the non-beings, but is removed even further from the Good than non-being; it is alien to it, even more distant from essence <note>the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing</note>. 

But one might say: where then does evil come from? For if there is no evil, then virtue and vice are the same—the whole of vice would be the same as the whole of virtue, and individual sins would be the same as their corresponding virtues; or, that which struggles against virtue could not be evil. And yet, temperance and intemperance, justice and injustice, stand in opposition to one another—and not merely as appearances in the just and the unjust, or the temperate and the intemperate. Rather, even before the difference between the virtuous man and his opponent appears externally, virtues and vices already stand far apart within the soul itself; the passions <note>irrational urges or emotions</note> rebel against the intellect, and from this it necessarily follows that one must grant an opposite to the Good: namely, Evil. For the Good is not in opposition to itself; rather, having sprouted from a primal ground <term>Urgrund: a fundamental, original source or first principle</term> and a primal cause, it delights in community, unity, and friendship.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether evil possesses any independent reality. Even a lesser good is not in opposition to a greater good, just as a greater degree of warmth or cold is not in opposition to a lesser degree of warmth or cold. One might then argue that evil is present within existing things and is itself an existing thing, standing in a hostile opposition to the Good. And if evil is the destruction of an existing thing, this still does not drive that thing out of being <term>Seyn; the state of existence itself</term>; rather, evil itself would be an existing thing and would contribute to the emergence of other existing things. For does the emergence of one thing not often arise from the destruction of another? In this view, evil would cooperate in the perfection of the whole, and through its own presence, make it possible for this whole not to be incomplete.

->§. 20.<-

To this, however, the discourse of truth <note>referring to the correct philosophical or theological argument</note> can respond: evil, as evil, produces neither essence <term>Wesenheit; the fundamental nature that makes a thing what it is</term> nor becoming <term>Werden; the process of coming into existence</term>. Instead, insofar as it is present, it merely degrades and destroys the substance of existing things. If someone were to say that evil is generative—and that through the destruction of one thing it allows another to come into being—the true answer is that it does not grant "becoming" *in its capacity as* destruction. Rather, as destruction and as evil, it only destroys and degrades; "becoming" and essence operate only through the power of the Good. Thus, evil is destruction in and of itself, but it appears generative only through the agency of the Good.

As evil, it is neither an existing thing nor a producer of existing things; however, through the Good, it is an existing thing, a good existing thing, and a producer of the Good. The same thing cannot, in the same relationship, be both good and evil at once; nor can the same power be both the destruction and the becoming of the same thing in the same relationship. This applies even to the primal power <term>Urkraft</term> or the primal destruction. For primal evil—evil in itself—is neither an existing thing, nor a good, nor a generative force, nor something that produces being and the Good. The Good, however, makes everything to which it [is] perfect... <note>The sentence is interrupted at the end of the page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the Good and its relationship to existence. The previous page established that "becoming" and essence are products of the Good, and that evil, as a form of destruction, does not possess its own generative power. This page specifically addresses how even seemingly "evil" or "deficient" things must retain a connection to the Good to remain in existence.</meta>

power to fight against it. Even that which is not at all within the thing is nevertheless that which exists <term>Seyende; the being or that which has existence</term> and can persist. But what is deprived of the Good in every way never was and never could be in any way; it is not, will not be, and cannot be. Take, for instance, the intemperate man <term>Unmäßige; one who lacks self-control or moderation</term>; even if he is partially deprived of the Good regarding his disordered desire <term>Begierde; passionate longing or lust</term>, he is indeed "non-existent" in this specific point and does not strive for true Being; nevertheless, he still participates in the Good through that faint echo of unification <term>Einigung; the state of being made one</term> and friendship. Even wrath <term>Zorn; anger or ire</term> participates in the Good precisely through its being moved and through its striving to set right and transform what appears evil to it according to what appears beautiful to it. And even he who strives after the worst life still participates in the Good because he strives for a "life" at all—which seems best to him—and he participates through the very fact that he strives, and strives for life, and looks toward what he perceives as the best life. And if one were to take away the Good entirely, there would no longer be essence <term>Wesenheit; the fundamental nature of a thing</term>, nor life, nor striving, nor movement; in short, absolutely nothing would exist. For even becoming <term>Werden; the process of coming into being</term>, which arises from destruction <term>Vernichtung; annihilation or perishing</term>, is not a power of evil, but rather a presence of a lesser good, just as sickness <term>Krankheit</term> is a deficiency in the constitution of the body; not of the whole constitution, for in that case the sickness itself could not persist. Instead, the sickness remains and exists because it possesses the most minimal constitution as its essence and persists within it. For that which is entirely without a share in the Good is neither a being nor among those things that exist; that which is mixed, however, is among the beings because of the Good, and is a being and among beings only insofar as it participates in the Good. In the same way, every being itself will stand on a higher or lower level according to the degree to which it participates in the Good. For even regarding existence <term>Seyn; the act of being or state of existence</term> itself: that which is in no way and nowhere a being will not exist. But that which is in one way and not in another "is not" only insofar as it has fallen away from the Eternally Existing <note>The author uses "eternally existing" to describe the divine or absolute reality compared to the transitory nature of worldly things.</note>.

<summary>This page argues that nothing can exist without participating in the Good, as evil is merely a deficiency rather than a positive force. It demonstrates that even negative states like wrath or sickness rely on a "faint echo" or a minimal structure of the Good to maintain their existence.</summary>

Insofar as it has participated in Being <term>Seyn; the pure state of existence or "to be"</term>, it exists; and Being itself overcomes and preserves even that which does not exist. But Evil, which has completely fallen away from the Good, is neither a good on a higher level nor on a lower level. That which is good in one respect but evil in another struggles against a part of the Good, but not against the Good in its entirety; and even this is still overcome by the presence of the Good. Thus, the Good gives essence <term>Wesenheit; the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</term> to its own deprivation <note>The author uses "deprivation" (Beraubung) to describe evil as a lack or a hole in something that should be there, rather than a substance in itself.</note>, insofar as that deprivation participates in it at all. For if evil were to vanish entirely, no Good, no mixed state, and no evil-in-itself would be possible at all. For if evil is an imperfect good due to the complete absence of the Good, then it is only imperfect because the perfect Good is distant. But evil will then only exist and be seen on its own when it is evil to those things which it opposes, having been removed from the Good. For like cannot be caught in mutual strife with like. Thus, evil is not a being <term>Seyendes; a specific thing that exists, such as a rock, a person, or an idea</term>.

->§. 21.<-

But evil is not within things that exist, either. For if everything that exists comes from the Good, and the Good is in all things and encompasses all things, then evil either cannot be in existing things, or it must be in the Good. But it cannot be in the Good (any more than cold can be in fire), and the capacity to be corrupted cannot dwell within that which makes even evil things good. But if it were to exist, how could evil be in the Good? If it were to come from the Good, that would be inadmissible and impossible. For a good tree, as the truth of Holy Scripture says, cannot bring forth bad fruit <note>original: "Matth. 7, 18." Reference to Matthew 7:18: "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit."</note>, nor can the reverse occur. Or, if that is not possible, then both Good and Evil must come from another principle <term>Prinzip; the fundamental source or origin from which something arises</term> and another cause. For no Duality <term>Dyas; a pair of two opposing or distinct principles</term> can be a principle; the Unity <term>Monas; the singular, undivided first cause</term> must be the principle of every Duality. 

Now, it is absurd to allow two completely opposite things to proceed and exist from one and the same source, and to represent the principle itself not as simple and unified, but as divided and twofold and opposed to itself, and in conflict with itself. It is not possible for there to be two mutually opposed principles of existence <term>Seyenden; the collective of all things that have being</term>, and for these to be in conflict with one another, within the whole, and against each other. 

For if this were granted, then God would also not be impassible <note>original: "leidenlos"; referring to the theological concept that God is perfect and therefore cannot be changed, harmed, or moved by external suffering</note> and not without discomfort, because something disturbing to him would be present. Then everything would be disordered and always in conflict with one another. 

The Good, however, imparts friendships to all existing things and is praised by the holy writers as the Primal Peace <term>Urfriede; the original, divine peace from which all harmony flows</term> and as the Giver of Peace. Therefore, all that is good is in friendship with one another and in harmony, having sprouted from one life, ordered together toward one Good, peaceful, similar, and friendly toward one another. 

Thus, evil cannot be in God, nor can it be anything divine. But it is also not *from* God. For either He is not good, or He creates good and brings the good into existence; and [one must ask] whether He brings it forth now and at another time not, or only some things and not all. For in this case, He would suffer a transformation and change, and specifically regarding the most divine aspect of all: namely, as the Cause. 

If the Good in God is a substance <term>Substanz; the underlying essence or reality of a thing</term>, then God, transforming away from the Good, would be at one time a being and at another time a non-being. If, however, He possessed the Good only through participation <note>The philosophical idea that a thing does not "be" the quality itself, but merely "shares" in it, as a window shares in the light of the sun</note>, and from another source, then He would sometimes have it and sometimes not. ### §. 22.

But evil is also not in the angels. For if the good angel proclaims the divine goodness, he is, through participation on the second rank, what the Proclaimed [Goodness] is as the Cause on the first rank. He is, therefore, an image of God, the manifestation of the invisible light, a pure and most transparent mirror—unmarred, unblemished, and undamaged—receiving (if it is permitted to say so) the entire beauty of the well-formed divine image and reflecting back within himself, unmixed (as much as he is able), the goodness of the silence in the secret sanctuary <note>original: "Heiligthum"; referring here to the "adyton" or the most sacred, hidden inner chamber of a temple, symbolizing the inaccessible nature of God</note>. Thus, evil is not in the angels; or [should we say] they are evil because they punish sinners? In the same way, then, those who discipline the errant would be evil, as would the priests who keep the uninitiated <term>Ungeweihten; those who have not been formally admitted into the sacred rites or mysteries</term> away from the divine mysteries. But it is not the act of being punished that is evil, but rather becoming worthy of punishment; and it is not being rightly barred from the holy customs that is evil, but rather becoming sacrilegious and unholy, and incapable of the pure mysteries <term>Geheimnisse; the sacred knowledge or sacraments of the faith</term>.

### §. 23.

Even the demons are not evil by nature. For if they were evil by nature, they would neither originate from the Good nor be counted among the things that have being <term>Seyenden; a philosophical term for all things that exist in the created order</term>. Nor would they have become bad from the Good, because they would be evil by nature and eternally. And furthermore, are they evil to themselves, or to others? If to themselves, then they would destroy themselves; if to others, in what manner are they destructive, and what are they destroying—the essence <term>Wesenheit; the fundamental substance or "whatness" of a thing</term>, the power, or the activity? If they destroy the essence, they would not be acting against nature; for they cannot destroy what is by nature indestructible, but only that which is susceptible to destruction...

But evil is also not found in irrational animals. Thus, it is not an evil that nature is not destroyed; rather, the destruction of nature—weakness and a deficiency of natural characteristics, activities, and powers—that is what is evil. And when everything existing in time becomes perfect through the process of becoming, then the imperfect will not exist at all within the whole of nature.

->§. 26.<-

Evil is also not found in nature as a whole. For if all natural relationships arise from Nature in general, then nothing is opposed to her. In individual cases, however, some things will be in accordance with nature, while others will not. For something is contrary to nature for one being that is not so for another; this is generally the case. But the wickedness <gloss>original Greek: κακία (*kakia*)</gloss> of nature is that which is opposed to it, the deprivation of what is its own, so that no "evil nature" exists; rather, something is only evil for a nature when it cannot achieve the perfection <term>Vollkommenheit; the state of being complete or reaching one's full potential as intended by the Creator</term> proper to that specific nature.

But evil is not in bodies either: for ugliness and disease are a lack of form and a deprivation of order. This, however, is not an absolute evil, but rather a lesser form of beauty. ->§. 28.<-

Nor is that frequently repeated claim correct—that evil resides in matter as matter, as some say. For matter itself partakes in and is receptive to adornment, beauty, and form. But if matter, existing apart from these qualities, were in itself without quality or form, how could matter actually *do* anything, since in and of itself it does not even have the power to be acted upon? And moreover, how could matter be evil? For if it exists in no way and nowhere, it is neither good nor evil. But if it exists in some way, and everything that exists comes from the Good, then matter must also come from the Good. ### §. 29.

Not even the often-mentioned <term>deprivation</term> <note>original: *Beraubung*, translating the philosophical concept of *privatio* or *steresis*. <meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of evil. ### §. 31.

The source of the Good is One. If evil is then set in opposition to the Good, then there are many causes of evil—not only those that produce evil as reasons and powers, but rather "un-power" <note>original: *Unkraft*, a state of impotence or lack of agency</note>, weakness, and the discordant mixing of things that are unlike each other. Evil is also not unmoving and always in the same state; instead, it is limitless, indeterminate, wandering among other limitless things. Even the origin and goal of all evil is the Good. For everything exists for the sake of the Good, both everything good as well as everything opposed to it. For we perform even evil in a longing for the Good (for no one does what they do with the intention of possessing evil); therefore, evil has no foundation or substance, but only a "sham substance" <note>original: *Scheinsubstanz*, likely translating the Neoplatonic concept of *parahypostasis*, an existence that is merely incidental, parasitic, or an unintended byproduct</note>, and it has come into being for the sake of the Good, not for its own sake.

### §. 32.

Thus, one must accept the being of evil as something accidental, which exists for the sake of another and not from its own cause; since in the process of becoming, it certainly [has] a right...
