<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of evil. The previous page established that evil is not an independent creative force and does not originate from matter itself, but rather exists as a parasitic "deprivation" of the Good. This section now examines whether the soul can be considered a cause of evil.</meta>

...it seems that because it occurs for the sake of the Good, it is not actually something "right" or "just," <note>original: *kein Rechtes*, implying it lacks legal or moral standing in the order of the universe</note> because we mistake the "non-good" for something good. It has been proven that that which is striven for is one thing, and that which actually occurs is another. — Evil is therefore outside the path, outside the goal, outside nature, outside the cause, outside the principle, outside the limit, outside the will, outside the substance <note>original: *Substanz*, referring to the fundamental essence of a thing</note>. Evil is thus deprivation, deficiency, and weakness; it is disharmony, failure, aimlessness, ugliness, lifelessness, irrationality, mindlessness, incompleteness, instability, causelessness, indeterminacy, un-begottenness, inactivity, sluggishness, disorder, dissimilarity, infinity, darkness, non-essentiality—nowhere and in no way having any being in itself. How then can evil achieve anything at all through its mixture with the Good? For whatever is entirely without a share in the Good is neither "something" nor can it "do" something. If the Good is a Being, a willing force, a power, and an activity, how can its opposite—which is deprived of essence, will, power, and activity—be capable of anything? Evil is not the same for everyone, in every way, or in the same manner. For a daemon <note>original: *Dämon*; in this philosophical context, this refers to a spiritual mediator or minor deity, not necessarily an evil spirit</note>, evil is to be outside the good-forming spirit; for the soul, it is to be outside of reason <note>original: *λόγος* (logos), the rational principle or intellect</note>; for the body, it is to be outside of its nature.

### §. 33.

But how can evil exist at all, given that there is a Providence? <note>the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note> Evil as "evil" is neither a Being nor is it found among those things that have Being. And no Being exists without the care of Providence. No "existing evil" exists unmixed with the Good; and since no Being is without some participation in the Good, while evil is the lack of Good—and yet no Being is entirely deprived of the Good—it follows that divine Providence is in all Beings, and no Being is without its care.

But even those who have become evil are kindly directed by Providence toward their own or the general good, and Providence cares for every being in a manner appropriate to its nature. Therefore, as the Providence which preserves each individual nature, it cares for those who move themselves as self-moving beings, and for the whole and the individual according to the whole and the individual, so far as the nature of those being cared for can receive the Good of Providence—which is communicated to each accordingly and spreads itself universally over the whole.

->§. 34.<-

Whatever the daemons <note>original: *Dämonen*; in this Neoplatonic Christian context, these are spiritual beings or fallen angels, not merely "monsters."</note> are, they are so from the Good and they are good. The evil in them comes from the falling away from their own Good; it is a change in their sameness <note>original: *Einerleiheit*; this refers to the consistency or integrity of their original spiritual essence.</note>, a weakness of their state, and of the angelic perfection that befits them. And they strive for the Good insofar as they strive for Being, for life, and for thought. And insofar as they do not strive for the Good, they strive for non-being. And this is not actually a striving, but a failure of actual striving.

I now desire to praise these divine names which proclaim Providence <term>Providence: *Vorsehung*; God's ongoing care and guidance of the universe</term>. We do not promise to express the primordial, supersubstantial <term>supersubstantial: *überwesentlich*; existing beyond or above the nature of created substance or essence</term> Goodness and Essence, nor the Life and Wisdom of the primordial, supersubstantial Godhead; for that is exalted in secret—as the Scripture says—above all goodness, and Godhead, and essence, and wisdom, and life. ### §. 9.

But if the philosopher **Clement** <note>Likely referring to Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Scripture.</note> asserts that Prototypes might also be assumed for other things which are among the higher beings, then his discourse does not proceed through proper, perfect, and simple names; yet even granting that this assumption might be correct, one must still always remember the Holy Scripture which says: "I have not shown you this so that you should go after them"; rather, we are led up to the Cause of all things, as much as we are able, through the knowledge that is appropriate to these matters. The beginning and end of all **being** <term>being: *Seyenden*; refers to everything that exists, whether physical or spiritual.</term> is thus the **Pre-existent One** <note>original: *Vorseyende*; a title for God expressing that He exists prior to and independent of all created things.</note>; He is the Beginning, as the Cause, and the End, as that for whose sake all things exist; as the Limit of all things, and as the Infinity of every infinity and limit, being exalted above both, as He is above all opposites. ## Chapter Seven.

### Of Wisdom, Mind, Understanding, Truth, and Faith.

**Contents.** The Wisdom of God is the Creatress of all wisdom, and exists unsearchably and incomprehensibly exalted above all wisdom; it is not to be measured by our wisdom.

From that Wisdom, the angels derive their intellectual (spiritual) nature, humans their rational nature, and other creatures their sensory nature. Why God knows all things without any activity, and how He anticipates everything in His knowledge and knows it within Himself through the knowledge of Himself; and how the angels also grasp sensory things in an intellectual manner.

God, as He is in Himself, is unknown to us; He is known partly through concepts and partly without concepts, and this knowledge is more divine and truer than the former.

### §. 2.

From this Wisdom, the intellectual and intelligible powers of the angelic spirits derive their simple and blessed intelligences. They do not gather divine knowledge through divided means, or from the divided, nor from sensory perceptions or logical deductions <note>original: *Schlußfolgen*. In this philosophical tradition, "discursive" reasoning—moving step-by-step from one thought to another—is considered a lower form of understanding than the immediate, intuitive "seeing" of the angels.</note>. Neither do they grasp this knowledge from anything common to many things; rather, being purely free from all that is material and from all physical mass, they recognize the intellectual nature of the Divine in a spiritual, immaterial, and singular way. They possess an intelligible power and activity that shines with unmixed, unstained purity. This power gazes upon divine knowledge in a state of undividedness and freedom from matter. Through the Divine One, they are shaped—according to their capacity—by divine wisdom and the "super-wise" Spirit and Mind. 

The souls of humans, by contrast, possess the power of understanding through logical deductions, moving in a circle around the truth of existing things. In their divided and multifaceted variety, they lose the singular unity of the angelic spirits. However, by gathering the "many" into "one," <note>This refers to the process of "synthesis" or "recollection," where the human mind tries to find the single underlying principle behind many different observations.</note> they also strive to emulate the angelic spirits, as far as is possible and attainable for souls. 

Furthermore, one would not stray far from the truth who called even sensory perceptions an echo of Wisdom. For even the spirit of demons, insofar as it is spirit, originates from this same Wisdom. But insofar as this spirit neither knows nor understands how to reach what it strives for—lacking both knowledge and right will—it may more properly be called a "falling away" from wisdom.

## Chapter Eight.

### Concerning Power, Justice, Salvation, and Redemption; also concerning Inequality.

**Content.** How God, who is nevertheless beyond all might and power, is still called Might and Power.
God is called Might or Power for this reason: because He is almighty and the Author <note>original: *Urheber*</note> of all might and power.
How the divine Omnipotence permeates all things.
It communicates to the angels all the power and strength that they possess.
In the same way, it strengthens humans, animals, and everything else, and maintains them in their proper state.
It is a sign of the highest power that God cannot deny Himself <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:13; in this theological context, God's "inability" to be inconsistent with His own nature is seen as the ultimate expression of His power, not a limitation</note>.
Why God is also called Justice, and how He fulfills that office.

### Why God allows the saints to be afflicted in this world.

->§. 1.<-

But, because the holy writers also praise divine Truth and all-wise Wisdom as Power and as Justice, and call them Salvation and Redemption, let us also explain these divine names to the best of our ability. That God is exalted above and beyond all power, however it may be or be conceived, will surely be known to anyone who has been nourished by the Holy Scriptures. For the Holy Scripture often calls Him "the Lordship" <note>This refers to God's absolute sovereignty, distinguishing Him even from the "Dominions" or "Powers" within the traditional angelic hierarchy</note> and distinguishes Him even from the super-celestial powers. How then can the holy writers praise Him, who is exalted above all power, as Power; or in what sense should we understand the name of Power in Him?

->§. 2.<-

We say, then, that God is Power because He contains all power within Himself beforehand and possesses it to a pre-eminent degree; as the Author <note>original: *Ursächer*</note> of all power, who brings everything into existence with unyielding, limitless power; and as the one who is the cause of the very being of power itself, whether in its totality or in its individual parts. He is infinitely powerful, not only because He brings all power into being, but also because He stands above all power and even above "Power-in-itself." Furthermore, He is able, to a super-exalted degree, to produce infinitely many other powers besides those that currently exist. He can do what limitless and infinitely produced powers can never do: He can never exhaust the "super-infinite" production of His power-giving strength. It is also through the ineffable, unknowable, and unfathomable <note>original: *undankbare*; in this archaic context, it suggests a quality that is so vast it cannot be "repaid" or fully grasped by the recipient</note> nature of His power that He towers over all things, and through the abundance of His strength, He [strengthens] the weak...

## Chapter Nine.

### Concerning Great, Small, One and the Same, Other, Similar, Dissimilar, Rest, Motion, and Equality.

**Contents.** God is called great, small, one and the same, and another in the Holy Scripture.
In what sense is God called "great"?
In what sense is He called "small," "one and the same," or "another"?
How should we understand it when length, breadth, and depth are used as predicates for God?
In what sense is God called "similar," given that the Cause and its effects are not actually similar?
In what sense is He called "dissimilar"?
How should we understand the description of Him standing or sitting?
How can God move, and what is His threefold motion?
Why is He called "the Equal"?

### §. 1.

**S**ince the All-Cause <term>Allursacher (the primary source of all existence)</term> is also given the epithets "great" and "small," as well as "the same" and "another," "similar" and "dissimilar," and "rest" and "motion," we shall also contemplate the images of these Divine Names as far as they are clear to us. God is praised in the Holy Scripture as "great" and as existing "in greatness"; and then again, He is found in the "gentle breeze," which signifies the divine "smallness" <note>This refers to the biblical story of Elijah (1 Kings 19:11-12), where God was not in the wind or earthquake, but in a "still, small voice."</note>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of divine attributes from Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite's *On the Divine Names*. Having discussed "Otherness" and symbolic dimensions on the previous page, the author now turns to the concept of "Divine Likeness" and the paradox of God being both like and unlike His creation.</meta>

...divine likeness to those who turn toward Him, by imitating—to the best of their ability—the One who is exalted above all limits and comprehension. This is the power of divine likeness: it turns all things brought into existence back toward the **Cause** <note>original: "Ursächlichen"; referring to God as the source from which all things originate.</note>. Because of this, we must say that the creature is like God and bears God's image and likeness. However, we must not say that God is like His creatures, just as we would not say that a man is "like" his own portrait. Things that exist on the same level can be like each other in a mutual way; they share a similar form that exists in both. But between the Cause and that which the Cause produces, we cannot assume this kind of reciprocity. God does not simply grant likeness to this or that individual; rather, He is the source of likeness for everyone who shares in it. He is the creator of **Primordial Likeness** <note>original: "Urähnlichkeit"; the original archetype or "first likeness" from which all other similarities are derived.</note> itself, and the likeness found in all beings is like a trace of divine likeness that brings about their union.

->§. 7.<-

But why do we speak of this? **Holy Scripture** itself says that He is "unlike," that He cannot be compared to anything, and that He is distinct from everything that exists. Most strikingly, the scriptures say that nothing is like Him. Yet, this statement does not contradict the possibility of being like Him. For God is simultaneously **like** and **unlike**: He is "like" in regard to our possible imitation of the **Inimitable** <note>original: "Unnachahmbaren"; referring to the paradox that we try to model ourselves after a God who is ultimately beyond any comparison.</note>, and "unlike" in consideration of the distance between the effect and its Cause—a distance characterized by boundless measures and indeterminable gaps that separate the two.

### §. 9.

What does it mean when the Holy Scriptures say further that the Unmoved extends over all things and is moved toward all? Must this not also be understood in a manner **worthy of God** <note>original: "Gottgemäßen"; a translation of the Greek "theoprepōs," meaning in a way that does not insult the divine nature with human limitations.</note>? For the pious man must believe that God moves not in spatial progress, nor in change, or becoming-other, or transformation, or local movement—whether it be straight or circular, or composed of both; nor in a mental, or soulful, or natural movement. Rather, God moves in that He brings all things into **being** <note>original: "Wesenheit"; essence or existence.</note>, preserves all things, and provides for all with manifold **Providence** <note>original: "Vorsorge".</note>, and is present to all in an incomprehensible embrace, and through His providential **outflows** <note>original: "Ausflüsse"; refers to the emanations or the "procession" of God's power into the world.</note> and activities upon all.

In this way, the movements of God the Unmoved can be praised in a manner worthy of God. The **straight movement** must then be understood as His unbending nature and the unswerving outflow of His activities, and the origin of the entire world from Him. The **oblique movement** <note>original: "schiefe Bewegung"; sometimes translated as "spiral" movement.</note> refers to His constant outflow and His generative stability. The **circular movement**, however, refers to His sameness, and the encompassing of the middle and the extremes—which encompass and are encompassed—and the **turning back** <note>original: "Hinwendung"; the Neoplatonic concept of "epistrophē," where the created effect turns back toward its divine Cause.</note> of that which has gone out from Him, back toward Him. —

### §. 10.

If, however, someone understands the names of **The One**, **The Same**, and **The Just** in Holy Scripture as though God were called **The Equal**, then it must be noted that God is called equal not only because He is without parts and subject to no deviation, but also because He brings His influence uniformly through all and into all things, as the Author of **Primal Equality** <note>original: "Urgleichheit"; the foundational principle of balance and symmetry in creation.</note>. Through this, He effects the uniform interpenetration of all things with one another, and the equal participation of all participants according to each one's capacity, and that equal distribution to all according to the worthiness of each individual. This encompasses the general equality of the **intelligible** <note>entities perceived by the mind alone</note> and **intellectual** <note>relating to the faculty of understanding</note>, of the rational, the sensible, the essential, the natural, and the voluntary—all of which He has pre-embraced in the highest sense and as a unity within Himself, according to the all-surpassing power of universal equality.

->§. 2.<-

One must, however, use "time," "day," "period" in general, and "eternity" in a **God-befitting** <note>original: "Gottgemäß"; in a way that is appropriate to the divine nature rather than human limitations.</note> manner for Him, as He who remains unchangeable and unmoved in all movement, and always remains in Himself in eternal motion, and is the Author of eternity, time, and days. Therefore, in the holy divine manifestations <note>original: "Gotterscheinungen"; theophanies or visions where God appears in human form, such as in the Book of Daniel.</note> of mystical visions, He is depicted both as an old man and as young; the first to designate the Ancient One who is from the beginning, the other to indicate Him who never grows old; or both shall teach that He passes through all things from the beginning to the end; or, as our divine teacher says, both reveal the age of God: the **Old One** points to the first in time, the **Young One** to the older according to number; for the **Monad** <term>Monas: the number "one," representing absolute unity and the source from which all other numbers flow.</term> and what is around the Monad holds a higher place than the number that has gone further out.

### §. 2.

He is called **One** because He is all-unifying according to the transcendence of the single Unity, and is the cause of the "one" for all things without, however, departing from Himself. # Chapter One.
## On the Divine Darkness.

**Contents.** Invocation of the Holy Trinity. To mystical contemplation one must ascend through the renunciation of ourselves and all things that exist.

How one must proceed in divine matters through affirmations and through negations <note>These refer to "Kataphatic" (positive) and "Apophatic" (negative) theology—speaking of what God is, versus what God is not.</note>.

What a concise and a detailed theology are; what darkness is, and how to reach it.

---

->§. 1.<-

Beyond-essential, beyond-divine, beyond-good Trinity, Overseer of Christian divine wisdom, lead us to the beyond-unknown, beyond-shining, highest summit of mystical sayings, where the simple, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of theology are unveiled in the beyond-light darkness of the mystically secret silence; which darkness shines most brightly in the deepest gloom and, in that which is completely untouchable and invisible, overfills the eyeless spirits with beyond-beautiful radiance. This is my prayer. 

But you, my dear Timothy, in your initial effort concerning mystical contemplations <note>original: *mystische Beschauung* — a deep, prayerful observation or experience of divine truth</note>, leave behind the sensory perceptions and the activities of the mind, and all things sensible and intelligible <note>original: *Intelligible* — things that can be understood by the intellect rather than the physical senses</note>, all non-being and being, and rise without the help of ordinary knowledge to union with Him who is beyond all essence and knowledge. For by detaching yourself from yourself and all others in an incomprehensible and absolute way, you will be led up to the ray of the divine darkness, once you have removed everything and been released from everything.

### §. 2.

But take care that none of the uninitiated <note>original: *Ungeweihten* — those who have not been admitted to the sacred mysteries</note> hear this—I mean those who are caught up in things that exist <note>original: *Seyenden* — the realm of created beings and material existence</note>, and who imagine that nothing "beyond-essentially" <note>original: *überwesentlich* — transcending the nature of essence or being itself</note> exists above existing things. These are people who believe they can grasp with their own understanding Him who has "made the darkness His dwelling place." If the holy mystical teachings exceed the reach of such people, what should one say of those even less initiated? They imagine the Cause of all things—which is exalted above all—to be like the lowest among created beings. They say this Cause is in no way superior to the godless forms they have fashioned, which are of many shapes. Yet one must attribute to this Cause everything that is found in created beings, as it is the Cause of all; and then one must again deny all these things to it in the most proper sense, as it is exalted above all. One should not believe that these negations contradict the affirmations, but rather that the Cause stands high above all privations <note>original: *Beraubungen* — a philosophical term for the lack or absence of a quality</note>, exalted above all affirmations and negations alike.

### §. 3.

Therefore, the holy Bartholomew says that Holy Scripture is at once much <note>original: *πολλὴν* — much or many</note> and very little; and the Gospel is wide and great, and yet at the same time condensed and narrow. It seems to me that he understood this in a supernatural sense: namely, that the good Cause of all is simultaneously many-worded, brief-worded, and wordless. It possesses neither speech nor intelligence because it lies beyond-essentially above all things. It appears unveiled and truly only to those who pass through all that is polluted and pure, and who climb beyond every ascent of all holy heights, leaving behind all divine lights and sounds and heavenly speech, and plunge themselves into the darkness where, according to Holy Scripture, He truly is who is beyond all. And not without reason is the holy Moses be—

<meta>This page concludes the third chapter of the treatise and begins the fourth. the more we turn toward the Sublime, the more words are compressed by the contemplation of spiritual objects; just as now, as we enter the darkness that transcends the mind, we will find not only brevity of speech, but total silence and the cessation of all mental understanding. In the first treatises, discourse descended from the highest things to the lowest and expanded into a corresponding fullness as it moved downward. Or is He not more truly Life and Goodness than air or stone? And is He not more speakable and thinkable than He is "drunken" or "angry"? <note>Dionysius argues that while God is beyond all words, it is "more true" to call Him Good than to call Him a rock; however, to reach the truth of God, one must eventually negate even the highest names like "Life."</note>

# Second Letter.
->To the same Monk Kaius.<- <note>As noted previously, "Therapeut" refers to a "servant of God" or member of an early ascetic community.</note>

*Contents: How God is the prime principle of divinity and goodness—specifically of that which is communicated and created.*

You ask how He who is exalted above all also stands above the prime principle of divinity and goodness. My answer is this: you must consider "divinity" and "goodness" as the very essence of the gift that makes us good and divine—as the inimitable imitation of Him who is exalted above God and above the Good, through which we are divinized and made good. For even if this gift is the principle by which we, the divinized and perfected, are made so, He who is exalted above every principle—and above all so-called divinity and goodness—stands higher than the principle of God and Goodness. He is higher insofar as He is inimitable and incomprehensible, lying beyond all imitation and grasping, and beyond both those who are imitated and those who grasp. <note>Dionysius distinguishes between God's unreachable essence and the "energies" or gifts (like goodness) that He shares with humanity. God is not just good; He is the source of the very concept of goodness.</note>

# Third Letter.
->To the same Kaius.<-

*Contents: What the word "suddenly" <note>original: *εξαίφνης* (exaiphnes)</note> signifies, especially when used in relation to the Incarnation.*

"Suddenly" refers to that which comes to light unexpectedly and out of the previously invisible. But when used in reference to the <term>Incarnation<note>The Christian doctrine of God becoming human in the person of Jesus Christ.</note></term> of Christ, I believe Holy Scripture intends to suggest that the <term>Super-essential<note>original: *Ueberwesentliche*. A core Dionysian term meaning "beyond all being" or "above all essence."</note></term> emerged from His hidden state to assume human essence, appearing visibly among us. Yet even after His appearance, He remains hidden—or to put it more divinely, He is hidden even within the appearance itself. For this "hiddenness" of Jesus remains concealed, and His mystery cannot be expressed by any word or any reason; even when spoken, it remains unutterable, and even when perceived, it remains unknown. <note>This highlights the "apostatic" or "negative" theology of the author: even when God reveals Himself in human form, the infinite mystery of His nature remains beyond human understanding.</note>

# Fourth Letter.
## To the same Gaius, the Servant of God. <note>The term "Therapeut" (servant/attendant) was used by Dionysius to describe a monk or a member of a dedicated religious community.</note>

**Contents.** Christ was at once truly human, and as the God-man, He took on human nature in a supernatural way.

You ask how Jesus, who is exalted above all, has stepped into the same rank as all men according to His essence. For He is not called "man" here merely as the Creator of men, but as one who, according to His entire essence, is a truly existing man. 

However, we do not define the concept of Jesus as that of a mere human; for He is not merely a human (not only <term>super-essential<note>Original: *überwesentlich*. This refers to the state of being beyond "essence" or "being" altogether, a state attributed only to the Divine.</note> alone and not human alone), but truly a human being, who out of immense love for humanity is at once above humanity and on the same level with them. He, the Super-essential one, has taken on essence from the essence of humans. Nevertheless, He, the eternally Super-essential, is overflowing with super-essence through its very abundance; truly entering into the realm of essence, He took it on super-essentially, and, while remaining exalted above men, He performs human actions. 

Evidence for this is found in the Virgin, who gives birth supernaturally, and the otherwise yielding, unstable water, which bore the weight of material earthly feet and did not give way, but stood firm in supernatural power without dissolving. <note>These are references to the Virgin Birth and the miracle of Jesus walking on the Sea of Galilee.</note> Who would wish to cite the many other examples! From these, the one who sees in a divine manner will recognize—in a way exalted above reason—that even what is said regarding the humanity of Jesus possesses the power of <term>overflowing negation<note>Original: *überschwengliche Verneinung*. This is a core concept in "apophatic" or "negative" theology: God is so great that we can only describe Him by "negating" or saying what He is not, because He exceeds all human categories.</note>. 

To put it briefly: He was not a man as if He were not a man, but as one born of men, He became truly human while remaining exalted above humans and existing far beyond them. Furthermore, He did not perform divine acts simply as God, nor human acts... <note>The text breaks off here; the author is likely about to explain that Christ performed "theandric" or "God-man" actions that combined both natures.</note>

## Fifth Letter.
->To Dorotheus the Liturgist.<-

---

**Contents.** An explanation of the Divine Darkness, which is discussed in the book *On Mystical Theology*.

The Divine Darkness is the "unapproachable light" in which, according to the Scriptures, God dwells. Thus, God is invisible because of the sheer abundance of light, and He is unapproachable because of the transcendence of His <term>super-essential<note>Original: *überwesentlichen*. This describes a state of being that is "above essence," meaning God exists beyond the very categories of "being" or "existence" as humans understand them.</note>> outpouring of light. Everyone who is deemed worthy to see and to know God arrives at this Darkness precisely through the act of "not-seeing" and "not-knowing," for they have entered a state that is exalted above all sight and knowledge. They recognize this very truth: that God exists beyond everything that can be perceived by the senses or the mind. In this way, the seeker agrees with the prophetic saying: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, and too high; I cannot attain it" (Psalm 139:6). 

So too do the Scriptures say that Saint Paul "knew" God by recognizing Him as the one who stands above all spiritual and intellectual knowledge. For this reason, Paul says that His ways are unsearchable (Romans 11:33), His judgments are incomprehensible, His gifts are unspeakable, and His peace surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7). Paul had found Him who is above all things; with a power higher than mere intellectual knowledge, he had recognized that the Cause of all is Himself exalted above all. <note>This "Divine Darkness" is a key concept in "Apophatic" or negative theology. It suggests that God is not "dark" because of a lack of light, but rather because His "light" is so intense it blinds the limited human intellect, appearing as darkness.</note>

# Sixth Letter.
## To the Presbyter Sosipater.

**Summary.** Sosipater should not occupy himself with the discovery and refutation of false opinions, but rather with the establishment of the truth.

Do not consider it a victory, venerable Sosipater, to strike out violently against a form of worship or a religious opinion that does not seem good. For even if you refute it with the utmost sharpness, your own cause, Sosipater, is not yet established because of that. For it is possible for the one <term>Being<note>Original German: *Seyende*. In this theological context, it refers to the ultimate Reality or God as the source of all existence.</note>>, the hidden and the true, to remain concealed from you and others amidst many errors and appearances of truth. For if something is not red, it is not therefore immediately white; or if something is not a horse, it is not necessarily and immediately a human being. If you follow my advice, you will do this: you will cease speaking against others, but instead speak for the truth in such a way that what you say is entirely irrefutable.

---

# Eighth Letter.
## To the monk <term>Demophilus<note>The name Demophilus literally means "friend of the people" in Greek.</note></term>, concerning one’s own work and grace.

**Contents.** The distinguished friends of God—Moses, David, Job, Abel, and Joseph—are praised especially for being gentle; in Jesus Himself, grace and gentleness shine above all else. In contrast, the harshness of Demophilus is rebuked, as he had treated a repentant person, who had been absolved by a priest, with cruel severity, and had behaved rashly toward the priest himself for granting that absolution. Dionysius frightens him with examples of those who were punished for such severity.
He presents the objections of Demophilus in the most plausible way and refutes them.
Inferiors, such as Demophilus, must never criticize their superiors or those who stand higher than they.
Order and subordination must be observed everywhere, following the example of the good and gentle shepherd, Christ.
One must imitate Christ’s gentleness more than the zeal of Elijah. The difference between the rewards of the gentle and the harsh.
Description of the vision which Saint Carpus had.

---

->§. 1.<-

The stories of the Hebrews say, my dear Demophilus, that even that holy Moses was deemed worthy of the vision of God because of his gentleness <note>original: *Sanftmuth*; often translated as "meekness" in biblical contexts regarding Moses.</note>. And if they ever report that he was outside the vision of God, they first report that he had departed from gentleness, and then they exclude him from the vision of God. For they say that when he became very proud and stubborn, and resisted the divine counsels, the Lord became angry. But when they praise him for the honors he received from God, they do so especially by mentioning his extraordinary effort to imitate divine goodness. For he was very gentle, and for this reason he is called a servant of God.

### §. 4.

Therefore, rein in your own speech, your zeal, and your passion as is fitting, and prescribe to them what is their due; but for yourself, look to the Liturgists <term>Liturgen: in the Dionysian hierarchy, this refers specifically to the rank of Deacons</term>, to these the Priests, to the Priests the Hierarchs <term>Hierarchen: the highest rank of the clergy, equivalent to Bishops</term>, and to the Hierarchs the Apostles and the successors of the Apostles. And if one of those fails in what is fitting for him, he shall be corrected by those believers who stand on the same level as him, so that one order is not thrown over the other, but each remains in his own rank and in his own service. This, then, is what we have to say to you.

# Ninth Letter.

## To the <term>Hierarch Titus<note>A high-ranking member of the church hierarchy. Titus was a companion of the Apostle Paul, to whom this fictionalized letter is addressed.</note></term>, who had asked him in a letter what the house of Wisdom was, what her cup, what her food, and her drink.

**Summary. *Symbolic theology* causes many absurd images and ideas among the uninstructed and ignorant. Herein is the explanation of various *symbols* occurring in Holy Scripture. Division of *theology* into *mystical* and *demonstrative*, and the parts of both *theologies*.**
**The various *symbols* are to be interpreted in different ways.**
**What one must think of fire when it is used for *God* and the *angels*. What food signifies.**
**Mystical meaning of the cup.**
**Meaning of liquid and solid food.**
**God's drunkenness and the reclining of the blessed in heaven.**
**Sleep and awakening of *God*.**

---

The holy *Hierotheus* <note>Hierotheus is presented as the teacher of Dionysius; scholars generally consider him a literary device to link these writings to the apostolic age.</note>, my dear *Titus*, surely heard all the *theological symbols* I explained before his departure. For in my work on *symbolic theology* <note>original: "symbolischen Theologie." Dionysius frequently refers to this treatise, though no such work by him has survived, leading some to believe it was a planned work or a literary reference to enhance his authority.</note>, I clearly set out for him everything that the Holy Scriptures seem to say about *God* that appears wondrous to the majority of believers. For the Fathers of unspeakable Wisdom <note>Referring to the biblical authors and early church teachers.</note> would stain the souls of the uninitiated with terrifying absurdity if they were to explain the divine, mystical truth—inaccessible to the uninitiated—through anything other than secret and bold riddles <note>original: "Räthselbilder." These are enigmatic images or allegories used to protect sacred truths from being trivialized.</note>. Therefore, we often do not believe the words that speak of divine mysteries, because we see them only through the sensory *symbols* forced upon them.

### §. 5.

This holy revelation of the feast simultaneously explains why God—the <term>Universal Cause</term> <note>original: "Allursächliche"; the source or primary cause of all that is good.</note> of all good—is represented as being <term>drunk</term> <note>original: "trunken"; in mystical theology, this is a metaphor for the "sober intoxication" of the soul or the overflowing abundance of the Divine.</note>. For just as with us drunkenness, taken in the negative sense, is an immoderate overfilling and a deprivation of sense and spirit, so must one think of drunkenness in God in a better sense. # Tenth Letter
## To the Theologian John, the Apostle and Evangelist, in his exile on the island of Patmos.

**Content.** Announcement to John, exiled on Patmos, that he will soon be freed and will return to Asia for the great benefit of his congregations.

<meta>This page transitions from the list of historical authorities (Le Nourry, Tillemont, etc.) to a critical discussion of the arguments regarding the authenticity of the Dionysian writings. It specifically addresses the scholarly debt owed to earlier critics and the importance of accurate dating for the history of Christian doctrine.</meta>

The treatise by **Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), also known as Dalläus, was a prominent French Protestant theologian who was among the first to prove that the works of Dionysius the Areopagite were later forgeries.</note> contains the primary arguments against the authenticity of the Areopagite writings. In the condensed summary that precedes the translation of these works, we have consistently presented them as the property of **Daillé**, although we are well aware that he owes the most striking of these arguments to **Morinus** <note>Jean Morin (1591–1659), a French priest and scholar whose work on liturgy and church orders influenced many later historians.</note>, who put them forward in his book ***On Holy Orders*** <note>original Latin: *de ordinibus*</note>. 

In our time, this question carries hardly any polemical interest, since even the reviewer of **Kaufmann’s** translation <note>A contemporary 19th-century translation of the Dionysian corpus into German.</note> of the *Heavenly Hierarchy* in the ***Literary Journal for Catholic Religious Teachers*** has recently and unreservedly admitted the later origin of these writings. When Protestant scholars speak of this with caution or doubt, however, it stems either from ignorance of the subject matter—as is the case in the *Letters on Ancient and Modern Mysticism*—or from a conscientiousness intimidated by the results of so-called **higher criticism** <term>A method of historical and literary analysis that seeks to determine the original context, date, and authorship of ancient texts.</term>, which treads softly on such uncertain ground to avoid any possible misstep. Or, finally, a preconceived hypothesis unhesitatingly pulls everything that might serve its purpose into its orbit for support. 

For this very reason, a complete exposition of all the external grounds that argue against the authenticity of the present writings and in favor of their later origin is not at all out of place right now. Regardless, the question always retains a purely scientific interest; for it cannot be a matter of indifference to determine at what time such a mass of **Neoplatonic ideas** <term>A school of mystical philosophy that originated in the 3rd century; its concepts of hierarchy and the "unknowable God" deeply influenced Christian theology.</term> penetrated the Church under the protection of a sacred name. Furthermore, the explanation of later phenomena in the field of the **history of dogma** <term>The study of how Christian doctrines and official teachings evolved and were codified over the centuries.</term> only becomes possible and productive through such a chronological determination.

<summary>The author argues that while the "Areopagite writings" are widely accepted as later forgeries, a detailed historical critique is still necessary to understand how Neoplatonic philosophy was integrated into early Church doctrine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the scholarly debate surrounding the authenticity of the writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, moving from Jean Daillé to the analysis of the Benedictine scholar Nicolas le Nourry.</meta>

— 208 —

According to **Daillé**, the excellent **le Nourry** <note>Denis-Nicolas Le Nourry (1647–1724) was a French Benedictine monk and scholar known for his rigorous historical analysis of early Christian texts.</note> has most carefully occupied himself with investigations into our writings in his ***Apparatus for the Great Library of the Ancient Fathers*** <note>original Latin: *adparatus ad bibliothecam maximam veterum patrum*, published in Paris, 1703</note>. From page 170 to 210 of his work, he first gives a condensed excerpt from the works of Dionysius in five paragraphs of the first chapter. The second chapter then presents the entire state of the controversy regarding Dionysius and indicates the course of the treatise. Namely, the author intends to fully state the arguments from both sides, examine them, and then add his own conclusions.

He then states that before the year 553, no one cited these works, although the defenders of these writings cited some passages in support of their opinion; however, these were taken from later, forged <note>original: *untergeschobenen* (placed underneath), referring to pseudonymous or spurious works</note> authors. Then he presents the main argument of the "friends" of the Areopagite writings: namely, that from the year 553 onwards, it has been the consistent opinion of the Church that these writings were the work of Dionysius. Here he provides citations of all authors from the sixth to the sixteenth century who refer to this matter.

He then follows with the reasons cited by **Daillé**, some of which he considers weak, but most of which he presents in all their strength, while bringing in the opinions of their opponents. At the conclusion, **le Nourry** gives us his own conjecture regarding the time in which these writings might have been written, and the causes that might have prompted them. Namely, he suggests that their author composed them when the Church was troubled by **Nestorian** <term>Followers of Nestorius (c. 386–450) who were accused of over-emphasizing the distinction between Christ's human and divine natures.</term> and **Eutychian** <term>Followers of Eutyches (c. 380–456) who argued that Christ's human nature was absorbed into his divine nature, a view known as Monophysitism.</term> errors, in order to protect the Catholic party; and to ensure them greater effectiveness, he made them known under the celebrated name of **Dionysius the Areopagite**. However, they did not become known immediately, but spread only gradually, and they did not reach general circulation until shortly before

...reached those conversations with the **Severians** <note>The Severians were a moderate Monophysite group; their 532 AD conference in Constantinople is the first historical record of the Dionysian writings being cited.</note>: this opinion is confirmed by the fact that no mention of them is made at either the **Council of Ephesus** <note>431 AD</note> or the **Council of Chalcedon** <note>451 AD</note>. The author may have taken much from **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note>.

At the end, after having spoken about the utility of the books and their editions, **le Nourry** adds the following nine remarks in a separate section.

The author did not understand Hebrew, as can be seen from the seventh chapter of the ***Celestial Hierarchy***.

It is uncertain whether the headings originate from the author himself, because they contain names of titles, such as **Presbyter** <term>Presbyter: an elder or priest in the early Church</term>, for example, which he uses nowhere else in his writings. Furthermore, it should be noted that these headings appear in all Latin and Greek manuscripts of the works.

The same observation applies to the tables of contents; it is particularly improbable that the author himself wrote them because the chapters frequently do not contain the content indicated in the summary.

If some believed that the name of an office lower than the diaconate <term>diaconate: the office or rank of a deacon</term> appeared in these writings—namely that of the **singers** <note>original Latin: *cantores*</note>—they are mistaken, because **Dionysius** uses this name only to represent the earthly Church hierarchy as being entirely similar to the heavenly one.

The sacred customs are not precisely specified. In the rite of **Confirmation**, the laying on of hands is missing, even though this practice originates from the Apostles.

He mentions some ceremonies that seem to have been in use only in his specific church, such as the covering of the altar with twelve feathers during the preparation of the holy **Chrism** <term>Chrism: a consecrated oil used in baptism, confirmation, and ordination</term>, and the washing of hands during the Mass after the reading of the names of the deceased.

In the eighteenth century, this dispute rested almost entirely, because it was viewed as nearly universally decided. No agreement had been reached regarding the specific time in which these writings were supposed to have been written, and opinions fluctuated between the fourth and sixth centuries; but on one point there was unanimity: that they were spurious <note>original German: *untergeschoben*</note> writings, and that they could by no means be attributed to **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A first-century Athenian convert mentioned in the Book of Acts; these mystical texts were later proven to be written by a "Pseudo-Dionysius" around 500 AD.</note>.

In most recent times, **Kestner** <note>August Kestner (1777–1853), a German diplomat and scholar who proposed controversial theories about early Christian secret societies.</note> (in his: *Agape, or the Secret World-Union of Christians Founded by Clement in Rome under Domitian's Reign*, Jena, 1819, 8vo.), in order to support a bold hypothesis regarding the method of Christianity's expansion, declared the Areopagite writings to be authentic—along with a multitude of other works generally held to be spurious. He claimed that they contained the ritual of mysteries for a **Johannine-Gnostic** <note>Refers to a theoretical fusion of the teachings of the Apostle John with Gnosticism, a movement emphasizing "secret knowledge" (gnosis) for salvation.</note> secret society, which he then provided in excerpts from these works. **Kestner** did not engage at all with the reasons provided by other writers against the authenticity of the writings of **Dionysius**, but only mentioned, as if in passing, that the opponents' main reason was the observation that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the primary historian of the early Church whose silence on a document often suggests it did not yet exist or was not accepted.</note> does not cite these writings. However, he singled out this one reason only because it was the easiest to refute based on his own assumptions. For throughout his entire book, he portrays **Eusebius** as an enemy of the so-called "Johannine Union," so that one cannot find it surprising if **Eusebius** made no mention of its primary document. But when **Kestner** suggests that the authenticity of the Areopagite writings in general could most easily be proven from the ten extant "genuine" letters of **Dionysius**, he has simply failed to provide us with the proof for the authenticity of these letters themselves. For according to—

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of August Kestner’s defense of the Dionysian corpus, noting its lack of academic support, and begins a detailed argument for a later authorship based on the texts' heavy reliance on the philosophy of Proclus (5th century AD).</meta>

In all investigations regarding the **Areopagite works** <note>A collection of mystical theological writings once attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, a first-century convert of St. Paul.</note> in general, the *Letters* appeared at the same time as the rest of the works. The same internal and external reasons that argue for a later origin of the entire collection apply in their full extent to these *Letters* as well.

This attempt by **Kestner** had to be mentioned because it belongs to the history of these works. A specific refutation of his claim is unnecessary, as it is already countered by the reasons previously mentioned, and because this new hypothesis has met with no success and gained no followers—rather, it has encountered significant opponents on specific points, such as **Eichstädt** <note>Heinrich Karl Eichstädt (1772–1848), a German philologist and professor at Jena.</note> and **Planck** <note>Gottlieb Jakob Planck (1751–1833), a prominent German Protestant theologian and church historian.</note>. —

While we refer to these and all previous points already contained in this volume regarding this matter, we will provide some additional information that may serve to strengthen these arguments.

We believe we can assert—as we have already expressed in an academic program: *On the Origin of the Areopagite Writings. Erlangen, November 1822.* <note>original: *de origine scriptorum Areopagiticorum. Erlangae, mense Nou. 1822.*</note>—that at the time of the Apostles, the Areopagite writings as we now have them could not have been written at all. Specifically, they are full of **Neoplatonic** <note>A mystical school of philosophy that began in the 3rd century AD; it sought to synthesize Plato's ideas with other spiritual traditions.</note> ideas, presented not in the manner that might have developed from the Gnostic systems of the apostolic age, but specifically those expressed by **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last great Greek philosophers; the striking similarities between his work and the Dionysian texts are a primary reason scholars date the latter to around 500 AD.</note>. How closely the alleged **Dionysius** agrees with Proclus—how principles, ideas, expressions, style, and everything pertaining thereto flowed into him from Proclus—a later essay in this book will seek to make clear and prove. Now, however, the philosophy of Proclus is not a system independent of all others, which developed completely from the spirit of this philosopher himself without predecessors; rather, it is a product of its time, a single link in that so-called—

the golden chain of Platonic philosophy. It constantly takes earlier works into consideration, cites them, explains them, and supplements them. — **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Saccas (3rd century AD), often considered one of the founders of Neoplatonism.</note> had first attempted to unite and merge the various older systems of the Greek philosophers, and among his students, **Plotinus** continued these efforts with the most admirable insight and an uncommon philosophical talent. **Porphyrius** and **Iamblichus** had introduced an abundance of Oriental <term>philosophemes</term> <note>Philosophical propositions or systems of thought.</note>, and just as this Platonic philosophy had been reshaped, modified, and expanded through these additions, **Proclus** took it up and developed it further. He seems to always start with **Plato**, but in his commentaries, every tenet of other philosophies appears, along with everything that could be adapted from previous philosophical acquisitions through a free, allegorical, and artificial mode of interpretation. 

And what had thus arisen for **Proclus**, which in his time and given his talents and knowledge had to manifest in this way and no other, was clearly utilized by the alleged **Dionysius**. Just as **Proclus** dared to link everything—even the most remote ideas—to simple Platonic principles and derive them from there, the **Areopagite** unhesitatingly juxtaposed what he had learned from this Platonic philosophy with biblical verses, whenever possible. He used the sayings of the **Holy Scriptures** for the explanation, confirmation, and authentication of what he had proposed. 

The fact that this was possible for him had its deeper reason in the reality that all contemplations on the highest objects of faith and knowledge always converge in a few simple ideas. Furthermore, Platonic philosophy had absorbed the fruits of Oriental **divine contemplation** <note>original: *Gottbeschauung*; a mystical state of looking upon or experiencing the divine.</note>—the very same fruits that, belonging to the most ancient times and originating from God Himself, also passed into the **Mosaic religion** <note>Judaism, as established through Moses.</note> and, in their highest transfiguration, into **Christianity**—

To assume that the <term>Areopagite writings</term> <note>The *Corpus Dionysiacum*, a collection of theological works once attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite (a 1st-century convert of St. Paul), but now recognized as the work of an anonymous 5th or 6th-century author known as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note> were written in the first or the beginning of the second century is to anticipate the entire development of Platonic philosophy brought about by centuries. It would mean magically conjuring **Proclus**—as he was shaped by the philosophical past in the fifth century—back into the time of the Apostles, thereby establishing a "Proclus before Proclus" in the person of the alleged Dionysius, if one considers him authentic.

These observations lead naturally to a conjecture which, even if it can be presented as nothing more than a hypothesis, still seems too probable for us not to express it.

We know that several of the most distinguished **Fathers** <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the intellectual foundations of Christianity.</note> were philosophically educated in Athens, and their writings bear witness that the Platonic ideas they drew from the instruction of philosophers mixed with their own views and gave them a particular color and modification. We mention only **Basil** <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), a leading figure in the early church.</note> and his friend **Gregory of Nazianzus**. The personalities of most Platonic philosophers are presented to us by their biographers—**Porphyry**, **Eunapius**, **Marinus**, etc.—as so amiable and engaging; they praise their eloquence and the purity of their morals in such a way that it cannot be surprising to us if Christian youths were captivated by their doctrine. However, personal respect for these teachers came into conflict with the Christian tenet that, as heathens, they were unworthy of God's grace and that they had not, after all, penetrated to the final stage of truth. <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the synthesis of Greek philosophy and early Christian theology. It follows a mention of the Church Father Basil of Caesarea, whose work reflects the influence of his Athenian education.</meta>

[...pla]tonic and Christian principles is striking, and it is not surprising that one or another Christian pupil of these Platonic sages attempted to unite the brilliance of philosophy with the truth of Christianity. In addition, in the turbulent times of the fifth and sixth centuries, many external reasons could have played a role. Heretical factions <note>Specifically referring to the Christological disputes (like Nestorianism or Monophysitism) that divided the early Church.</note> confused the Church, and through the usual path of synods and imperial decrees, external coercion was indeed achieved, but not internal conviction. 

What if a pupil of **Proclus**, a zealous Christian who took a lively interest in the suffering of the Church, became convinced that he could—through his philosophy in connection with Christian doctrine—overcome all opponents and secure victory for the pure teachings of the Church? Should he not do it? But to venture into the stormy activity of the factions as a weak individual with an unknown name seemed risky; and his prudence might seem excusable, or even justified by the pressure of the times themselves, if he took the name of a celebrated disciple of the Apostles to gain respect and entry for his writings. But who could have more readily occurred to him—being an Athenian or someone living in Athens—and to whom could he more fittingly attribute his works, than to the Athenian **Dionysius the Areopagite**, the disciple of **Paul**? —

Thus far our conjecture, the probability of which we leave to stand, while we speak only of another conjecture which would view **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop known for blending Neoplatonic thought with Christian faith.</note> as the author of these writings. We would have little to object to this if we knew nothing else of **Synesius** than his ten hymns. For in these, indeed, the greatest agreement with the Areopagite’s style and character cannot be overlooked; the same intimate familiarity with the <term>Alexandrian-Platonic theosophical ideas</term> <note>A school of thought that combined Plato's philosophy with mystical elements, often seeking a direct, meditative knowledge of God.</note>, the same

--- Page 264 ---
<meta>This page continues the comparison between the writings of Synesius of Cyrene and the mystical works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, focusing on their stylistic similarities and philosophical differences regarding the nature of matter.</meta>

There is a similar bombast of expression, the same repetitions, the same air of mystery, and the very same ecstasy into unnamable, inexpressible spheres of light. We especially notice that idea which asserts that all that exists is permeated by the Divine, and exists and endures only through the Divine; this is repeated to the point of exhaustion in the hymns of **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Hypatia who later became a Christian bishop. His work represents a unique bridge between Hellenic philosophy and early Christianity.</note>. This is the very idea that serves as the actual pillar of the **Dionysian system** <note>Referring to the "Corpus Areopagiticum," a body of influential mystical texts written by an anonymous author known today as Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>. However, the **Areopagite** stands higher in this regard: he considers matter as necessary and even views evil as serving the good, whereas the verses of Synesius contain incessant sighs for liberation from the weight of the body and of material substance.

Nonetheless, the probability would be great that Synesius, or a philosopher related to his spirit, also wrote the Areopagite works, were it not for the fact that we must take Synesius’s prose works into consideration. These, however, completely contradict such a suspicion. For where they provide an account, they are clear and without any bombast; the speeches are fluid, written with rhetorical skill, without exaggeration, and without the superfluous and bombastic ornament of epithets; his letters are bright, natural, and witty—excellent in their narratives and descriptions—and throughout show no trace of "Areopagite" affectation or mysteriousness.

Yet the hymns are important evidence for that mindset which expresses itself in the writings we have examined. We therefore provide the first three of them (which constitute the largest part of the hymns overall) in a literal, metrical translation. Regarding this, we must only note that—especially in the third hymn, which proceeds quite monotonously in the same verses—we have occasionally taken some liberty with the <term>meter</term> <note>The rhythmic structure of a poem.</note> in order to render the meaning quite literally. In a work such as this, literal accuracy must always be regarded as the primary requirement.

<meta>This page begins the first section of the treatise regarding the Areopagite writings. It establishes the foundational conflict between "Mysticism"—which seeks internal, hidden truths in Scripture—and the "historical-grammatical" academic method of the author's time, which views the Bible primarily as a historical and cultural document.</meta>

### 1.

What we call <term>mysticism</term> <note>original: *Mystik*. In this context, it refers to the practice of seeking direct, internal experience of the divine.</note> is occupied entirely with the interior—with internal experiences, inner feelings, contemplations, and insights. From the slightest and most ordinary impulse toward the good, up to the contemplation of God Himself, the mystic, as such, is always turned within; he experiences something hidden and secret, which he can only inadequately describe with words and can, at most, only hint at in ordinary language. Yet, he must recognize the <term>Holy Scripture</term> <note>original: *heilige Schrift*. The Bible.</note> as an epitome of divine pronouncements. If his inner experiences are to be considered divine, they must harmonize with the pronouncements of the Bible; indeed, since he unconditionally accepts the divine inspiration of the Scripture, every passage of the text must contain a divine meaning for him. 

This, however, is not possible through the ordinary path of <term>historical-grammatical interpretation</term> <note>original: *historisch-grammatischer Auslegung*. A scholarly approach that interprets the Bible as a historical document by focusing on the original language and the specific era in which it was written.</note>. For this method, ordinary history remains just history. It treats the imagery of the poets as mere "poetic ornament" and similarly categorizes the <term>ecstasies</term> <note>original: *Entzückungen*. These are the visionary or trance-like states experienced by the biblical prophets.</note> of the prophets in this same class. When God’s own pronouncements appear, this method always remarks that they were shaped and arranged according to the local customs, the era, and the level of education of those to whom they were originally addressed. 

Through this scholarly approach, however, every mystical sense is excluded. While the interpreters display a great deal of <term>erudition</term> <note>original: *Gelehrsamkeit*. Deep academic learning or scholarship.</note>, and succeed in making every detail quite clearly understood, they do so by preventing any further allusions or hints. They restrict each individual book to the specific time and purpose for which it was written. On the other hand, common experience teaches that every book requires its own particular mood, its own particular disposition, in order to—

Even for some outstanding <term>secular books</term> <note>original: *profanen Büchern*. And who is unaware of what every art lover knows regarding the clear, unfathomable depth in the masterpieces of the visual arts by **van Eyck** and **Raphael**, or even of other lesser masters? 

If we must have developed a political sense within ourselves to understand political writers, or a poetic sense to understand poets, and if artworks of all kinds require a sense for art, we may then ask: what kind of sense is required, what must be developed, in order to understand the **Bible**, this collection of divine writings? 

Many answer this question by suggesting a critical and historical sense—the former to distinguish the authentic from the inauthentic, the latter to place oneself precisely within the situation, time, and environment. Others, however, who (according to the teachings of the Church and our <term>symbolical books</term> <note>original: *symbolischen Bücher*. In theology, these are the official creeds and confessions that define a church’s doctrine.</note>) regard Scripture as <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>original: *von Gott eingegeben*. The doctrine that God is the ultimate author of the biblical text through human instruments.</note>, speak thus: if it is absolutely necessary for the understanding of any work that we liken ourselves to the spirit of the author we wish to understand, and if God Himself speaks as the author in the biblical books, then surely a **divine sense** will be necessary for their understanding. One might also accept, in a certain sense, that language itself is often too clumsy to accurately and suitably express inner feelings or higher experiences, and that ultimately, in every word and sentence, there is only that which the individual reader appropriates for themselves and what they think during the process. Among the later <term>mystics</term> <note>Those who seek direct, personal experience of the divine or absolute truth through intuition or insight rather than logic.</note>, we very often find that when they wish to speak of the point that promises us the most enlightenment—namely, how they arrived at the actual light and vision—they suddenly break off and excuse themselves by citing the <term>ineffability</term> <note>original: *Unaussprechlichkeit*. The quality of being beyond the power of words to describe.</note> of these experiences. The Word must always remain the standard, and individual parts must be explained from the whole of the Christian spirit; only that which harmonizes with this spirit are we to regard as correct and binding.

### 3.

The allegorical and mystical interpretation, just like the historical-critical rationalist one, both proceed from principles that are not, in and of themselves, to be rejected. One might say that it is only when both are applied together in their simple and authentic manner that true <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially of religious scripture.</note> actually emerges. Both, however, have rarely or almost never remained in the middle ground, but have instead lost themselves to a greater or lesser degree in extremes on both sides. If one side used internal spiritual experiences for a better understanding of Scripture and attempted to explain it through them, one could not say they were wrong; but when they twisted and turned Scripture itself according to individual experiences and dreams, they fell into the error of judging its value based on how well it agreed with their own experiences. If this could not be easily demonstrated from the Bible itself, they took refuge in a secret tradition of the initiated, and where even this no longer sufficed, they assumed a continuous new revelation of the Holy Spirit, which would be equal to the first revelation. In doing so, they approached the claims of those Jews whom **Schöttgen** <note>Christian Schöttgen (1683–1751), a German theologian and scholar who sought to explain the New Testament through the lens of ancient rabbinic writings.</note> cites in the preface to his *Hebrew and Talmudic Hours*. <note>original Latin title: *horis hebraicis et talmudicis*</note> These people said:

> Do not believe that the written law is the foundation of our faith; on the contrary, the oral law is its foundation, and it is upon the oral law that the covenant of the Israelites with God was established, as it is written in Exodus 34:27: "For according to these words, I have made a covenant with you and with Israel." And these words of the oral law are the hidden treasure of the Holy God. For it was well known to Him that the Israelites would one day be exiles among the nations, and

This is not even to mention how the **Catholic Church** soon utilized this view of tradition to present itself as the only competent interpreter; just as the **Councils** claimed for themselves a continuous, specific activity of the **Holy Spirit**, which for the Church even became a legislative power.

...they then place the Bible on the same level as all other books; they demonstrate how everything within it occurs so naturally in the spirit of that time, uncovering its errors, oversights, and contradictions. But it is precisely this desire to make it clear to the common intellect that leads them astray. It is one thing to consider the Bible as an ordinary book—as a historical source, for instance—where such a view is exactly correct; it is quite another to view it as a book of religion upon which all of Christianity depends. In the latter case, entirely different needs emerge and seek satisfaction than those of the intellect, which asks only whether everything fits together externally or whether it can be explained satisfactorily through logic. Yet, with this **rationalistic** sense, one can always guard against the path of vain and empty fanaticism <term>Schwärmerei: A derogatory term used in the 18th and 19th centuries to describe religious "enthusiasm" or "frenzy" that lacked intellectual grounding</term>; and the possession of the **mystical sense**—to call it that for lack of a better word—will protect against that path which leads to the profane, the dull, and the superficial. —

### 4.

Thus, one can well prophesy that in the reawakened struggle between the soul and the intellect—between mystics and rationalists—no party will achieve a decisive victory, as each hopes; rather, both fundamental dispositions will persist side-by-side and will always take on new forms according to the character of each age.

### 5.

Allegorical interpretation originated in the East <note>original: "Oriente"</note>, where a very flexible imagination and the wit of the creative faculty easily turn sensory appearances into images of the non-sensory, or exchange one sensory thing for another through metaphorical expression. Furthermore, we find that whenever spiritual views spread among more educated peoples through philosophy and deeper reflection, these views are carried back into earlier, revered works, which, in their sensory and poetic innocence, had not yet considered such ideas. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 241 regarding the history of interpretation methods. The opening word "trachtung" is the conclusion of "Betrachtung" (contemplation or view) which began on the preceding page.</meta>

view was recognized, it should not be missing from the nation's masterpieces; and where common views manifested themselves in sensory images, these were to be refined through an underlying explanation, so that every blemish might be removed from the beloved and revered work. However, to imbue sensory images with spiritual meaning is to explain them allegorically, and thus allegorical interpretation became the means to this stated end. This method of explanation was applied both to Homer <note>Early Greek scholars often used allegory to explain away scandalous behavior of the gods in Homer's epics</note> and to the Bible.

As the Jews were widely dispersed through the Babylonian captivity <note>The period in the 6th century BCE when the elite of the Kingdom of Judah were exiled to Babylon, leading to significant cultural and religious shifts</note> and moved beyond the narrow confines of the Promised Land, they gradually had to incorporate the ideas of foreign peoples into their sphere of knowledge. Later, a great number of this mercantile people gathered in the new global center of trade, Alexandria, where both treasures and the ideas of the entire civilized world flowed together. It was here, in the effort to link modern ideas to the sacred records, that the allegorizing exegesis <term>Exegese: From the Greek for "to lead out," this refers to the critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture</term> developed, of which such a rich supply has been preserved for us in the works of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who famously used allegorical methods to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy</note>.

The manner in which these exegetes conducted their work may be made clear by a longer passage from Philo himself; it is surely better to let him speak for himself than to merely suggest his style through a deficient description, which often leaves the reader with a different impression than the author intended. For this, we choose his treatise on the Giants, in an interpretation of Genesis 6:1–4—

...the fire has the fire-born <note>original: "Feuergeborne." For these stars are also souls, entirely immortal and divine, which is why they also possess the circular motion <note>In ancient Greek and Hellenistic cosmology, circular motion was considered the most perfect and divine form of movement, reserved for the celestial spheres</note> that is most closely related to the movement of the mind. For their mind is the purest.

It is therefore necessary that the air also be full of living beings. These, however, are invisible to us, since the air itself cannot be seen by our senses. But one cannot say that there are no souls in the air just because our sight cannot perceive the form of these souls. They must necessarily be grasped by the mind, because like is perceived by like <note>A fundamental principle in Greek philosophy—that the human mind can only perceive the divine or the spiritual because it shares the same essential nature</note>. Must we not say that all land and water animals live by air and breath? Do not pestilential diseases occur when the air is corrupted, precisely because the air is the cause of all animation? And when it is harmless and incorruptible, as it tends to be especially during north winds, does it not contribute to an enhanced and more vigorous life when we breathe in the pure air? 

And is it likely that the very thing by which other water and land animals are animated should itself have no part in souls? On the contrary, even if everything else produced nothing living, the air alone would have to do so, since it received the seeds of the soul through the special grace of the Creator of the world. Now, of these souls, some descend into bodies, while others never wished to have anything in common with any part of the earth. These latter souls, who are consecrated and appointed to the service of the Father, the Creator of the world is accustomed to use as ministers and assistants for the administration of mortal things. But the others, who descended into the body as if into a river, are sometimes swept away and submerged by the vortex of a mighty whirlpool; yet at other times they are able to struggle against the power of the current, first surfacing by swimming, and then flying back again to the place from whence they started. <meta>This page continues the interpretation of Genesis 6:3 ("My spirit shall not remain in man forever, for he is flesh"). ...worthy of being **Elders** <term>Elders: In the biblical Book of Numbers, seventy leaders were chosen to share the burden of leadership with Moses; Philo interprets this as a sharing of spiritual wisdom.</term>, if they have not received that all-wise Spirit. For it is said: **"I will take of the Spirit that is upon you and will put it upon the seventy Elders."** <note>Numbers 11:17</note> But do not imagine this "taking away" as a separation or a division, but rather like what happens with **fire**; which, even if one lights a thousand torches from it, is by no means diminished, but remains in the same state. 

The nature of **knowledge** <term>knowledge: Philo uses the term "Wissenschaft" (science/knowledge) to describe spiritual and intellectual understanding.</term> is of the same kind. For even when it has made its students and acquaintances experienced, it is not diminished in any part. Indeed, it often increases, just as is said of **springs** from which water is drawn. For it is said of these that they then become sweeter. The ongoing conversations, which provide the occasion for reflection and practice, effect a complete perfection. 

If **Moses'** own spirit, or that of any other created being, had to be shared with such a large number of acquaintances, it would likely have diminished by being divided into so many parts. But the Spirit resting upon him is the wise, divine, indivisible, and inseparable one—the glorious Spirit that fills everything everywhere. When it shares itself for the benefit of others, it suffers no loss; when it communicates itself, it loses nothing of its understanding, its knowledge, or its wisdom. 

The divine Spirit can thus indeed remain in the soul, but it is impossible for it to persist there permanently, as we have said. Why should we wonder at this, since no other possession is firm and permanent? For human things eternally waver and shift, constantly absorbing other changes. 

The primary cause of ignorance, however, is the **flesh** and our association with the flesh—as he <note>Moses, as the presumed author of Genesis.</note> himself confesses when he says: **"Because they were flesh, the divine Spirit could not remain in them."** <note>Genesis 6:3</note> Also **marriage**, the raising of children, the providing of **necessities**, a lack of reputation <note>original: "Ruhmlosigkeit"</note>, and **poverty**; private and public...
