<meta>This page continues Philo's exploration of why the divine Spirit cannot dwell permanently in human beings. Having established that the Spirit is like a flame that is not diminished when shared, he now identifies the "flesh" as the primary obstacle to spiritual wisdom, contrasting the tethered physical life with the free, incorporeal life of the soul.</meta>

Affairs of business and a thousand other things cause **wisdom** <term>wisdom: For Philo, "Sophia" (wisdom) is the highest human achievement, a divine gift that allows the soul to see the truth of the universe.</term> to wither before it has even bloomed. But nothing is so great a hindrance to it as the nature of the **flesh**. For this serves as a foundation of ignorance and lack of knowledge—indeed, the first and greatest foundation upon which every one of the aforementioned obstacles is built. 

For those **souls** that are incorporeal and fleshless, dwelling in this theater of the universe, enjoy divine visions and divine sounds; they possess an insatiable love for these things, and no one hinders them. But those who bear the heavy burden of the flesh, weighed down and shackled, cannot gaze upward at the heavenly spheres. Instead, with their necks forcibly pulled down, they are rooted to the earth like four-legged animals. Therefore, the **Lawgiver** <term>Lawgiver: Philo’s standard term for Moses, whom he regards as the ultimate philosopher and legislator.</term>, wishing to abolish unlawful and forbidden intimacy and intercourse, speaks thus:

> "The man, the man shall not approach his near kinswoman to uncover her nakedness, for I am the Lord." <note>Leviticus 18:6. Philo notes the repetition of "the man" in the Greek/Hebrew text as a significant allegorical detail.</note>

How could one more strongly call for the contempt of the flesh and all that belongs to it than in this manner? And he not only warns against it, but also declares with certainty that the true human being never voluntarily approaches the friendly and intimate pleasures of the body, but rather always thinks of keeping a distance from them. 

And the fact that he says "the man, the man" twice, not just once, is a sign that he does not mean the human made of body and soul, but rather the one who possesses **virtue**. For that is that true human of whom one of the ancients <term>Diogenes: Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BCE), a Cynic philosopher who famously carried a lamp in broad daylight, claiming to be looking for a single "real" or "honest" human being.</term>, lighting a lantern at midday, said to a questioner: he was looking for a human. 

That one should not go toward all the ugliness of the flesh has a necessary reason. For some things must be permitted, such as those necessities we use to live healthily and without disease; but the superfluous must be sent to the vultures <note>original: "zum Geyer zu schicken" — a German idiom for discarding something as worthless or consigning it to destruction.</note>, as it is by the superfluous that the **desires** are ignited...

<summary>Philo argues that the physical nature of the flesh is the primary obstacle to divine wisdom, contrasting the earth-bound human condition with the freedom of incorporeal souls. He uses the biblical repetition of "the man" in Leviticus and the anecdote of Diogenes the Cynic to distinguish between the physical person and the virtuous "true" human.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Philo of Alexandria’s allegorical commentary on the Book of Leviticus. ...banish <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page: that the influence of the flesh can suddenly drive away all virtuous impulses.</note> and everything virtuous in a single attack. Therefore, **desires** should not be stirred up for everything that is dear to the **flesh**. For untamed lusts, though they often fawn like dogs, frequently turn back and bite incurably. Thus, if we adopt **frugality** <term>frugality: Philo uses the term "Genügsamkeit," reflecting the Greek "autarkeia" (self-sufficiency), a core Stoic and Platonic virtue meaning being satisfied with the bare essentials.</term>, which is the friend of **virtue**, and prefer it to the needs of the body, we defeat the countless host of bitter enemies. Even if circumstances should forcibly demand that we take more than what is measured and suitable, let us not go toward them. 

For he says, he shall not "approach to uncover his nakedness." <note>German: "Schaam aufzudecken." In this context, Philo is interpreting the Hebrew/Greek biblical idiom for "nakedness" as a symbol for shameful or illicit exposure of the soul's lower nature.</note> It is worth the effort to reveal what this means. Often, those who had acquired no possessions had rich abundance; others, who did not strive for fame, were deemed worthy of public praise and reward; and to those who hoped for not even the slightest power, the greatest strength came. Let all these learn that no one should "approach" such things in spirit; that is, they should not admire them, or gaze at them with excessive wonder. One should regard each of them—**wealth**, **fame**, and **physical strength**—not merely as a good, but also as the greatest evil <note>Philo argues that these external "goods" become evils if the soul seeks them out of greed or vanity, rather than receiving them as gifts from God to be used wisely.</note>. 

For the greedy find access to money, the fame-seekers to glory, and those eager for combat and gymnastics to physical strength. They have surrendered the better part of the **soul** to the inferior, soulless things. But those who remain "within themselves" subject these glittering and envied external structures of fortune to the **mind** <term>mind: Here referring to the "Logos" or "Hegemonikon," the ruling part of the soul that should guide human behavior.</term> as their leader, accepting them for proper use if they come to them; yet if they are far off, they do not go toward them, being people who can be happy even without these goods. 

But whoever approaches them and wishes to follow their trail fills **philosophy** with shameful delusion—which is why it is said that he "uncovers nakedness." For should not the disgrace of those be clear and obvious, who call themselves **wise** while they sell **wisdom** for a pittance...

It harms when it gives, and it benefits and blesses when it takes away. Therefore, O soul, if one of the magic charms of pleasure calls you to itself, turn away from it, avert your gaze, and look upon the genuine beauty of **virtue**, and persist in this looking until the longing softens you and attracts you like a magnet, leads you closer, and binds you to the object of your desire. <meta>This page continues Philo of Alexandria’s allegorical commentary on the Book of Leviticus. The previous page ended with the idea that it is beautiful not to abandon the contemplation of the divine spirit, the God of the whole.</meta>

...**am the Lord**; <note>original: "bin der Herr." A reference to the recurring phrase in Leviticus, "I am the LORD your God."</note> this is not only to be understood as if He were saying, "I am the Perfect, the Imperishable, and the truly Good, and whoever holds to me leaves behind the imperfect and that which clings to the flesh," but also as if He were saying: "I am the Ruler, the King, and the Sovereign." When leaders are present, their subordinates do not dare to do anything evil; when masters are present, the servants do not. For when those who have the power to punish are nearby, those among them who are incapable of higher insight are kept within the bounds of reason by fear. Since God is near and fills everything, we must worship Him especially, for He surveys all and is present everywhere; and if we do not do so out of love, we should at least cautiously honor the immovable power of His dominion—the terrifying and inescapable nature of His punishments—by considering what kind of chastising power He can employ. In this way, we will separate ourselves from injustice so that the divine spirit of wisdom does not easily depart and distance itself from us, but remains with us for a long time, just as it remained with the wise Moses. 

For he [Moses] possesses the most peaceful conditions; whether standing or sitting, change or movement is by no means natural to him. It says: **Moses and the Ark did not move** <note>A reference to Numbers 10:35–36, which Philo interprets as the stability of the soul that has reached a state of virtue.</note>, either because the wise man is inseparable from virtue, or because virtue is not movable and the virtuous man is not changeable, but both stand in the firmness of right reason. Elsewhere it then says: **Stand here by me** <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 5:31. Philo interprets God’s command to Moses as an invitation into the eternal "standing" or stability of the Divine.</note>. This pronouncement was communicated to the prophet, signifying the rest and stillness which reigns unchangeably with God, who stands eternally unchangeable. For whatever is placed against a flawless <term>measure: German "Maaßstab," referring to an absolute standard of truth or morality.</term> must necessarily become straight. <meta>This page continues Philo of Alexandria’s allegorical interpretation of the life of Moses and the nature of the soul. On the previous page, Philo discussed the stability of the virtuous man and the ARK, suggesting that the wise person remains firm in right reason.</meta>

<page-num>— 252 —</page-num>

...and so to ask: "Why do you stand alone?" For if someone perceives the ongoing war during peace—a war that is directed not just against nations, regions, and cities, but also against households and even the individual person; indeed, if one sees the unspeakable and heavy storm in souls, which is constantly assailed by the extreme corruption of life's affairs, then he naturally wonders how anyone, in the midst of the storm, can enjoy stillness, and in the midst of the swirling roar of the sea, find peace.

Now you also understand why not even the High Priest—that is, **Reason**—who is always able to remain with and occupy himself with the sacred doctrines, has the freedom to approach them at any time, but barely once a year. For the spoken word is not secure, because it becomes a duality <note>original: "Zweiheit." Philo suggests that vocalizing a thought splits it between the mind and the air, creating a division, whereas pure thought remains a unified "one."</note>. Beholding the Being <note>original: "das Seyende," a philosophical term for the ultimate, unchanging reality of God.</note> with the soul alone and without voice is the most secure path, because it exists in undivided unity. 

Just as the divine spirit does not remain among the "Many"—that is, among those who set many different purposes for their lives—even if it turns toward them for a brief moment, it appears only to that one form <term>form or essence (εἴδει)</term> of humanity that has stripped away everything related to the world of "becoming" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "becoming" (Werden) refers to the temporary, changing physical world, as opposed to the eternal "being."</note>. This person has cast off even the innermost coverings and veils of mere opinion <term>opinion or appearance (δόξα)</term> and strives toward God with a carefree, naked mind <term>intellect or thought (διανοίᾳ)</term>. 

Thus, Moses pitches his tent outside the camp and the physical army; that is, he established his unmoved power of knowledge <term>judgment or purpose (γνώμην)</term> and began to prostrate himself before God. By entering into the darkness, into the invisible place, he remains there and completes the holiest of initiations. And he becomes not only an initiate <term>initiate (Myste)</term>, but also a revealer <term>hierophant or sacred teacher (Hierophante)</term> of the holy rites and a teacher of the Divine, which he proclaims to those who have purified ears. The divine spirit is now always with him, guiding him constantly on the right path. From others, as already mentioned, the spirit quickly departs, and completes their life in one hundred and twenty...

<summary>Philo explains that divine truth is found in the silence of the soul's unity rather than in spoken words or worldly distractions. He presents Moses as the ideal philosopher-mystic who leaves the "camp" of physical life to enter the divine darkness and become a teacher of sacred mysteries.</summary>

How does it happen, then, that those burdened with guilt live for the same length of time as the all-wise prophet? In this place, it suffices to say that things sharing the same name are not necessarily identical in nature. Often, completely different types—the wicked and the virtuous—may share the same numbers and spans of time when they are listed together, even though they possess the most separate and distant powers. Now to the next part of our passage: **There were also tyrants** <note>original: "γίγαντες" (gigantes), usually translated as "giants." For this reason, he also banished the celebrated and decorative arts of painting and sculpture from his state; these arts merely counterfeit the nature of reality and use the eyes to craft deception and fraud for easily-led souls. He makes no mention of any "giant-fable" at all; rather, he uses the term to suggest that some humans are earthly, others are heavenly, and others are divine.

**Earthly** men are those who hunt after the pleasures of the body, desiring their enjoyment and participation, and striving for everything that serves to satisfy every single lust. **Heavenly** men are the craftsmen, the scholars, and the friends of study. For our heavenly part is the spirit <note>original: "Geist," referring to the intellect or the higher mind (Greek: *nous*).</note>. The spirit concerns itself with the celestial revolutions; it sharpens and whets all other arts and exercises and strengthens itself in spiritual matters. **Divine** men, however, are the priests and prophets,

Such a person belongs to the only God, becomes His follower, and straightens the path of his whole life by making use of the true way of the single King and Ruler of all, neither deviating nor turning away to any side.

The "sons of the earth," however, depart from their intellect and dig into the soulless, immobile nature of the flesh. For *they both became one flesh*, as the Lawgiver <note>Moses, traditionally regarded as the author of the Pentateuch</note> says. Just like Dionysius, he also cites apocryphal writings to which he attributes full authority, and asserts that the whole of Holy Scripture has an allegorical sense, an assertion he proves with passages from the Old and New Testaments themselves. He has strikingly imitated the exegetical style of **Philo** and provided several reasons why Scripture expresses itself in a secret manner. In this way, Clement was able to trace everything he found in the philosophers that was similar to Christianity back to the Old Testament.

## 9.

We make an intermediate remark here, which refers to the era of **Dionysius**, since we are discussing the exegesis of the earliest Fathers. It is, namely, probable that these earliest Fathers did not yet possess the Epistles and Gospels of the New Testament, as they prove all the Christian dogmas they touch upon—the nature of Christ, his resurrection, the abolition of the Mosaic law by him—merely through allegorical explanations of the Old Testament. It is only with **Clement of Alexandria** that we find, as stated, the citation of all the books of the New Testament; from this, the conclusion regarding the **Areopagite writings** <term>Areopagite writings: The "Corpus Areopagiticum," a collection of mystical texts once attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite (1st century) but now dated much later.</term>—which are familiar with all New Testament books without exception—follows of its own accord. —

## 10.

Regarding Tertullian’s statement against Marcion <note>Marcion of Sinope was a 2nd-century figure who rejected the Old Testament; Tertullian was a prolific early Christian author who argued against him.</note>—who had said that one ought not believe certain things about God because they were unbelievable and foolish—Tertullian replied that one must believe precisely for that reason: because it is unbelievable and foolish. When reading this, one is involuntarily reminded of the Areopagite way of conceiving God *through negation* or *removal* <note>original: *per negationem* or *ablationem*; this refers to "apophatic theology," which describes God by what He is not, rather than what He is.</note>. It is the same when he says: "The Son of God was born; we are not ashamed of it, precisely because it demands shame. The Son of God died; it is entirely believable, because it is foolish. He was buried and rose again; it is certain, because it is impossible."

Origen also reminds us entirely of Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> through his principle: To recognize and demonstrate the hidden causes and reasons of divinely revealed dogmas through philosophy should not be undertaken by all Christians, but only by those who are wiser and more insightful than the common crowd; those who are filled with the peculiar gifts of the Holy Spirit and have attained wisdom and knowledge through Him. For those things necessary for eternal salvation are presented most clearly for all Christians in Holy Scripture.

And here we also recall the passage in the *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: *praeparatio*; a work by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea.</note> by Eusebius (Book XI, Chapter 21), where the phrase so often found in the Areopagite appears: that the Father is not an *essence* <note>original Greek: οὐσία (ousia)</note> but rather *beyond essence* <note>original Greek: ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας (epekeina tēs ousias)</note>. This is because this passage fully encompasses that negative explanation of the nature of God.

## 11.

Justin <note>Justin Martyr, an early Christian apologist.</note>, likewise devoted to allegorical interpretation, cites Josephus and Philo as the wisest of men. At the same time, he lived in Alexandria at a period when Clement and Pantaenus were practicing the entire Philonic method of interpretation <note>Referring to the style of Philo of Alexandria, who used Greek philosophical categories to interpret Jewish scripture.</note>. We also know of Athenagoras that he twists and turns passages of the Old Testament according to his needs, in order to import into them whatever he had learned elsewhere or devised himself.

## 12.

Thus, in 그 century in which the so-called Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century whose writings were long attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite mentioned in Acts 17:34.</note> appeared, allegorical exegesis <term>allegorical exegesis: the method of interpreting the Bible by seeking a hidden spiritual or symbolic meaning rather than a literal one</term> was something commonplace, handed down from older times and recognized as valid. He employs this method without hesitation, seeing it as a way of explanation for which he expects no opposition. On the contrary, in the eleventh paragraph of the fourth chapter of *On the Divine Names*, he looks down with contempt on those who remain fixed on the external words of Holy Scripture and do not penetrate to the inner and deeper sense. This is the primary passage that clearly expresses his principles of scriptural interpretation, by which he consistently guided himself.

## 13.

Dionysius regards Holy Scripture as the primary source from which everything relating to God and providing information about divine matters must be drawn (*On the Divine Names* 1, 1). Therefore, in this regard, one must say nothing except what is contained in Holy Scripture (ibid. 1, 2. 3.). Whoever is opposed to the holy scriptures can also understand nothing of mystical theology, and it is impossible to guide anyone who does not concern themselves with the theosophy <term>theosophy: here meaning "divine wisdom" or the knowledge of God revealed through sacred texts</term> contained in the Scripture to higher theological science at all (ibid. 2, 2.). Holy Scripture is the most beautiful rule of truth, and one must use its pronouncements without changing, diminishing, or increasing them. We shall see how little our author has kept this last principle in mind—though he expressed it himself—as it is impossible to observe it as soon as allegorical interpretation is applied; in that process, modification, removal, and addition occur right from the start.

### 17.

One must be suited for the interpretation of Holy Scripture. It requires a certain constitution, a certain talent. Above all, it requires an uncommon purity, a special disposition of the soul (ibid. 1, 2.). The right interpretation is a gift of God and comes from God alone (ibid. 1, 3.). The interpreter must behold the God-like visions with a God-beholding understanding <term>dianoia: a Greek term for the faculty of reason or thought; here used to describe a spiritualized intellect</term> (<term>διανοίᾳ</term>) and lend holy ears to the revelations of the holy names of God. From this it follows naturally that interpretations obtained in such a way must be kept away from the uninitiated and their mockery. Because of this, however, exegesis <term>exegesis: the critical explanation or interpretation of a religious text</term> remains the property of a few initiates, likewise a mystery <note>original: "Mysterium"</note>, that only the holy, unblemished spirit preserves (ibid. 2, 2.). An introduction to interpretation could perhaps be given by a lesser person, but its actual understanding requires one’s own intuition of the spiritual utterances of the Scripture; for this, and for the clear overview that this requires, a higher power of those mature in faith is needed (ibid. 3, 2.). The common people cannot grasp the sense of Holy Scripture. It has indeed used words that are appropriate for the common people, but only to stimulate them through these words and lead them to something higher; (this is now nothing else than saying that the Holy Spirit has accommodated itself <note>The "doctrine of accommodation" suggests that God simplifies divine truths so they can be understood by the limited human mind.</note>). <meta>This page continues the discussion from Section 17 regarding the requirements for a qualified interpreter of Holy Scripture. It highlights a perceived contradiction in Dionysius's theology concerning the authority of the Church versus the Bible, before transitioning into Section 18 to examine his specific methods of citing and paraphrasing biblical texts.</meta>

...have knowledge of divine things at all, <unclear>know what</unclear> is understood by the divine utterances of Holy Scripture. — It is particularly from this that Dionysius's self-contradiction emerges: on one hand, he identifies Holy Scripture as the sole source, but then places Tradition <note>The "Tradition" here refers to the unwritten teachings and practices of the Church passed down through the ages.</note> alongside it, and furthermore demands a "higher understanding." This understanding would then necessarily hold the same authority as Holy Scripture—which is indeed the case, since by these "understanding ones," no one is meant but the higher clergy, who, as such, represent the only correctly interpreting Church.

### 18.

Regarding the nature of his exegesis <term>exegesis: the critical explanation or interpretation of a religious text</term>, it must first be noted that his citations from Scripture are, for the most part, not literal. He apparently cited passages from memory and modified individual verses according to the ideas he was currently explaining, so that they fit precisely into his discourse as illustrations or proofs. 

When he cites the passage 1 Corinthians 2:4 in the first paragraph of the first chapter of his work "On the Divine Names" <note>original: "von den göttlichen Namen"; this refers to *De Divinis Nominibus*, a key work by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, it is not enough for him to simply provide it as it is; instead, he paraphrases the end of the biblical verse so that he can apply the "demonstration of power" stirred by the Spirit in the holy writers, in order to derive the ineffable knowledge of God as a consequence. 

Earlier and later mystics <note>A mystic is one who seeks direct, personal experience or union with the Divine, often seeing deeper spiritual meanings behind literal texts.</note> have very frequently—indeed, almost always—employed this type of exegesis. A thought would take possession of their soul, and through their intimate familiarity with Holy Scripture, they would quickly find a passage that stood in some connection with that thought. While expressing the thought itself, they would allow the biblical passage to flow in as an allusive citation. Thus, the passage took on the color of their own thought, and the result was what one cannot exactly call a fal— <note>The text breaks off mid-word, likely intended to be "falsche" (false) or "falsche Auslegung" (false interpretation).</note>

...ical, yet a sense removed from the literal understanding—an unusual and often surprisingly deep meaning. One cannot exactly call this type of interpretation allegorical or typical. The interpreter, in this case, possesses a specific, holistic view within himself and then allows the individual biblical elements to take shape according to it. He permeates, as it were, the individual part with the spirit of his view—which he holds in his mind and soul—and thereby turns the individual element into something else, or at least presents it in a different light. 

This becomes clearer if we consider the principle that Bengel <note>Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752) was a prominent German Lutheran clergyman and scholar whose "Gnomon" remains a foundational work in New Testament studies.</note> expressed in his *Gnomon*: "Apply yourself wholly to the text; apply the whole matter to yourself" <note>original: "Te totum applica ad textum; rem totam applica ad te."</note>. For as the individual, with the greatest reverence for Holy Scripture, applies all its passages to himself, an individual relationship must emerge between him and these passages. In such a process, one cannot think of a general meaning that is equally clear to everyone—I mean, one that would present itself to everyone as the only correct and exclusive interpretation. 

Even in ordinary life, we find examples of this, where individual biblical passages are applied on specific occasions and are thereby placed in a unique connection and a unique light. This applies not only to biblical passages but often also to passages from classical writers in general. How often is a conversation about a specific subject conducted between educated men, into which passages from poets or orators—with which one or the other is familiar—flow from time to time? These passages then take their context from the conversation itself. In such cases, one cannot demand that a precise philological <term>philological: the branch of knowledge that deals with the structure, historical development, and relationships of a language or languages</term> interpretation be satisfied, as long as they have achieved their effect in this particular instance and contributed to the cultivation and refinement of the dialogue. The same can be said of the proverbs or mottos <note>original: "Sinnsprüche oder Mottos"</note> that writers sometimes place at the beginning of their works, which then, in all brevity, nonetheless...

...are there to express and introduce the thoughts of the book. At first glance, these often seem entirely foreign, and only a deeper engagement—a finer intuition, a mind capable of connecting distant things—discovers all or many of their relationships. Indeed, if we open the Bible, as used to be the custom, to seek comfort or counsel in a specific case, it is this same **creative application** <note>original: "Witz der Anwendung." In this historical context, "Witz" (wit) refers to an ingenious mental faculty or the ability to find hidden connections, rather than modern humor.</note> that teaches us, being full of a particular subject, to apply every single part of the discovered <term>oracle</term> <note>oracle (Orakelspruch): A term used here to describe a biblical verse treated as a direct, prophetic answer to a personal problem.</note> to our own situation in the most detailed manner. — In judging **mystical exegesis**, I believe one must not forget the observation that it is one thing to engage with Holy Scripture as a scholar—as a grammatical exegete—and another to apply it edifyingly to oneself in individual cases. In the first instance, any explanation not contained in the words themselves must be avoided, and only that which has a firm **philological** <note>philological: based on the literal, historical, and linguistic study of the text.</note> basis should be provided. 

Upon this foundation, the individual believer then builds their own structure for their particular needs; and insofar as they are a lover of Holy Scripture, it should not surprise us that, beyond serious study, they occasionally claim the right to *play* with the beloved object—a truth that can also be said, in the best sense, of the lovers of the most serious sciences. I hardly need to add that such play must remain far from the **fundamental articles of faith**, as indeed it usually does; we have found all such writers known to us to be most firmly and warmly convinced of the actual pillars of **Christian doctrine**.

Often he uses his proof-texts in a rather clumsy way, choosing those which have only the most distant allusion to a meaning suitable to him. To prove that Holy Scripture always speaks of the whole of God, he cites **Revelation 1:4**, **Psalm 102:28** <note>original: "Pſalm 101, 28." Particularly characteristic are the cases where he cites passages of the Bible and then explains how the holy writers *must actually have meant* them, where he naturally always attributes his **own opinion** to them.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Pseudo-Dionysius’s literary and exegetical style. The most frequent case is that a lengthy explanation of a specific subject comes first, and then—either inserted into the discussion itself or summarizing everything at the end—there is a biblical saying, though not exactly quoted word-for-word. This saying is usually of such a nature that, according to the first, ordinary view, Dionysius’s intended meaning does not seem to lie within it at all; yet, it can be sensed, felt, or suspected there. (Compare ibid. 4, 13. in its entirety).

Sometimes he poses difficulties for himself, which he then proceeds to solve. At this point, it is appropriate to remark that the New Testament writers did not necessarily have in mind every possible meaning a word could have, nor the multiple senses in which it might be used. However, when an interpreter arrived in later times with knowledge drawn from elsewhere—as is the case here with **Neoplatonic philosophy** <note>Neoplatonism was a school of thought that combined Plato's ideas with mysticism; it heavily influenced early Christian theology.</note>—he sought to prove that the ideas which involuntarily associated themselves in his mind with New Testament words were actually inherent in the words themselves and intentionally placed there. Thus, Dionysius (ibid. 4, 14.) attempts to demonstrate that the distinction between <term>eros</term> <note>original Greek: ἔρως; often translated as "desire" or "passionate love."</note> and <term>agape</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγάπη; usually translated as "brotherly" or "unconditional love."</note> is a biblical one. The words were intended to be significant and rich in references, and it could not fail that someone who searched so eagerly would find whatever meaning and reference he needed or desired within them.

Although Dionysius protects himself by frequently stating that he wishes to put forward nothing but what is scriptural and resting on the foundation of Holy Scripture, his proofs are nevertheless entirely **dialectical** <note>Dialectics here refers to a method of logical argument and philosophical debate.</note> and philosophical. He brings in his biblical citations merely as allusions for confirmation and illustration. He does this with that aforementioned talent of an **ingenious wit** <note>original: "Witz." In this context, it refers to a sharp mental faculty for finding clever or hidden connections between ideas.</note>, which knows how to find distant similarities of meaning in a passage and apply them to a given case, identifying the finer...

**Corderius** <note>Balthasar Corderius (1592–1650) was a Jesuit scholar and editor known for his influential commentaries on the works of Dionysius.</note> provides the following remark in a note (regarding *The Divine Names* 5, 9) concerning the author's <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture.</note>. The author had cited the passage from **Exodus 25** <note>original: 2 Mos. 25.</note>, which according to the **Vulgate** <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the standard for the Catholic Church.</note> reads: *I have shown those things to you.* <note>original Latin: "Nota ostendi illa tibi."</note> Corderius adds: *Note that he was not quoted word-for-word by Dionysius, but according to the sense. For indeed, the apostolic disciples learned from the holy apostles to sometimes cite scripture in this way, just as the holy Apostles themselves occasionally do.* <note>original Latin: "Nota, illum non ad verbum a Dionysio citatum, sed secundum sensum. Sic nimirum apostolici discipuli a sanctis apostolis didicerunt, citare aliquando scripturam, sicut ipsi sancti Apostoli interdum faciunt."</note>

There is also occasionally the use of one or a few words from Holy Scripture without the intention of proving anything, or without any other special purpose in mind.

He seeks to resolve apparent contradictions in Scripture based on his own principles. When he has established the proposition that "God can do all things," he confronts the contradiction found in **2 Timothy 2:13**, which says: "God cannot deny himself," and then resolves it in his own manner. General principles guide his exegesis. One such principle is cited in ***The Heavenly Hierarchy*** **2, 4**, stating that divine things are not signified through similar things, but through dissimilar ones. He also provides the reason why this occurs and then explains what some of these "dissimilar" qualities—such as **wrath**, **impotence**, and so on—mean when they are attributed to God, and in what sense they must be understood when applied to divine matters.

He often falls into direct contradiction with Holy Scripture. An example of this is provided by the eleventh chapter of ***The Heavenly Hierarchy***. There, he finds that in **Psalms 24, 80, and 103** <note>The German text cites Psalms 23, 79, 102; these follow the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering common in older German scholarship, which usually differs by one from modern English Bibles.</note>, classes of angels are called "Powers," which according to his theory are something entirely different; he then helps himself out through his own subtle distinctions.

### 20.

In order to judge the nature of his <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of a religious text.</note> in detail, some examples of particularly characteristic modes of interpretation now follow.

In the book *On the Divine Names* (1, 6), he uses the passage **Genesis 32:29** <note>original: 1 Mos. 32, 29.</note> as proof that Holy Scripture sometimes depicts God as nameless. However, according to the text of the **Septuagint** <note>The influential Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note>, the passage reads: *Tell me your name;* <note>original Greek: "ἀνάγγειλόν μοι τὸ ὄνομά σου"</note> and in another passage, **Judges 13:18** <note>original: Richt. 13, 18.</note>, which Dionysius allows to blend into his work in his usual manner, Manoah asks the angel of the Lord: *What is your name?* <note>original Greek: "τί ὄνομά σου;"</note> and the angel answers: *Why do you ask my name, since it is wonderful?* <note>original Greek: "ἵνατί τοῦτο ἐρωτᾷς τὸ ὄνομά μου, καὶ αὐτὸ ἐστὶ θαυμαστόν"</note> where Dionysius writes: *And why do you ask my name? And this is wonderful.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἵνατί ἐρωτᾷς τὸ ὄνομά μου; καὶ τοῦτο ἔστι θαυμαστόν."</note>

At this point, we must note that the **Areopagite** <note>The name given to the anonymous author of these works, who wrote as if he were the Dionysius mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note> did not use the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament at all—indeed, he could not have used it. His citations of Hebrew words such as the **Seraphim** and the **Cherubim** <note>Traditional names for orders of angels; Seraphim means "burning ones" and Cherubim "full of knowledge."</note> show that he understood nothing of Hebrew. He even admits this himself, for in the very passage where he speaks of the meaning of these angelic names, he refers to those who are "masters of the Hebrew language." This observation does not bring any discredit to the author of the Areopagite writings, as it is well known how rare a knowledge of the Hebrew language was among the **Church Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian theologians and writers.</note>; almost only **Jerome** and **Origen** are cited as being passably knowledgeable in it. At the same time, the cited passage provides evidence for our earlier remark that Dionysius did not quote literally at all, nor did he stick to a single passage, but rather, according to his needs, he took several passages together and, as it were, fused them.

**Ephesians 1:21** <note>original: Ephes. 1, 21.</note> has the text: *far above —— and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the one to come* <note>original Greek: "ὑπεράνω —— καὶ παντὸς ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένου, οὐ μόνον ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι"</note> and Dionysius, who evidently

...keeping this passage in mind, he renders it as: **established high above every name that is named, whether in this age or in the one to come** <note>original Greek: "ὑπεριδρύμενον ὀνόματος ὀνομαζομένου, εἴτε ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, εἴτε ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι"</note> — which demonstrates both his freedom in quoting and his tendency to introduce his beloved **compound words** wherever possible.

From the saying in **Matthew 19:17** (ibid. 2, 1), Dionysius manages to extract the idea that the entire **divine-ruling existence** <note>original Greek: "Θεαρχικὴ ὕπαρξις" (thearchikē hyparxis). His entire treatise *On the Divine Names* actually has an **exegetical** <note>Relating to the critical interpretation of scripture.</note> purpose, but at the same time a **dogmatic** <note>Relating to the established doctrines or beliefs of the church.</note> one. He explains, on the one hand, how these individual names that Holy Scripture uses for God are actually to be understood, and how one must proceed in order not to misunderstand them.

The passage in **Matthew 20:15** (ibid. 2, 1) from the parable of the laborers in the vineyard, "**because I am good,**" is immediately applied by Dionysius as if it were spoken by God Himself; he regards this **good** <note>original Greek: "ἀγαθός"</note> as the attribute of God as the "**primal-good.**"

Regarding **Psalm 103:3** <note>In modern English Bibles, this is usually Psalm 104:30.</note> (ibid. 2, 1), **You shall send forth your spirit, and they shall be created** <note>original Greek: "ἀποστελεῖς τὸ πνεῦμά σου, καὶ κτισθήσονται"</note>, he interprets it as if the passage were speaking specifically about the **Holy Spirit**.

In the same work (2, 2), he expresses his thoughts on Jesus and the Holy Spirit using various figurative expressions, in order to make clear how he seeks to explain the relationship between the two.

To him, **Paul** is (ibid. 2, 11) **he who is great in divine things** <note>original Greek: "ὁ πολὺς τὰ θεῖα"</note> and **the light of the world** <note>original Greek: "τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου"</note>; and in the same place, in the citation of **1 Corinthians 8:5**, he writes simply **of earth** <note>original Greek: "γῆς"</note> instead of **the earth**, and instead of **as**, he uses **as if** <note>original Greek: "ὡσπερὲν" instead of "ὥσπερ".</note>.

**Peter** is called (ibid. 3, 2): **the highest and most senior summit of the theologians** <note>original Greek: "ἡ κορυφαία καὶ πρεσβυτάτη τῶν Θεολόγων ἀκρότης"</note>.

He finds his entire dialectically subtle doctrine of evil, which he drew from the philosopher **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) whose complex systems of logic heavily influenced early Christian mysticism.</note>, in the passage concerning the good and the bad tree in **Matthew 7:18**. The passage (ibid. 5, 8) likewise serves to provide a more precise understanding of his **exegesis** <term>exegesis: the critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture</term>. In this section, he explains why God is described as **multiplied** <note>original: "πολλαπλασιάζεται" (pollaplasiadzitai). This refers to the idea of the One God manifesting in many forms or names.</note> in the Scriptures, and why it is said of Him: **He was, He is, He shall be** <note>original: "ἦν, ἔστι, ἔσται" (ēn, esti, estai)</note>, and **He became, He becomes, He shall become** <note>original: "ἐγένετο, γίνεται, γενήσεται" (egeneto, ginetai, genēsetai)</note>. His common and frequently recurring maxim—that God knows everything, is above all, etc.—is proven (ibid. 7, 2) by citing **Daniel 13:42** <note>In the Septuagint/Catholic Bibles, this is the Story of Susanna, where God is described as the "knower of secrets."</note>.

In the same place (7, 3), he cites Proverbs 8:30 and the Wisdom of Solomon (chapters 7 and 8) in the same allusive manner mentioned above. —

His method of interpreting scripture is shown very clearly (ibid. 7, 4) where he attempts to explain the **Logos** <note>original: "λόγος". In Christian theology, the Divine Word or Reason. Dionysius's explanation here is criticized by the author as being overly vague.</note> and loses himself entirely in expansive and tedious digressions.

All the names bestowed upon God in Holy Scripture, which Dionysius explains, he traces back—with only minor variations—to his concept of the all-sustaining, all-creating **Godhead** that stands above all things; consequently, in this regard, his writing is full of frequent repetitions.

Regarding the passage **Hebrews 4:12**, which is cited (ibid. 9:3), Dionysius adds: "moreover, of all things that are" <note>original: "μᾶλλον δὲ τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων" (mallon de tōn ontōn hapantōn)</note> and explains the verse in terms of the "smallness" of God—likely referring to a spiritual subtlety that permeates all things. —

A strictly **hermeneutical** <term>hermeneutical: relating to the method of interpreting a text, especially scripture</term> observation is found (ibid. 10:3): that Holy Scripture sometimes calls "eternal" <note>original: "αἰώνιον" (aiōnion)</note> that which merely lasts for a long time. As proof, the passage from **Psalm 24:7–9** <note>The text cites Psalm 23 per the Septuagint numbering; in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 24.</note> is cited from the **Septuagint** <term>Septuagint (LXX): The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, used by early Christians.</term>: "Be lifted up, you eternal gates" <note>original: "ἐπάρθητε πύλαι αἰώνιοι" (eparthete pylai aiōnioi)</note>. Dionysius adds: "He calls 'time' <note>original: "χρόνον" (chronon)</note> that which is in birth and decay, in change, and which exists differently at different times." Holy Scripture generally designates "that which truly is" <note>original: "τὰ ὄντα" (ta onta)</note> with the word **aeon** <note>original: "αἰών" (aiōn), often translated as eternity</note>, while designating "things in a state of becoming" <note>original: "τὰ ἐν γενέσει" (ta en genesei)</note> with the word **time** <note>original: "χρόνος" (chronos)</note>. —

Occasionally, we find elaborations on individual scriptural passages which gain a broader meaning and their own particular light through the citation of another passage. For example, in *The Celestial Hierarchy* (1, 1), he interprets the words "Every good and perfect gift comes down from above..." <note>A reference to James 1:17.</note> in such a way that he says: the light proceeds from the Father to us, drawing us upward as a unifying force and filling us. Thus, it leads us toward the Father’s gathering unity and deifying simplicity, which he then proves with the other saying, "that all things are from Him and unto Him" <note>A reference to Romans 11:36.</note>. This could be called an **exegesis through opposites**; for the meaning Dionysius draws from both passages is this: Not only does everything come down from the Father according to the first saying, but according to the second, everything also goes up to Him—at least, everything that is good.

I shall add a few more points concerning both the exegesis and the **dogma** <term>dogma: the established beliefs or doctrines of a religious group</term> of Dionysius, which are included here simply to more fully understand the perspectives through which he judged and utilized Holy Scripture.

### 21.

From these individual passages drawn from the writings of Dionysius, the nature of his <term>exegesis</term> <note>exegesis: the critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture</note> can be sufficiently understood. This method of interpretation remained common among all subsequent mystics; they developed it even further and, in particular, pushed its playful application to the highest degree. I will cite a few examples of this expansion, choosing first the first treatise from the works of the famous mystic Richard of Saint Victor, which deals with "The Eradication of Evil and the Promotion of Good." The entire treatise is a mystical interpretation of the fifth verse of the hundred and fourteenth Psalm; it reads as follows:

### 9.

Let us also consider how the seawater—those bitter waves—is out of the way for some and in the way for others. Who doubts that this life is the way to the future life? One person fears for the things of the present life, another for those of the future. For the one who fears for the things of this life, the sea is in the way. For the one who fears for what lies beyond this life, the sea is beside the way. In this life, good and evil exist together; in that life, there is only good or only evil. This life, however, lies between the things of the future life—between the good and the evil—as if in the middle, because it approaches both with some similarity and has good and evil mixed together. ### 10.

Sorrow for certain goods is the sea on the right; sorrow for certain evils is the sea on the left. <note>In this allegory, the "right" represents the fear of losing spiritual or worldly blessings, while the "left" represents the fear of falling into suffering or sin, mirroring the walls of water that flanked the Israelites.</note> Certainly, if we are otherwise in our right minds, we must fear for both, be anxious, and overflow in bitter tears. We should fear losing those [the goods], and we should fear falling into these [the evils], and thus we have a double sea that strongly protects us on both sides. In the right manner, I believe, we strike the sea that blocks our way, hinders our journey, and cuts off our course with the <term>rod of righteous severity</term> <note>The "rod" is a reference to Moses' staff, here interpreted as a disciplined and rigorous spiritual life.</note>; we terrify it with the contemplation of divine punishment and push it aside by renewing our focus on the future trial. 

Thus, all our fear and all our sorrow should be removed from the path, and for this useless life—the concern for worldly life—our anxiety should be divided between the two, so that through the sorrow of fear we make eternal evils vanish, and through the tears of longing we exchange them for eternal goods. Happy are those who pass through this double sea of double sorrow, who leave all doubt and fear of future expectation far behind them, and who overcome the general mourning of mistrust with the certainty of a sure hope. May such fear and such sorrow also be annihilated in us by the overwhelming security of trust. Let this sea also flee and give way, so that we too may sing with the Prophet:

In such an expansive manner does <term>Richard of Saint Victor<note>A 12th-century theologian and prior of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris, famous for his works on mystical contemplation.</note></term> interpret and paraphrase a single verse, in order to attach what he wished to present, precisely in the manner of <term>Dionysius<note>Referring to Dionysius the Areopagite (or Pseudo-Dionysius), a highly influential mystical author whose 5th-century writings merged Christian doctrine with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note></term>. One notices in him, as in the Areopagite, an extraordinary knowledge of the Bible and an almost even greater talent for twisting and interpreting individual passages to suit his aims. We note that this is only the first foundation upon which Richard then erects his systematic structure of mystical theology; but how greatly he already agrees with the Areopagite in these few points! Everything is intended to establish a contempt for all things earthly and to elevate the soul into the higher **intelligible regions** <note>The realm of spiritual reality that can only be understood by the intellect or the soul, rather than the physical senses.</note>. Every passage—no matter how distinct, clear, or obviously historical and narrative it may be in itself—must take its share of the light and warmth that emanate from the mind and imagination of the mystical interpreter. Indeed, this passage does not lack the words that are so characteristic of the Dionysian writings, such as the word <term>unlikeness<note>original Latin: *dissimilitudo*; original Greek: *ἀνομοιότης* (anomoiotēs). A central concept in "negative theology," where God is described by how He differs from created things to emphasize His transcendence.</note></term>

# 1.

The manner of Dionysius’s presentation is characterized by the unusually frequent use of <term>superlatives</term> <note>Words expressing the highest degree of a quality, such as "most high" or "most radiant."</note> and words compounded with the <term>alpha privative</term> <note>original: "α privativum"; a Greek prefix (a- or an-) indicating negation or absence, similar to the English "un-" or "in-," as in "infinite" or "invisible."</note>, by his pompous circumlocutions for the names of holy things, by the general turgidity of his expression, by the length of his sentences, by the recurring formulas and expressions of modesty, by the disorder in which he jumbles his sentences together, by the warmth with which he speaks, and by the preciousness with which he transforms simple expressions of simple concepts into more unusual and elevated ones.

All these characteristics arise from the very purpose and essence of his writings.

# 2.

By far the greater part of his treatises is concerned with suggesting and explaining the incomprehensibility, the exuberance, and the absolute sublimity of God. Because of this, he was forced to use superlatives; indeed, he seeks to further elevate these superlatives through compounding and accumulation, in order to express through language itself the infinite height at which the divine essence resides. Above matter, above the inorganic and the organic, above plants and animals, above man himself, above understanding, imagination, and spirit, he exalts the God of whom he hardly dares to speak, and can therefore only speak of Him in

### 3.

Directly connected to this is the use of words compounded with the <term>alpha privative</term> <note>original: "a privativo"; a Greek and Latin prefix (a- or an-) that negates the word following it, such as "in-" or "un-" in English.</note>. God is nothing of that which man can see, feel, imagine, think, or sense. His concept is an eternal negation and privation <note>The state of being deprived of or lacking a quality; in theology, this refers to describing God by what He is NOT.</note>, and all that exists must be marked, as it were, with that negative letter in order to distinguish it from God. But because He is not "not-everything-thinkable" out of deficiency, but rather out of unfathomable sublimity above all things, there are also compounds with <term>hyper</term> <note>original: "ὑπὲρ"; meaning "above," "beyond," or "over."</note>, which express this sublimity with a slightly changed sense, just as the negative compounds did. And to indicate the actual essence and being of God even more clearly, compounds with <term>auto</term> <note>original: "αὐτὸ"; meaning "self."</note> and <term>arche</term> <note>original: "ἀρχὴ"; meaning "origin," "source," or "first principle."</note> are called upon for help, indicating that God is perfect, self-sufficient in Himself, and the source and essence of the entire universe.

<meta>This page continues the stylistic analysis of Dionysius, moving from his use of superlatives to his creation of a specialized, "mysterious" vocabulary designed to distinguish initiates from the common crowd.</meta>

## 4.

Everything connected with the service of God and the Church he never names with the actual, conventional words, but with others he has fashioned himself, which carry the appearance of mystery. With him, the ordinary classes of clergy do not have their customary names, but others. He calls them Hierarchs, Priests <note>original: "ἱερεῖς" (*hiereis*)</note>, Hierophants <note>A priest who interprets sacred mysteries or esoteric principles.</note>, and Liturgists. To baptism, the Lord's Supper, Holy Scripture, and the sacred writers, he gives his own names; these are easy enough to decipher, but they fit his purpose perfectly: to appear as a "consecrated one" or a teacher of secrets. For he does not write for the masses, nor for an unvetted, unseparated heap, but for a few highly-consecrated <term>mystai</term> <note>original: "Mysten"; initiates into secret religious rites.</note> who have penetrated into the depths of divine mysteries. Their knowledge of sacred objects relates to the expressions he uses for them in exactly the same way that the dark ignorance of the masses relates to the common expressions with which they must content themselves. Herein lies the entire character of the Areopagite style of writing.

What he writes are mysteries. Just as in all secret orders, alliances, and societies, signs of recognition have always been bound to certain names, titles, and expressions—which the confidant alone could then connect to the true and striking meaning—so it is here. Indeed, just as the initiated members themselves changed their names (as happened with monks who received a new name upon entering an order), Dionysius speaks as an <term>epopt</term> <note>original: "Epopte"; from the Greek *epoptes*, meaning an eyewitness or one who has attained the highest level of initiation.</note> for those who know. Through his unusual terminology, he separates his "high theosophy" <note>A system of philosophy or religion which proposes to establish direct, personal knowledge of the divine.</note> from anything common.

## 5.

These previously mentioned peculiarities give his style that turgid appearance which, to all those who occupy themselves with him, is evident at first glance—

strikes one in a startling way. This effect is further increased by the fact that he generally prefers to use compound words of all kinds. Even the most fleeting glance at any page reveals words such as **moved by the Father** <note>original: "πατροκινητός" (*patrokinētos*)</note>, **manifestation of light** <note>original: "Φωτοφανεία" (*photophaneia*)</note>, **giver of good** <note>original: "ἀγαδοδότης" (*agathodotēs*)</note>, **unifying** <note>original: "ἑνοποιός" (*henopoios*; literally "making one")</note>, **deifying** <note>original: "θεοποιός" (*theopoios*; literally "making divine")</note>, and **handed down from the Father** <note>original: "πατροπαραδοτός" (*patroparadotos*)</note>, among others. Listing them all here is unnecessary, as they have been carefully preserved in the translation itself and rendered to reflect the full peculiarity of the original.

->6.<-

The length of his sentences also strikes one unpleasantly. This is explained by the fact that he always feels an inner urge to say everything he knows, possesses, and senses about a subject. Particularly in the book *On the Divine Names*, within his definitions—or rather his explanations—of the individual titles of God, he repeatedly cites everything that God is under that specific name, how He cannot be thought of, and everything over which He is exalted. In seeking to satisfy this urge, he does not easily find an end; to exhaust the subject, he draws everything he can possibly grasp into his circle. Thus, because the sophisticated and rich language of the **Platonic philosophers** <note>referring to Neoplatonists like Proclus, whose complex terminology heavily influenced Dionysius</note> did not easily fail him, and because his extraordinary knowledge of the Bible was at his command, he stretches his sentences to an improper length.

->7.<-

Furthermore, the modesty with which he expresses himself is characteristic, manifesting in the recurring use of restrictive phrases. He hardly dares to touch such highly holy things; he hardly dares to utter even an echo of them. Human nature in general is not capable of true insight into these matters—much less he himself, who only timidly approaches with...

with the weakest of strengths, he set about a work that was far too heavy and high for him. Therefore, to understand his manner, one must look particularly at those expressions that signify precisely what was just mentioned. He explains divine truths only **according to what is permitted** <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ θεμιτὸν" (*kata to themiton*)</note>, **as far as is attainable** <note>original: "ὡς ἐφικτόν" (*hōs ephikton*)</note>, **sufficiently for our capacity** <note>original: "ὡς καθ' ἡμᾶς ἱκανῶς" (*hōs kath' hēmas hikanōs*)</note>, **as far as possible** <note>original: "ὡς δυνατόν" (*hōs dynaton*)</note>, and **to the extent of one’s power** <note>original: "ὅση δύναμις" (*hosē dynamis*)</note>; he says of himself: **"and for us, who fall far short of many good men"** <note>original: "καὶ ἡμῖν πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀπολειπομένοις" (*kai hēmin pollōn andrōn agathōn apoleipomenois*)</note>.

### 8.

One cannot think of an ordered method of presentation in the way such order is conceived in our own times when reading Dionysius. He does indeed have a certain order in his books *On the Celestial Hierarchy* and *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where the subject matter itself dictated the sequence in which he had to let the individual parts of his treatise follow one another. One misses this order all the more in the writing *On the Divine Names*. There, a few simple sentences placed at the beginning would have saved him from countless repetitions. For fundamentally, in the aforementioned treatise, using ever-recurring words and sentences, only the simple assertion is made: that all the names of God in the Holy Scriptures are different only in appearance, while in themselves and in their actual sense, they are merely synonyms. 

He needed only to put forward the **Platonic concept of God** <note>the philosophical idea of God as the ultimate, simple source of all reality</note> and explain it in its individual parts, so that he could then, referring back to it, say in a few pages that this concept is expressed in all those names of God—**the Good** <note>original: "ἀγαθός" (*agathos*)</note>, **the One** <note>original: "ἕν" (*hen*)</note>, and so on—and why and how it can be demonstrated in them without any effort. But the importance he gave to his work and the air of mystery did not allow for that. To maintain this mystery, the "initiate" had to interpret everything for the "laypeople" in proper order, in great detail, and with continued solemnity.

### 9.

How this type of style was prepared among the Church Fathers from Clement of Alexandria onwards <note>Clement (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who integrated Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine</note>, how it had already reached a high level especially with Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople, known for his eloquent "golden-mouthed" preaching</note> and shows itself as closely related to the Dionysian manner of expression, others before us have demonstrated—particularly Dalläus <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Protestant scholar</note> in the treatise we have cited, and Casaubonus <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar</note> in the sixteenth of his *Exercitationes* <note>original: "Exercitationen"; refers to scholarly refutations</note> against Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian</note>. Speculative mysticism has always made use of this style, since Dionysius was constantly regarded by it as a high, unsurpassable model, and it has occasionally fallen into even more abstruse and obscure territory. But we need not add that we consider this mysticism and this style as by no means recommendable.

Expression and language appear quite differently in the practical mystics of all centuries. Their language is the language of hearty, deep, inward emotion, of a lively feeling, and of a deeply inspired view of the inner life. It is the language of experience. One can assert that these mystics were always ahead of their centuries in language in terms of clarity, intimacy, and freedom from affectation. Of these actually practical mystics, however, who kept themselves pure from excessive enthusiasm and fanaticism, there are relatively few. They always express themselves most beautifully in those works where they give an unadorned account of their own lives, of their experiences, and of their spiritual guidance. From the *Lives of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: "Leben der Altväter"; refers to the *Vitae Patrum*, stories of early Christian hermits</note> down to the most recent times, we have a rich supply in this regard; and the more excellent of these works are, following Luther's example, also almost universally recognized. It goes without saying that one should separate out everything superstitious, meddlesome, and everything based on self-deception, and not forget to measure every individual detail against the standard of Holy Scripture, which for us Protestants alone

He highlights that practical mystical accounts of personal experience are highly valued in the Protestant tradition, provided they are measured against Scripture.</summary>

is the rule and guide. But for this very reason, a history of mysticism is so necessary. Even in our own time, people lump together the noble and the ignoble, the true and the false, inspiration and madness, the warmth of inner religion and absurdity into the broad category of mysticism; and after throwing everything into one pile, one is quick to condemn the entire mass. 

It is certainly more difficult to separate the fanatics and the ecstatic <note>original: "Exaltirten"; referring to those in states of religious trance or intense emotional excitement</note>, the chiliasts <note>term: Chiliasts; those who believe in a literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ, often used here to imply radical or apocalyptic groups</note> and the visionaries, the erring and the wavering, from the good, and to present them in distinct categories. However, a proper judgment of this significant part of church history is not possible at all unless one examines the individual classes separately—without bias, but with a love for eternal truth, and without any hatred except for that of superficiality and unjust condemnations, whether they come from church council tribunals or elsewhere—recognizing the good wherever it is found and discarding the bad wherever it is encountered. 

The true source for understanding the mystical sense in general lies in these mentioned biographies of individuals. However, applying sober and just criticism to them is harder than one might think without having tried it.

# Marsilio Ficino.

->(Concerning the ninth book of the sixth Ennead of Plotinus).<-

Insofar as every unity exists within its multiplicity <note>The "many" or the various parts that make up a whole</note>, it preserves its essence <term>Wesenheit: the intrinsic nature or indispensable quality of something that determines its character</term>, which is lost once unity is dissolved. Unity, therefore, sustains essence, and it likewise completes both essence and Being. The unity that reigns within its opposite multiplicity neither consists of itself, nor has it emerged from that opposing multiplicity; rather, it originates from the pure Unity, which exists simply in itself above all manifold essence. When one says: "a body" and "a soul," or "a heat" and "a cold," the unity predicated here is neither a body—otherwise it could not apply to the soul—nor a coldness—otherwise it would not fit the heat. Through a similar conclusion, one finds that the One in itself is higher than any essence; it is through the power of the One that everything which participates more in Unity thereby also shares more in essence.

Moreover, the highest perfection of Being <note>original: "Seyenden"</note> in itself consists in identity <note>original: "Einerleiheit"; the state of being the same or having a unified nature</note> and constancy; but these have their ground in Unity, just as diversity and motion have their ground in number. Therefore, the Unity which is the cause of motion for Being is higher than Being itself. One says now either that Being is one and the same as Unity, or that it is distinct from it. It must certainly be admitted that Unity is the ground of identity; if one therefore asserts the former—that Being is one and the same with Unity—then there certainly exists, prior to this unity, a Unity that is earlier than it, by which it is made one and the same. If, however, one asserts the latter—that Unity is distinct from Being—then Unity in itself is indeed prior, one and—

# The Ninth Book of the Sixth Ennead
### of
## P l o t i n u s.

---

->§. 1.<-

All beings <note>original Greek: ὄντα (onta)</note> exist through the One; both those that are primary beings, and those which are said to exist in any way among beings. For what could anything be, if it were not one? If the "one" is taken away, a thing is no longer what it was said to be. For an army is no longer an army if it is not a single unit; nor is a choir or a herd, if they are not one. Even a house or a ship cannot exist if they do not possess unity, for the house is a single thing and the ship is a single thing; if they lose this unity, the house is no longer a house, and the ship is no longer a ship. 

Therefore, continuous <note>original Greek: συνεχῆ (synechē)</note> magnitudes would not exist at all if the One were not within them. If they are divided—insofar as they lose their unity—they also change their very being. Is it not then the case that for every individual thing that is partially (<note>original Greek: κατὰ μέρος (kata meros)</note>) one, its <term>essence</term> (<note>German: Wesenheit. In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the true nature or substance of a thing.</note>) and the One are one and the same? And in the case of <term>Being</term> (<note>German: Seyende</note>) and essence, are its essence, Being, and the One not all one and the same? If so, whoever has found Being would also have found the One, and essence would be the same as the One. What then! If the <term>Intellect</term> (<note>German: Geist. Plotinus uses this term to refer to the "Nous," the divine mind or second hypostasis in his system.</note>) were essence, the Intellect would also be the One—the Intellect being that which is Primarily Being and the Primary One. And by communicating Being to others, it would simultaneously and to the same degree communicate the One to them.

For what else besides these (Intellect and essence) could one call "the One"? For "man" and "a man" are one and the same; or, just as every individual thing has a number—as when you say of something that there are two—so one says "the One" of a single thing (<note>original Greek: μόνον τινὸς (monou tinos)</note>). Now, if there is a number of Beings, then clearly there is also the One, and it must be investigated what it is. If counting is merely an activity that the Soul performs, then the One will not exist within the things themselves. But it was said (<note>original Greek: ἔλεγεν ὁ λόγος (elegen ho logos) – literally "the argument said"</note>) that if an individual thing loses the One, it can no longer exist at all.

Now we must see whether the individual "one" and "Being" are one and the same, and whether <term>universal</term> (<note>original Greek: ὅλως (holōs)</note>) Being and the One are the same. But if the Being of each individual thing is a <term>multiplicity</term> (<note>German: Vielheit</note>), whereas the One cannot possibly be a multiplicity, then the two must be different. Man, for instance, is a "living being" (<note>original Greek: ζῶον (zōon)</note>) and "rational" (<note>original Greek: λογικόν (logikon)</note>) and many parts. And this many-ness is bound together by the One. Thus, man is one thing and the One is another. For the One is

And if it is at once the thinking subject (<note>original Greek: νοοῦν (nooun)</note>) and the object being thought (<note>original Greek: νοούμενον (nooumenon)</note>), it will be double and not simple, and therefore it cannot be the One. 

If it looks at something different from itself, it looks entirely at that which is higher and precedes it. But if it looks both at itself and at that which is higher, it is likewise a "Second"; and one must posit the Intellect as that which stays with the Good and the First, gazing upon it, while also staying with itself, thinking itself, and thinking that it is itself the totality of Being. 

Since the Intellect is so manifold, it is far from being the One; thus the One will not be "all things," for then it would no longer be the One. Nor is the One the Intellect, for then it would be all things (since the Intellect is all things); nor is it Being, for Being too is all things.

### §. 3.

But what should the One be? And what nature should it have? It is not surprising that this cannot be easily expressed, since it is not easy even in the case of <term>Being</term> (<note>German: Seyenden. In Neoplatonism, this refers to the realm of true existence or the Intelligible world.</note>) and <term>Form</term> (<note>German: Gestalt. Referring to the Platonic Ideas.</note>), and indeed our knowledge (<note>original Greek: γνῶσις (gnōsis)</note>) is based on forms. When the soul approaches the formless, which it cannot grasp—because it is neither limited nor shaped (<note>original Greek: τυπῶσθαι (typōsthai)</note>) by a manifold shaper—it wavers and fears that it will find (<note>original Greek: ἔχει (echei)</note>) nothing there. Therefore, such things are difficult for the soul, and it gladly descends, often falling away from everything until it reaches the realm of sensory perception; there it rests as if on solid ground, just as the eye (<note>original Greek: ὄψις (opsis)</note>), when exhausted by small things, gladly alights upon the large. 

When the soul wants to look into itself, seeing itself alone through being-together, and being one because it is one with it <note>The soul becomes one with the object of its contemplation, the Intellect or the One</note>, it does not believe it possesses what it seeks, because it is not distinct from that which is thought. The same must be done by those who wish to philosophize about the One. Because it is the One we seek, and because we look toward the <term>Origin</term> (<note>German: Ursprung. Plotinus uses this for the 'Arche,' the ultimate source.</note>) of all things—the Good and the First—we must not stay far from what surrounds the First by falling into the lowest of all things. Instead, striving for the First, we must lead ourselves away from the lowest sensory existences; we must be removed from all sin, like those hurrying toward the Good. We must ascend to the Origin within ourselves and become "one" out of many, if we wish to become beholders of the Origin and the One. 

The seeker must become <term>Intellect</term> (<note>German: Geist. Representing 'Nous,' the divine mind that is the second level of reality below the One.</note>), entrusting their soul entirely to the Intellect and grounding it there, so that what the Intellect sees, the soul also receives with wakefulness, beholding the One through the Intellect. One must add no sensory perception, nor let anything of it pass into that which is to be perceived, but rather see the Purest with the pure Intellect, and with the highest part of the Intellect. For all these things belong to the realm of Being and make it a multiplicity. 

But why does it not "stand" if it is not moved? Because for a Being, it must be one of these two or both. That which stands is standing by virtue of <term>Rest</term> (<note>original Greek: στάσει (stasei)</note>), but it is not one and the same as Rest itself; therefore, "standing" would belong to it as an attribute (<note>original Greek: συμβήσεται (symbēsetai)</note>), and it would no longer remain simple. Even when we call the One the "First Cause," we do not mean to assert that an attribute (<note>original Greek: συμβεβηκός (symbebēkos)</note>) belongs to it, but only that we receive something from it, while it remains within itself. This simultaneous plurality is the intelligible world, which stands closest to the First <note>The One</note>. This First must necessarily exist if it can be proven that a soul exists, and this First must be more essential and higher <note>original Greek: *kyriōteron*; more primary or authoritative</note> than the soul. Yet, even this Mind is not the ultimate First, because it is not truly One and not simple. But the One is simple and is the origin of all things. 

What, then, exists before the most precious of all Beings? If something must exist before the Mind—which desires to be One, but is not One, being instead merely uniform <note>original German: *eingestaltig*</note> because it is not dispersed within itself, but is truly in and with itself, and does not fracture itself because it stands so close after the One—even though it "dares," in a sense, to distance itself from the One? That which exists before these is a wonder: the One, which is not a "Being" <note>In Plotinian philosophy, the One is "beyond being" (*epekeina tēs ousias*); if it were a "being," it would be one of many things, rather than the source of all.</note>, lest this "One" be spoken of as a property of something else. In truth, no name actually belongs to it. But if we must name it, it is, generally speaking, appropriately called "the One."

<meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically Book VI, Chapter 9. ...be named, not as if it were some other thing and then "the One." For this reason, it is difficult to recognize; yet it is best recognized through its product, which is Essence <term>Wesenheit</term> <note>original: *Wesenheit*; this refers to the Greek *ousia*, the true substance or being of things</note>. The Mind <note>original: *Geist*; the divine Intellect or *Nous*</note> leads toward this Essence, and its nature is such that it is the source of everything best, a power that generates all that exists <note>original: *das Seyende*</note>. This power remains within itself and is never diminished, nor is it contained within the things that have come into existence beneath it. Because it exists before these things, we must necessarily call it the "One," so that we may designate it with a name among ourselves and lead ourselves toward an undivided understanding <note>original Greek: *ἔννοιαν* (ennoian)</note>; and we do this because we desire the soul itself to be one. When we call it the "One" and "indivisible," we do not mean it in the same sense as a point or a unit <term>Monad</term> <note>original: *Monas*; the basic unit in mathematics</note>. For that which is "One" in a mathematical sense is merely the origin of quantity, which could never exist if Essence did not exist first—and this source is prior even to Essence. Therefore, we must not think of the One in those terms, but rather consider it as being represented by them only through analogy, by its simplicity and its rejection of multiplicity and division.

### §. 6.

How then should we name the One, or in what way can we adapt it to our spiritual thinking? We must posit it as being "One" in a far higher degree <note>original Greek: *πλειόνως* (pleionōs)</note> than we assume the unit or the point to be one. For in the case of a point or unit, the soul strips away physical magnitude and the multiplicity of numbers to arrive at the smallest possible thing; it rests upon something that is indeed indivisible, but which was formerly part of something divided and which still exists within something else. But the One is not within another thing, it is not within a divided whole, and it is not "indivisible" in the sense of being the "smallest" part. On the contrary, it is the greatest of all—not in terms of physical size, but in power. It is "sizeless" in its power, just as those things that exist after it are undivided in their powers, rather than being indivisible in their physical mass.

<summary>This page explains that "the One" is the ultimate source of reality, distinguished from mathematical units or points because it exists prior to all quantity and essence. It characterizes the One as a supreme, indivisible power rather than a physical or numerical "smallest part."</summary>
