One must also assume it to be the Infinite—not as something that cannot be traversed in size or number, but as something that cannot be encompassed in its power. For if you think of it as Mind <note>original: *Geist*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the Divine Intellect or *Nous*</note> or God, it is still more; and if you unify it through the faculty of reason <note>original Greek: *διάνοια* (dianoia); this refers to the human ability to think through things logically or discursively</note>, it is more even there; even if you think of it as a God and raise it up to the most unified point of your spiritual thought. For it is within itself, and nothing is added to it. Even through the concepts of the self-sufficient and the unity of itself, one cannot sufficiently define the One. For it must be the most sufficient of all, the most self-sufficient, the most without need. 

But everything that is many and not One is needy, since it is not one thing but has become out of many. Its essence <term>Essence</term> <note>original: *Wesenheit*; this is the German translation for the Greek *ousia*, meaning the true substance or "being" of a thing</note> thus requires the state of being one. This [the One], however, does not need itself, for it *is* itself; but whatever is many needs as much as it is. And every individual part of that which is within it—since it exists because of others and not in itself—is in need of those others; and in relation to the One and the whole, it reveals itself as something lacking. If, then, something must be most self-sufficient, it must be the One, since it alone is such that it needs neither itself nor another. 

For it seeks nothing so that it may be, or so that it may be well, or so that it may have something to lean upon. Since it is the cause of others, it does not receive what it is, or its well-being, from those others. For what should come to it from the outside? Therefore, well-being does not "belong" to it as an external quality; for it is well-being itself. It also has no place, for it needs no support; unlike inanimate things that cannot carry themselves and are therefore supported, or a physical mass that falls if it is not held up. For everything else is supported by that through which it exists, and it occupies the place where it has been set. Thus, that which seeks a place is also needy. But the origin <term>Origin</term> <note>original: *Ursprung*; referring to the *arche*, the first principle from which all things flow</note> is not in need of that which comes after it. And the origin of

<summary>Plotinus argues that "the One" is defined by its absolute self-sufficiency and infinite power, existing beyond the needs and spatial limitations that define all other beings. Unlike the "Many," which depend on parts and external support to exist, the One is the uncaused cause that requires nothing from its own creations.</summary>

--- Page 383 ---
<meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s Enneads, Book VI, Chapter 9, Section 6. The previous page discussed how the One is the most self-sufficient of all things, needing neither itself nor any other, while all multiple things are inherently needy.</meta>

...be, it absolutely needs nothing from anything. For that which is in need is in need because it strives toward its origin <term>Origin</term> <note>original: *Ursprung*; in Neoplatonic thought, this is the *arche*, the starting point or source from which all reality flows</note>. Now, if the One were in need, it would clearly no longer be seeking to be One; it would thus be in need of that which would destroy its own nature. Everything that is said to be in need, however, is in need of its own well-being and that which preserves it. 

To the One, therefore, nothing is "a good," and thus it has no will or desire toward anything; rather, it is supra-good <note>original: *übergut*; this translates the Greek *hyperagathon*, suggesting a reality that does not just possess "goodness" as a quality, but is the very source beyond the concept itself</note>. It is not good for itself, but rather good for others, should anything be able to participate in it. There is no intellectual thinking <note>original: *geistiges Denken*; this refers to the activity of the *Nous* or Divine Mind</note> within it, so that no "otherness" exists within it, nor is there any movement. For the One exists prior to movement and prior to intellectual thinking. 

For what should it think? Itself? In that case, it would have been ignorant before the act of thinking and would have needed thinking in order to know itself, even though it is already self-sufficient within itself. But because it does not "know" and does not "think" itself, no ignorance will be found within it. For ignorance only occurs in the presence of "another"—when one thing knows nothing of another. But that which stands alone neither knows, nor has anything that it does not know. Since it is One, and is present with itself, it does not need to think of itself. 

For one does not even need to add this concept of "being present with itself" in order to preserve its status as One. One must also strip away the acts of thinking and understanding <note>original: *συνιέναι* (sunienai); to perceive or comprehend together</note>, as well as the thinking of itself and of any other. One must not categorize Him—God—according to the one who thinks <note>original: *κατὰ τὸν νοοῦντα* (kata ton noounta); according to the thinking subject</note>, but rather according to Thought itself. But this Thought does not think; instead, it is the cause of thinking for another. 

The cause, however, is not one and the same as the effect; this Cause of all things is therefore none of those things which it causes. Therefore, we must not call it "the Good" simply because of the benefit it gives to others, but rather "the Good" in another sense—a Goodness that sits above all other goods.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the One is so perfectly self-sufficient that it lacks even the "need" to think or know itself, as thinking would imply a division between the thinker and the object of thought. He concludes that the One is the "supra-good" cause of intellect, but remains distinct from all its effects.</summary>
<keywords>The One, Neoplatonism, self-sufficiency, intellectual thinking, supra-good, Divine Mind, causality, Plotinus</keywords>

## §. 17.

But if, because God <note>The translator uses "God" here to refer to "The One," the absolute source of reality in Plotinus's philosophy.</note> is none of these things, you are uncertain in your knowledge, then direct your attention toward yourself; and from yourself, direct it toward God. But as you direct yourself toward God, do not cast aside the discursive intellect <note>original: *mê epirriptōn tēn dianoian*; the faculty of the mind that reasons step-by-step</note>; for he is not "nowhere" in such a way that he deprives everything else of his presence. Rather, he is present to whoever is able to touch him "there" <note>original: *ekeî*; a term Neoplatonists used for the higher, intelligible realm beyond the physical world</note>; but to those unable to do so, he is not present. Just as in other cases no specific thinking occurs if the thinker is contemplating something else or is focused elsewhere, so too must one understand here: one must not add anything to the object of thought for it to be what it is. Likewise, one who holds another mental image <note>original: *typon*; a stamp or impression</note> in the soul cannot think of God as long as that image is active. 

Just as the soul, when preoccupied and held by other things, cannot be shaped according to the image of the opposite, so too must the soul become completely "without quality" <note>original: *apoion*; a technical term in ancient physics. For matter to receive the form of "hot," it must not already be "cold."</note> if it is to receive the images of everything. Even more so, the soul must become formless <note>original: *aneideon*</note> if it is to have no hindrance within itself for its fulfillment and illumination by the "First Nature" <note>The One, the highest principle of reality.</note>. If this is the case, the soul must release itself from everything external and turn entirely inward; it must not lean toward anything on the outside, but instead must ignore everything—first in terms of its own disposition, and then even in terms of forms. It must not even know itself, but exist entirely in the beholding of that One. It must be with him, and only after it has spent enough time in his company should it come back and, if possible, announce this communion to others. 

Minos <note>In Greek mythology, the King of Crete and a judge in the underworld, famous for his wisdom and lawgiving.</note> likely enjoyed such communion in the past, and for this reason, it is said that he was a companion <note>original: *oaristēs*; an intimate friend or one who speaks face-to-face</note> of Zeus. Remembering this communion, and having been touched by the Divine, he produced the after-images of it: the laws. By this touch of the divine law-

In this dance, however, he sees the source of life, the source of the mind <note>German: *Geist*; in Plotinus’s philosophy, this usually refers to *Nous*, the Divine Intellect</note>, the origin of being, the cause of the Good, and the root of the soul; yet these do not flow out from God in such a way as to diminish Him. There the soul finds rest and is beyond evils, having ascended to the place free from evils; there she thinks <note>original Greek: *noei*; refers to pure intellectual contemplation</note>, and is free from every impression <note>original Greek: *apathēs*; meaning impassivity or being unaffected by external stimuli</note>, and there is true life <note>original Greek: *alēthōs zēn*</note>. For the life that is now lived without God is only a trace of life, which merely imitates that life. The life there, however, is an activity of the mind <note>German: *Wirksamkeit des Geistes*; the Greek *energeia* of *Nous*</note>, and this activity also produces gods by touching that One (God) in peace and stillness <note>original Greek: *en hēsychō*</note>; it produces beauty, it produces justice, it produces virtue. For this is what the soul conceives <note>original Greek: *kyei*</note> when she is filled with God, and this is her origin and her goal. Origin, because she is from there; but goal, because her Good is there, and because when she arrives there, she becomes what she was.

### §. 11.

This was the meaning intended by the law of the Mysteries <note>original: *Mysterien*; referring to the ancient Greek "Mystery Cults" like the Eleusinian Mysteries, which required initiates to keep their experiences secret</note>, that the secret should not be made known to the uninitiated. For that realm should not be made public, and therefore the law forbade revealing the Divine to another who has not himself been granted the happiness of seeing it. Since they were not two, but the seer and the seen were one—as the seen was not an "object of vision" but a thing unified—if one who was mingled with it remembers it, he will hold the image of it within himself. He was one and the <unclear>same</unclear>, and was in himself not at all different, nor was he different in relation to others; for nothing moved within him, no anger, no desire for another was in him, he who had already ascended; but there was also no Reason <note>original: <term>Logos</term>; the principle of rational thought or logical discourse</note>, no spiritual thinking—indeed, not even he himself, if one may say so. Instead, as if carried away or inspired, he stood quietly in an unmoving, silent state, in no way turning away from his own essence, nor turning around himself, but standing entirely and, as it were, having become Stillness <note>original Greek: *stasis* (στάσις); meaning a state of standing, stability, or a complete lack of motion</note> itself. Even from beautiful things <note>original Greek: *tōn kalōn* (τῶν καλῶν)</note> he no longer turns; for he goes even beyond the Beautiful <note>original Greek: *to kalon* (τό καλόν)</note> itself. He even steps beyond the circle of the virtues,

<meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s Enneads, Book VI, Chapter 9, Section 11. Plotinus is using the metaphor of a temple's inner sanctuary (the adyton) to describe the soul's mystical union with "the One" or the "Origin."</meta>

...as when one enters into the interior of the sanctuary, leaving behind the statues in the temple. Upon leaving the sanctuary, these statues are the first things that encounter him again, following his vision within and his communion <note>original: *συνουσίαν* (synousia); meaning a deep being-together or spiritual intercourse</note> there. Once inside, he looks upon no statue and no image, but upon the thing itself—the Archetype; these statues and images are merely secondary objects of sight. 

But the "Origin" itself is perhaps not even an object seen; rather, there is another kind of seeing there: ecstasy, becoming simple <note>original: *Einfachwerden*; referring to the Neoplatonic concept of *haplosis*, or the soul stripping away all complexity to reach unity</note>, a surrendering of oneself to it, a longing for its attainment, and a state of stillness and contemplation to be in harmony with it. For if someone sees it in this way within the sanctuary, he truly sees; but if he looks in any other way, nothing is present to him. 

These imitations are also hinted at by the wise prophets, who show how that God is to be beheld. The wise priest, who understands the riddle <note>original: *αἴνιγμα* (ainigma)</note>, possesses the true vision of the sanctuary when he is there. If he has not yet reached it, he considers this sanctuary to be something invisible, and he will understand the "Source and Origin" only as an abstract starting point. But if he is within it, then he sees the Origin and is together with it—like joined with like—leaving aside nothing of the divine that the soul is capable of possessing. 

Before the vision, the soul asks for what remains to be gained from the vision; but for the one who has gone beyond everything, that which remains is simply that which exists before everything. For the nature of the soul will not pass into absolute non-existence. Rather, if it descends, it will come to evil, and thus to non-being—but not to a state of total non-existence. If the soul takes the opposite path, it will not come to something "other," but to itself; and if it is not in something other, it is in nothing but itself. However, to not be in "beings" <note>existing, separate things</note> but to be alone in itself, is to be in Him (God). For one does not become "Essence" <note>original: *Wesenheit*; likely translating the Greek *Ousia*</note>, but rather something exalted above Essence, by virtue of this communion with God.

<summary>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a priest entering a temple's inner sanctum to describe the soul's mystical union with the One, emphasizing that the soul must leave behind all "images" to achieve a state of absolute simplicity and ecstasy.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Neoplatonism, Mysticism, The One, Ecstasy, Sanctuary, Soul's Journey, Non-being, Essence, Communion</keywords>

--- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page concludes the translation of Plotinus’s Enneads, Book VI, Chapter 9, Section 11. It completes the thought from the previous page regarding the soul's movement beyond the physical and intellectual realms into a final state of mystical union.</meta>

...goes beyond. If one sees that they have become this, then they possess themselves as an image similar to Him <note>Referring to "the One" or God</note>. And when they go out from themselves, as an image returning to its Archetype <note>original: *Urbild*</note>, they will reach the goal of their journey. If they should fall away from this divine contemplation <note>original: *Schauen*; refers to the intuitive vision of the divine</note>, they reawaken the virtue <term>Virtue (Tugend): In Neoplatonism, virtues are not just moral rules but purifications that help the soul shed its "heaviness" to rise higher.</term> within them; and seeing themselves fully adorned by it, they become light once more, ascending through virtue to the Intellect <term>Intellect (Geist): Often translated as "Spirit" or *Nous*, this is the realm of pure, eternal thought.</term> and to wisdom, and through these to Him. And such is the life of gods and of divine and blessed men: a life unconcerned with the pleasures of this world—the flight of the alone to the Alone <note>original: "die Flucht des Einen zu dem Einen"; this is one of the most famous phrases in Western mysticism, translated from the Greek *phygē monou pros monon*.</note>.
